author: Albert Einstein
text: Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.
citation: Repeated throughout his life (with variants); see: [http://quoteinvestigator.com/2011/05/13/einstein-simple/ Quote Investigator]

author: Albert Einstein
text: Un homme heureux est trop content du présent pour trop se soucier de l'avenir.
citation: A happy man is too satisfied with the present to dwell too much on the future. From "Mes Projets d'Avenir", a French essay written at age 18 for a school exam (18 September 1896). The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein Vol. 1 (1987) Doc. 2

author: Albert Einstein
text: The mass of a body is a measure of its energy content.
citation: Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energieinhalt abhängig? ("Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy content?") Annalen der Physik 18, 639-641 (1905). Quoted in Concepts of Mass in Classical and Modern Physics by Max Jammer

author: Albert Einstein
text: We shall, therefore, assume the complete physical equivalence of a gravitational field and a corresponding acceleration of the reference system.
citation: Statement of the equivalence principle in Yearbook of Radioactivity and Electronics (1907)

author: Albert Einstein
text: Es ist bequem mit dem Einstein. Jedes Jahr widerruft er, was er das vorige Jahr geschrieben hat.
citation: It's convenient with that fellow Einstein, every year he retracts what he wrote the year before. Letter to Paul Ehrenfest, 26 December 1915. Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Vol. 8, Doc. 173.

author: Albert Einstein
text: Unser ganzer gepriesener Fortschritt der Technik, überhaupt die Civilisation, ist der Axt in der Hand des pathologischen Verbrechers vergleichbar.
citation: Our entire much-praised technological progress, and civilization generally, could be compared to an axe in the hand of a pathological criminal. Letter to Heinrich Zangger (1917), as quoted in A Sense of the Mysterious: Science and the Human

author: Albert Einstein
text: The most beautiful fate of a physical theory is to point the way to the establishment of a more inclusive theory, in which it lives on as a limiting case.
citation: (1917) as quoted by Gerald Holton, The Advancement of Science, and Its Burdens: the Jefferson Lecture and Other Essays (1986)

author: Albert Einstein
text: Ich habe auch manchen wissenschaftlichen Plan überlegt, während ich Dich im Kinderwagen spazieren schob!
citation: I have also considered many scientific plans during my pushing you around in your pram! Letter to his son Hans Albert Einstein (June 1918)

author: Albert Einstein
text: Geh Recht viel spazieren, dass Du Recht gesund wirst und lies nicht gar zu viel sondern spar Dir noch was auf bis Du gross bist.
citation: Make a lot of walks to get healthy and don't read that much but save yourself some until you're grown up. Letter to his son Eduard Einstein (June 1918)

author: Albert Einstein
text: I lie on the beach like a crocodile and let myself be roasted by the sun. I never see a newspaper and don't give a damn for what is called the world.
citation: Letter to Max Born, 1918, from The Born-Einstein Letters: Friendship, Politics and Physics in Uncertain Times, Macmillan (2005 edition), pg 7.

author: Albert Einstein
text: Liebe Mutter! Heute eine freudige Nachricht. H. A. Lorentz hat mir telegraphiert, dass die englischen Expeditionen die Lichtablenkung an der Sonne wirklich bewiesen haben.
citation: Dear mother! Today a joyful notice. H. A. Lorentz has telegraphed me that the English expeditions have really proven the deflection of light at the sun. Postcard to his mother Pauline Einstein (1919)

author: Albert Einstein
text: Wie lieb ich diesen edlen Mann Mehr als ich mit Worten sagen kann. Doch fürcht' ich, dass er bleibt allein Mit seinem strahlenden Heiligenschein.
citation: How much do I love that noble man More than I could tell with words I fear though he'll remain alone With a holy halo of his own. Poem by Einstein on Spinoza (1920), as quoted in [http://docs.google.com/viewer?a=v&q=cache:i-4Gd4RHW3gJ:press

author: Albert Einstein
text: I am neither a German citizen nor do I believe in anything that can be described as a "Jewish faith." But I am a Jew and glad to belong to the Jewish people, though I do not regard it in any way as chosen.
citation: Letter to Central Association of German Citizens of the Jewish Faith, 3 [5] April 1920, as quoted in Alice Calaprice, The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (2010), p. 195; citing Israelitisches Wochenblatt, 42 September 1920, The Collected Papers

author: Albert Einstein
text: Es ist das schönste Los einer physikalischen Theorie, wenn sie selbst zur Aufstellung einer umfassenden Theorie den Weg weist, in welcher sie als Grenzfall weiterlebt.
citation: No fairer destiny could be allotted to any physical theory, than that it should of itself point out the way to the introduction of a more comprehensive theory, in which it lives on as a limiting case. Über die spezielle und die allgemeine R

author: Albert Einstein
text: Raffiniert ist der Herrgott, aber boshaft ist er nicht.
citation: Subtle is the Lord, but malicious He is not. Remark made during Einstein's first visit to Princeton University (April 1921) as quoted in Einstein (1973) by R. W. Clark, Ch. 14. "God is slick, but he ain't mean" is a variant translation of t

author: Albert Einstein
text: Insofern sich die Sätze der Mathematik auf die Wirklichkeit beziehen, sind sie nicht sicher, und insofern sie sicher sind, beziehen sie sich nicht auf die Wirklichkeit.
citation: In so far as theories of mathematics speak about reality, they are not certain, and in so far as they are certain, they do not speak about reality. Geometrie and Erfahrung (1921) [http://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007%2F978-3-642-49903-6

author: Albert Einstein
text: I have come to believe that the motion of the Earth cannot be detected by any optical experiment.
citation: How I Created the Theory of Relativity, speech at Kyoto University, Japan, December 14, 1922, as cited in Physics Today, August, 1982.

author: Albert Einstein
text: May they not forget to keep pure the great heritage that puts them ahead of the West: the artistic configuration of life, the simplicity and modesty of personal needs, and the purity and serenity of the Japanese soul.
citation: Comment made after a six-week trip to Japan in November-December 1922, published in Kaizo 5, no. 1 (January 1923), 339. Einstein Archive 36-477.1. Appears in The New Quotable Einstein by Alice Calaprice (2005), p. 269

author: Albert Einstein
text: Whether you can observe a thing or not depends on the theory which you use. It is the theory which decides what can be observed.
citation: Objecting to the placing of observables at the heart of the new quantum mechanics, during Heisenberg's 1926 lecture at Berlin; related by Heisenberg, quoted in Unification of Fundamental Forces (1990) by Abdus Salam <small> {{ISBN|052137140

author: Albert Einstein
text: Ich glaube an Spinoza's Gott, der sich in der gesetzlichen Harmonie des Seienden offenbart, nicht an einen Gott, der sich mit Schicksalen und Handlungen der Menschen abgibt.
citation: I believe in Spinoza's God, Who reveals Himself in the lawful harmony of the world, not in a God Who concerns Himself with the fate and the doings of mankind. 24 April 1929 in response to the telegrammed question of New York's Rabbi Herbert

author: Albert Einstein
text: I should unconditionally refuse every direct or indirect war service and try to induce my friends to adopt the same attitude, irrespective of the general opinion of the causes of war.
citation: When asked what his attitude would be in the event of another war, at a meeting of the Council of War Resisters in Zurich. As quoted in [https://www.jta.org/archive/einstein-would-refuse-any-war-services-no-matter-what-the-cause Einstein Wo

author: Albert Einstein
text: Science is international but its success is based on institutions, which are owned by nations. If therefore, we wish to promote culture we have to combine and to organize institutions with our own power and means.
citation: When asked the question, "Why a 'Jewish' University?" when Einstein was assisting Chaim Weizmann in fundraising for The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. As quoted in [Albert Einstein, Letter "Einstein in Singapore." Manchester Guardian, Octo

author: Albert Einstein
text: Sometimes one pays most for the things one gets for nothing.
citation: Quoted in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein by Alice Calaprice (2010), p. 230

author: Albert Einstein
text: I am a determinist. As such, I do not believe in free will. The Jews believe in free will. They believe that man shapes his own life. I reject that doctrine philosophically. In that respect, I am not a Jew.
citation: Quoted in [http://books.google.com/books?id=dJMpQagbz_gC&lpg=PP1&pg=PA387#v=onepage&q&f=false Einstein: His Life and Universe] by Walter Isaacson, p. 387

author: Albert Einstein
text: No one can read the Gospels without feeling the actual presence of Jesus. His personality pulsates in every word. No myth is filled with such life.
citation: As reported in Einstein — A Life (1996) by Denis Brian, when asked about a clipping from a magazine article reporting his comments on Christianity as taken down by Viereck, Einstein carefully read the clipping and replied, " That is what I

author: Albert Einstein
text: It is quite possible to be both. I look upon myself as a man. Nationalism is an infantile disease. It is the measles of mankind.
citation: When asked by Viereck if he considered himself to be a German or a Jew. A version with slightly different wording is quoted in [http://books.google.com/books?id=dJMpQagbz_gC&lpg=PP1&pg=PA386#v=onepage&q&f=false Einstein: His Life and Univer

author: Albert Einstein
text: I am fascinated by Spinoza's pantheism, but I admire even more his contribution to modern thought because he is the first philosopher to deal with the soul and body as one, and not two separate things.
citation: Did not appear in the Saturday Evening Post story, but quoted in [http://books.google.com/books?id=dJMpQagbz_gC&lpg=PP1&pg=PA387#v=onepage&q&f=false Einstein: His Life and Universe] by Walter Isaacson, p. 387, in the section discussing Vier

author: Albert Einstein
text: Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance you must keep moving.
citation: Letter to his son Eduard (5 February 1930), as quoted in Walter Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe (2007), p. 367

author: Albert Einstein
text: I believe that whatever we do or live for has its causality; it is good, however, that we cannot see through to it.
citation: Interview with Rabindranath Tagore (14 April 1930), published in The Religion of Man (1930) by Rabindranath Tagore, p. 222, and in The Tagore Reader (1971) edited by Amiya Chakravarty

author: Albert Einstein
text: The really good music, whether of the East or of the West, cannot be analyzed.
citation: Interview with Rabindranath Tagore (14 April 1930), published in The Religion of Man (1930) by Rabindranath Tagore, p. 222, and in The Tagore Reader (1971) edited by Amiya Chakravarty

author: Albert Einstein
text: I never think of the future. It comes soon enough.
citation: Attributed in [http://books.google.com/books?id=Af84fBmzmVYC&pg=PA305&dq=Belgenland The Encarta Book of Quotations] to an interview on the Belgenland (December 1930), which was the ship on which he arrived in New York that month. According

author: Albert Einstein
text: Besides agreeing with the aims of vegetarianism for aesthetic and moral reasons, it is my view that a vegetarian manner of living by its purely physical effect on the human temperament would most beneficially influence a lot of mankind.
citation: From a letter to Hermann Huth, Vice-President of the German Vegetarian Federation (27 December 1930). Supposedly published in German magazine Vegetarische Warte, which existed from 1882 to 1935. Einstein Archive 46-756. Quoted in The Ultima

author: Albert Einstein
text: Die Diktatur bringt den Maulkorb und dieser die Stumpfheit. Wissenschaft kann nur gedeihen in einer Atmosphäre des Freien Wortes.
citation: A dictatorship means muzzles all round and consequently stultification. Science can flourish only in an atmosphere of free speech. "Science and Dictatorship," in Dictatorship on Its Trial, by Eminent Leaders of Modern Thought (1930) - later

author: Albert Einstein
text: Everyone sits in the prison of his own ideas; he must burst it open, and that in his youth, and so try to test his ideas on reality.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=cvlOAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Everyone+sits+in+the+prison+of+his+own+ideas+he+must+burst+it+open+and+that+in+his+youth+and+so+try+to+test+his+ideas+on+reality%22&pg=PA104#v=onepage Miscellaneous], Cosmic Religion, p. 1

author: Albert Einstein
text: I see a clock, but I cannot envision the clockmaker. The human mind is unable to conceive of the four dimensions, so how can it conceive of a God, before whom a thousand years and a thousand dimensions are as one?
citation: From Cosmic Religion: with Other Opinions and Aphorisms (1931), Albert Einstein, pub. Covici-Friede. Quoted in The Expanded Quotable Einstein, Princeton University Press; 2nd edition (May 30, 2000); Page 208, {{ISBN|0691070210}}

author: Albert Einstein
text: As an eminent pioneer in the realm of high frequency currents... I congratulate you on the great successes of your life's work.
citation: [http://www.teslasociety.com/einsteinletter.jpg Einstein's letter] to Nikola Tesla for Tesla's 75th birthday (1931)

author: Albert Einstein
text: Only a life lived for others is a life worthwhile.
citation: In answer to a question asked by the editors of Youth, a journal of Young Israel of Williamsburg, NY. Quoted in the New York Times (June 20, 1932), [http://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F40617F83B5A13738DDDA90A94DE405B828FF1D3 p.

author: Albert Einstein
text: It can scarcely be denied that the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience.
citation: "On the Method of Theoretical Physics" The Herbert Spencer Lecture, delivered at Oxford (10 June 1933); also published in Philosophy of Science, Vol. 1, No. 2 (April 1934), pp. 163-169., p. 165. [thanks to Dr. Techie @ www.wordorigins.org a

author: Albert Einstein
text: I never failed in mathematics. Before I was fifteen I had mastered differential and integral calculus.
citation: Response to being shown a "Ripley's Believe It or Not!" column with the headline "Greatest Living Mathematician Failed in Mathematics" (1935). Quoted in Einstein: His Life and Universe by Walter Isaacson (2007), [http://books.google.com/boo

author: Albert Einstein
text: The whole of science is nothing more than a refinement of every day [sic] thinking.
citation: "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0016003236910475 Physics and Reality]" (as translated by Jean Piccard) in the Journal of the Franklin Institute Vol. 221, Issue 3 (March 1936), at p. 349

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: We, the disinherited of this land, we who have been oppressed so long, are tired of going through the long night of captivity. And now we are reaching out for the daybreak of freedom and justice and equality.
citation: Montgomery Bus Boycott speech, at Holt Street Baptist Church (5 December 1955)

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: True peace is not merely the absence of tension: it is the presence of justice.
citation: In a 1955 response to an accusation that he was "disturbing the peace" by his activism during the Montgomery Bus Boycott in Montgomery, Alabama, as quoted in Let the Trumpet Sound : A Life of Martin Luther King, Jr (1982) by Stephen B. Oate

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Let no man pull you so low as to hate him.
citation: [https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/king-papers/documents/most-durable-power-excerpt-sermon-dexter-avenue-baptist-church-6-november-1956#fn1 Sermon at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church (Montgomory, Alabama 6 Nov 1956)]

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The decision which we must make now is whether we will give our allegiance to outmoded an unjust customs we owe our ultimate allegiance to God and His will, rather than to man and his folkways
citation: Stride Toward Freedom (1958)

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The decision we must make now is whether we will give our allegiance to outmoded and unjust customs or to the ethical demands of the universe. As Christians we owe our allegiance to God and His will, rather than to man and his folkways
citation: Stride Toward Freedom (1958)

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: I feel that segregation is totally unchristian, and that it is against everything the Christian religion stands for.
citation: In his letter to Sally Canada (19 September 1956), as quoted in The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr (1992), by Carson & Holloran, Volumes 2-3, p. 373

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: In the struggle for human rights and justice, Negros will make a mistake if they become bitter and indulge in hate campaigns.
citation: Speech delivered in Finney Chapel at Oberlin College (7 February 1957), as reported in [http://chronicle.northcoastnow.com/2008/01/21/when-mlk-came-to-oberlin/ "When MLK came to Oberlin" by Cindy Leise (The Chronicle-Telegram; January 21, 2

text: We know that there are many things wrong in the white world, but there are many things wrong in the black world too. We can't keep on blaming the white man. There are things we must do for ourselves.
citation: Address to a black congregation in St. Louis, published in "The Dangerous Road Before Martin Luther King", Harper's magazine (February 1961); quoted by James Baldwin, in "Highroad to Destiny," a chapter in Martin Luther King, Jr.: A Profile

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: They are honoring a great one in Clemente. I have been watching his career ever since he joined the Pittsburgh club. Roberto should wind up as one of the all-time stars before he is through.
citation: Speaking with Pittsburgh Post-Gazette sports editor Al Abrams on July 9, 1961, at Forbes Field, while both waited to speak at the second annual Freedom Jubilee, sponsored by Pittsburgh's Central Baptist Church; as quoted in [https://news.go

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The time is always right to do what's right.
citation: "The Future of Integration", address in Finney Chapel at Oberlin College (22 October 1964), as quoted in "When MLK came to Oberlin" by Cindy Leise, The Chronicle-Telegram (21 January 2008); he also used a slight variant of this "the time is

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Call it democracy, or call it democratic socialism, but there must be a better distribution of wealth within this country for all God's children.
citation: Speech to the Negro American Labor Council (May 1965), as quoted in From Civil Rights to Human Rights : Martin Luther King, Jr., and the Struggle for Economic Justice (2009), by Thomas F. Jackson, p. 230

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in healthcare is the most shocking and inhumane.
citation: Speech to the Second National Convention of the Medical Committee for Human Rights – Chicago (25 March 1966), as quoted in Dan Munro, [http://www.forbes.com/sites/danmunro/2013/08/28/americas-forgotten-civil-right-healthcare/ "America's For

text: I'm getting sick and tired of people saying that this movement has been infiltrated by Communists. There are as many Communists in this freedom movement as there are Eskimos in Florida.
citation: [https://web.archive.org/web/20080706183244/http://www.playboy.com/arts-entertainment/features/mlk/04.html Interview in Playboy (January 1965)]

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: What happens in Johannesburg affects Birmingham, however indirectly. We are descendants of the Africans. Our heritage is Africa. We should never seek to break the ties, nor should the Africans.
citation: [https://web.archive.org/web/20080706183244/http://www.playboy.com/arts-entertainment/features/mlk/04.html Interview in Playboy (January 1965)]

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: If a city has a 30% Negro population, then it is logical to assume that Negroes should have at least 30% of the jobs in any particular company, and jobs in all categories rather than only in menial areas.
citation: from a 1968 Playboy magazine interview{{fix cite}}

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: We know of no more crucial civil rights issue facing Congress today than the need to increase the federal minimum wage and extend its coverage.
citation: [http://www.aft.org/yourwork/tools4teachers/bhm/mlktalks.cfm Statement on minimum wage legislation (18 March 1966)], as quoted in Now Is the Time. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. on Labor in the South: The Case for a Coalition (January 1986)

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The backlash is merely the surfacing of prejudices . . . that already existed and . . . are just now starting to open.
citation: Rev. Martin Luther King, Jr., Seventh Annual Gandhi Memorial Lecture, Howard Univ., Washington, D.C. (6 November 1966), quoted in [http://www.freedomtomarry.org/document.asp?doc_id=2030 What do the election results mean for the move toward

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The evils of capitalism are as real as the evils of militarism and evils of racism.
citation: As quoted in [https://books.google.it/books?id=DNId6HxkzQwC&pg=PA247&dq=%22The+evils+of+capitalism+are+as+real+as+the+evils+of+militarism+and+evils+of+racism%22 The Myth of American Diplomacy: National Identity and U.S. Foreign Policy] (196

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: I am not interested in power for power's sake, but I'm interested in power that is moral, that is right and that is good.
citation: As quoted in The Civil Sphere (2006) by Jeffrey C. Alexander, p. 388

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The greatness of our God lies in the fact that He is both toughminded and tenderhearted.
citation: Ch. 1 : A tough mind and a tender heart

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Human salvation lies in the hands of the creatively maladjusted.
citation: Ch. 2 : Transformed nonconformist

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Nothing in the world is more dangerous than sincere ignorance and conscientious stupidity.
citation: Ch. 4 : Love in action, Sct. 3

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: The means by which we live have outdistanced the ends for which we live. Our scientific power has outrun our spiritual power. We have guided missiles and misguided man.
citation: Strength to Love, Chapter 7

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Hatred paralyzes life; love releases it. Hatred confuses life; love harmonizes it. Hatred darkens life; love illuminates it.
citation: Last paragraph of section III of Antidotes for fear, page 122 (see link at top of the section)

author: Martin Luther King Jr.
text: Let us be dissatisfied until America will no longer have a high blood pressure of creeds and an anemia of deeds.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: And down the long and silent street, The dawn, with silver-sandalled feet, Crept like a frightened girl.
citation: "The Harlot's House", st. 12, in The Dramatic Review (11 April 1885)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Be warned in time, James, and remain, as I do, incomprehensible: to be great is to be misunderstood.
citation: Letter to James McNeill Whistler (23 February 1885) [http://www.artsandartists.org/exhpages/whistler.html]{{deadlink}} Last clause quotes Emerson, "Self-Reliance"

author: Oscar Wilde
text: A thing is not necessarily true because a man dies for it.
citation: "The Portrait of Mr. W. H.", in Blackwood's Magazine (July 1889) [http://www.planetmonk.com/wilde/portrait/wh01.html]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Consistency is the last refuge of the unimaginative.
citation: "The Relation of Dress to Art", [http://www.gutenberg.org/files/14062/14062-h/14062-h.htm The Pall Mall Gazette] (February 28, 1885) Reprinted in Aristotle at Afternoon Tea: The Rare Oscar Wilde (1991)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: A poet can survive everything but a misprint.
citation: "The Children of the Poets", The Pall Mall Gazette (October 14, 1886) [http://www.online-literature.com/wilde/1307/]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Most modern calendars mar the sweet simplicity of our lives by reminding us that each day that passes is the anniversary of some perfectly uninteresting event.
citation: "A New Calendar", The Pall Mall Gazette (February 17, 1887) [http://www.online-literature.com/wilde/1307/]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: A simile committing suicide is always a depressing spectacle.
citation: "The Poets' Corner III", The Pall Mall Gazette (30 May 1887) [http://www.online-literature.com/wilde/1307/]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: And, after all, what is a fashion? From the artistic point of view, it is usually a form of ugliness so intolerable that we have to alter it every six months.
citation: "The Philosophy of Dress", The New-York Tribune, 1885. For an analysis see [http://www.oscarwildeinamerica.org/quotations/fashion-a-form-of-ugliness.html Fashion a Form of Ugliness], oscarwildeinamerica.org (retrieved 9 May 2026)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: We have really everything in common with America nowadays, except, of course, language.
citation: The Canterville Ghost (1887). For history and analysis of the quote see [http://oscarwildeinamerica.org/quotations/common-language.html "Common Language"], oscarwildeinamerica.org (retrieved 9 May 2026)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: All charming people, I fancy, are spoiled. It is the secret of their attraction.
citation: "The Portrait of Mr. W. H.", Blackwood's Magazine (July 1889)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: It is always a silly thing to give advice, but to give good advice is absolutely fatal.
citation: "The Portrait of Mr. W. H."

author: Oscar Wilde
text: The more we study Art, the less we care for Nature. What Art really reveals to us is Nature's lack of design, her curious crudities, her extraordinary monotony, her absolutely unfinished condition.
citation: Intentions (1891)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Art finds her own perfection within, and not outside of herself. She is not to be judged by any external standard of resemblance. She is a veil, rather than a mirror.
citation: Intentions (1891)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: He is really not so ugly after all, provided, of course, that one shuts one's eyes, and does not look at him.
citation: "The Birthday of the Infanta", The House of Pomegranates (1892) [http://emotionalliteracyeducation.com/classic_books_online/hpomg10.htm]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Death must be so beautiful. To lie in the soft brown earth, with the grasses waving above one's head, and listen to silence. To have no yesterday, and no tomorrow. To forget time, to forgive life, to be at peace.
citation: The Canterville Ghost (1887) [http://www.planetmonk.com/wilde/savile/canterville.c1.html]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I put all my genius into my life; I put only my talent into my works.
citation: J'ai mis tout mon génie dans ma vie; je n'ai mis que mon talent dans mes œuvres. Conversation with André Gide in Algiers, quoted in letter by Gide to his mother (30 January 1895); popularized by Gide and often subsequently quoted in Gide's

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I summed up all systems in a phrase, and all existence in an epigram.
citation: Written in a letter from Reading Prison to Lord Alfred Douglas (early 1897){{citation needed}}

author: Oscar Wilde
text: People who count their chickens before they are hatched act very wisely because chickens run about so absurdly that it's impossible to count them accurately.
citation: Written in a letter to Robert Ross from Paris (31 May 1898){{citation needed}}

author: Oscar Wilde
text: It is better to have a permanent income than to be fascinating.
citation: The Model Millionaire (1912)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: He to whom the present is the only thing that is present, knows nothing of the age in which he lives.
citation: "Oscariana" (1907), Complete Works, p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=-CtXAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA32 32]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: I have the kiss of Walt Whitman still on my lip.
citation: In a journal or later note by George Cecil Ives recording a meeting with Wilde in 1900, Oscar Wilde: Myths, Miracles and Imitations (Cambridge University Press,1996), John Stokes

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Prayer must never be answered: if it is, it ceases to be prayer and becomes correspondence.
citation: The Epigrams of Oscar Wilde, edited by Alvin Redman (1952) [http://books.google.com/books?id=qUjQAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Prayer+must+never+be+answered+if+it+is+it+ceases+to+be+prayer+and+becomes+correspondence%22&pg=PA106#v=onepage]

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Keep love in your heart. A life without it is like a sunless garden when the flowers are dead. The consciousness of loving and being loved brings warmth and richness to life that nothing else can bring.
citation: The Epigrams of Oscar Wilde, edited by Alvin Redman (1952) [http://books.google.com/books?id=qUjQAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Keep+love+in+your+heart+a+life+without+it+is+like+a+sunless+garden+when+the+flowers+are+dead+the+consciousness+of+loving+and+bein

author: Oscar Wilde
text: An idea that is not dangerous is unworthy of being called an idea at all.
citation: The Epigrams of Oscar Wilde, edited by Alvin Redman (1954)

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Starvation, and not sin, is the parent of modern crime.
citation: The Epigrams of Oscar Wilde, edited by Alvin Redman (1954)

author: Francis Bacon
text: Nay, number (itself) in armies, importeth not much, where the people is of weak courage; for (as Virgil saith) it never troubles the wolf how many the sheep be.
citation: Essays or Counsels Civil and Moral (1597), XXIX: "Of the True Greatness of Kingdoms and Estates."

author: Francis Bacon
text: Knowledge, that tendeth but to satisfaction, is but as a courtesan, which is for pleasure, and not for fruit or generation.
citation: Valerius Terminus: Of the Interpretation of Nature (ca. 1603), in Works, Vol. 1, p. 83; The Works of Francis Bacon (1819), Vol. 2, [https://books.google.com/books?id=xgE9AAAAYAAJ&pg=PA133 p. 133]

author: Francis Bacon
text: Aristotle (…) a mere bond-servant to his logic, thereby rendering it contentious and well nigh useless.
citation: Rerum Novarum (1605)

author: Francis Bacon
text: Riches are a good handmaid, but the worst mistress.
citation: De Augmentis Scientiarum, Book II, "Antitheta" (1623)

author: Francis Bacon
text: Audacter calumniare, semper aliquid haeret.
citation: Hurl your calumnies boldly; something is sure to stick. De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623)

author: Francis Bacon
text: I bequeath my soul to God (…). My body to be buried obscurely. For my name and memory, I leave it to men's charitable speeches, and to foreign nations, and the next age.
citation: His will (1626)

author: Francis Bacon
text: It is true that may hold in these things, which is the general root of superstition; namely, that men observe when things hit, and not when they miss; and commit to memory the one, and forget and pass over the other.
citation: Sylva Sylvarum Century X (1627)

author: Francis Bacon
text: Ne mireris, si vulgus verius loquatur quam honoratiores; quia etiam tutius loquitur.
citation: Do not wonder, if the common people speak more truly than those of high rank; for they speak with more safety. Exempla Antithetorum, [http://books.google.com/books?id=C9cQAAAAYAAJ&q="Ne+mireris+si+vulgus+verius+loquatur+quam+honoratiores+qu

author: Francis Bacon
text: He that defers his charity 'till he is dead, is (if a man weighs it rightly) rather liberal of another man's, than of his own.
citation: Ornamenta Rationalia, http://books.google.com/books?id=VHNUAAAAYAAJ&q="He+that+defers+his+charity+'till+he+is+dead+is+if+a+man+weighs+it"+"rather+liberal+of+another+man's+than+of+his+own"&pg=PA298#v=onepage §55

author: Francis Bacon
text: Whence we see spiders, flies, or ants entombed and preserved forever in amber, a more than royal tomb.
citation: Historia Vitæ et Mortis; Sylva Sylvarum, Cent. i. Exper. 100, reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

author: Francis Bacon
text: There is no excellent beauty that hath not some strangeness in the proportion.
citation: Of Beauty https://www.authorama.com/essays-of-francis-bacon-43.html

author: Francis Bacon
text: For a man to love again where he is loved, it is the charity of publicans contracted by mutual profit and good offices; but to love a man's enemies is one of the cunningest points of the law of Christ, and an imitation of the divine nature.
citation: Of The Exaltation of Charity

author: Francis Bacon
text: You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God" This canon is the mother of all canons against heresy; the causes of error are two; the ignorance of the will of God, and the ignorance or not sufficient consideration of his power.
citation: Of Heresies

author: Francis Bacon
text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
citation: Of Studies

author: Francis Bacon
text: Read not to contradict and confute, nor to believe and take for granted, nor to find talk and discourse, but to weigh and consider.
citation: Of Studies

author: Francis Bacon
text: For all knowledge and wonder (which is the seed of knowledge) is an impression of pleasure in itself.
citation: Book I, i, 3

author: Francis Bacon
text: Let great authors have their due, as time, which is the author of authors, be not deprived of his due, which is, further and further to discover truth.
citation: Book I, iv, 10

author: Francis Bacon
text: The sun, which passeth through pollutions and itself remains as pure as before.
citation: Book II

author: Francis Bacon
text: Sacred and inspired divinity, the sabaoth and port of all men's labours and peregrinations.
citation: Book II

author: Francis Bacon
text: Cleanness of body was ever deemed to proceed from a due reverence to God.
citation: Book II

author: Francis Bacon
text: They are ill discoverers that think there is no land, when they can see nothing but sea.
citation: Book II, vii, 5

author: Francis Bacon
text: But men must know that in this theater of man's life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on.
citation: Book II, xx, 8

author: Francis Bacon
text: We are much beholden to Machiavel and others, that write what men do, and not what they ought to do.
citation: Book II, xxi, 9

author: Francis Bacon
text: For man seeketh in society comfort, use, and protection: and they be three wisdoms of divers natures, which do often sever: wisdom of the behaviour, wisdom of business, and wisdom of state.
citation: Book II, xxiii

author: Francis Bacon
text: Primum quaerite bona animi; caetera aut aderunt, aut non oberunt.
citation: Seek first the virtues of the mind; and other things either will come, or will not be wanted. Book II, xxxi

author: Francis Bacon
text: For the inquisition of Final Causes is barren, and like a virgin consecrated to God produces nothing.
citation: Book III, viii

author: Francis Bacon
text: Man, being the servant and interpreter of Nature, can do and understand so much and so much only as he has observed in fact or in thought of the course of nature. Beyond this he neither knows anything nor can do anything.
citation: Aphorism 1

author: Francis Bacon
text: Human knowledge and human power meet in one; for where the cause is not known the effect cannot be produced. Nature to be commanded must be obeyed; and that which in contemplation is as the cause is in operation as the rule.
citation: Aphorism 3

author: Francis Bacon
text: It would be an unsound fancy and self-contradictory to expect that things which have never yet been done can be done except by means which have never yet been tried.
citation: Aphorism 6

author: Francis Bacon
text: The logic now in use serves rather to fix and give stability to the errors which have their foundation in commonly received notions than to help the search for truth. So it does more harm than good.
citation: Aphorism 7

author: Francis Bacon
text: The cause and root of nearly all evils in the sciences is this — that while we falsely admire and extol the powers of the human mind we neglect to seek for its true helps.
citation: Aphorism 9

author: Francis Bacon
text: There is a great difference between the Idols of the human mind and the Ideas of the divine. That is to say, between certain empty dogmas, and the true signatures and marks set upon the works of creation as they are found in nature.
citation: Aphorism 23

author: Francis Bacon
text: But the best demonstration by far is experience, if it go not beyond the actual experiment.
citation: Aphorism 70

author: Francis Bacon
text: It is not possible to run a course aright when the goal itself has not been rightly placed.
citation: Aphorism 81

author: Francis Bacon
text: But by far the greatest obstacle to the progress of science and to the undertaking of new tasks and provinces therein is found in this — that men despair and think things impossible.
citation: Aphorism 92

author: Francis Bacon
text: Truth will sooner come out from error than from confusion.
citation: Aphorism 20

author: Francis Bacon
text: My Lord St. Albans said that Nature did never put her precious jewels into a garret four stories high, and therefore that exceeding tall men had ever very empty heads.
citation: No. 17

author: Francis Bacon
text: Hope is a good breakfast, but it is a bad supper.
citation: No. 36

author: Francis Bacon
text: Like strawberry wives, that laid two or three great strawberries at the mouth of their pot, and all the rest were little ones.
citation: No. 54

author: Cicero
text: Equidem ad pacem hortari non desino; quae vel iniusta utilior est quam iustissimum bellum cum civibus.
citation: As for me, I cease not to advocate peace. It may be on unjust terms, but even so it is more expedient than the justest of civil wars. Epistulae ad Atticum (Letters to Atticus) Book VII, Letter 14, section 3; as translated by E.O. Winstedt i

author: Cicero
text: They are such fools that they seem to expect that, though the Republic is lost, their fish-ponds will be safe.
citation: Letters to Atticus, Book I, 18.

author: Cicero
text: Quidem concessum est rhetoribus ementiri in historiis ut aliquid dicere possint argutius.
citation: Indeed rhetoricians are permitted to lie about historical matters so they can speak more subtly. Brutus, 42

author: Cicero
text: Nemo enim fere saltat sobrius, nisi forte insanit.
citation: Almost no one dances sober, unless he is insane. Pro Murena (Chapter VI, sec. 13)

author: Cicero
text: Etenim, iudices, cum omnibus virtutibus me adfectum esse cupio, tum nihil est quod malim quam me et esse gratum et videri. Haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum.
citation: In truth, O judges, while I wish to be adorned with every virtue, yet there is nothing which I can esteem more highly than being and appearing grateful. For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other v

author: Cicero
text: O di immortales! non intellegunt homines, quam magnum vectigal sit parsimonia.
citation: O immortal gods! Men do not realize how great a revenue parsimony can be! Paradoxa Stoicorum; Paradox VI, 49

author: Cicero
text: Id quod est praestantissimum, maximeque optabile omnibus sanis et bonis et beatis, cum dignitate otium.
citation: That which is most excellent, and is most to be desired by all happy, honest and healthy-minded men, is dignified leisure. Pro Publio Sestio; Chapter XLV

author: Cicero
text: Etiamne hoc adfirmare potes, Luculle, esse aliquam vim, cum prudentia et consilio scilicet, quae finxerit vel, ut tuo verbo utar, quae fabricata sit hominem? Qualis ista fabrica est? ubi adhibita? quando? cur? quo modo?
citation: Can you also, Lucullus, affirm that there is any power united with wisdom and prudence which has made, or, to use your own expression, manufactured man? What sort of a manufacture is that? Where is it exercised? when? why? how? Academica, B

author: Cicero
text: Laudandum adulescentem, ornandum, tollendum.
citation: The young man should be praised, honored, and made immortal. Ad Familiares 11.20.1; the reference is to Octavian, with tollendum carrying the implication of the youth's being slain and thus "made immortal".

author: Cicero
text: Si hortum in bibliotheca habes, deerit nihil.
citation: If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need. To Varro, in Ad Familiares IX, 4

author: Cicero
text: Adsiduus usus uni rei deditus et ingenium et artem saepe vincit.
citation: Constant practice devoted to one subject often prevails over both ability and skill.[https://archive.org/stream/probalbo00ciceuoft#page/n5/mode/2up] Variant translation: Constant practice given to one matter often conquers both genius and a

author: Cicero
text: Nonne, ut ignis in aquam conjectus, continuo restinguitur et refrigeratur, sic refervens falsum crimen in purissimam et castissimam vitam collatum, statim concidit et extinguitur?
citation: Does not, as fire dropped upon water is immediately extinguished and cooled, so, does not, I say, a false accusation, when brought in contact with a most pure and holy life, instantly fall and become extinguished? Cicero, Pro Roscio Comodeo

author: Cicero
text: Sic submissa voce agam tantum ut iudices audiant; neque enim desunt qui istos in me atque in optimum quemque incitent; quos ego, quo id facilius faciant, non adiuvabo.
citation: I will speak in a low voice, just so as to let the judges hear me. For men are not wanting who would be glad to excite that people against me and against every eminent man; and I will not assist them and enable them to do so more easily. Ci

author: Cicero
text: Lex est summa ratio insita a natura, quae iubet ea, quae facienda sunt, prohibetque contraria.
citation: Law is the perfection of reason implanted in us by nature, which enjoins what should be done, and forbids what we should not do. Book I, section 18; J. W. Jones, A Translation of all the Greek, Latin, Italian, and French Quotations which oc

author: Cicero
text: Est enim unum ius quo deuincta est hominum societas et quod lex constituit una, quae lex est recta ratio imperandi atque prohibendi. Quam qui ignorat, is est iniustus, siue est illa scripta uspiam siue nusquam.
citation: For there is but one essential justice which cements society, and one law which establishes this justice. This law is right reason, which is the true rule of all commandments and prohibitions. Whoever neglects this law, whether written or u

author: Cicero
text: Quid enim foedius auaritia, quid immanius libidine, quid contemptius timiditate, quid abiectius tarditate et stultitia dici potest?
citation: For what is there more hideous than avarice, more brutal than lust, more contemptible than cowardice, more base than stupidity and folly? Book I, section 51; translation by C.D. Yonge [http://books.google.com/books?id=AdAIAAAAQAAJ&q=%22For+

author: Cicero
text: Nam et qui bene imperat, paruerit aliquando necesse est, et qui modeste paret, videtur qui aliquando imperet dignus esse.
citation: For in order to command well, we should know how to submit; and he who submits with a good grace will some time become worthy of commanding. Book III, section 2; translation by Francis Barham

author: Cicero
text: Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?
citation: To what length will you abuse our patience, Catiline? Variant translation: "When, O Catiline, do you mean to cease abusing our patience?" by Charles Duke Yonge (M. Tullius Cicero. The Orations of Marcus Tullius Cicero, B. A. London. Henry G

author: Cicero
text: Quodsi ea mihi maxime inpenderet tamen hoc animo fui semper, ut invidiam virtute partam gloriam, non invidiam putarem.
citation: I have always been of the opinion that infamy earned by doing what is right is not infamy at all, but glory. Speech I

author: Cicero
text: Sed ita a principio incohatum esse mundum, ut certis rebus certa signa praecurrerent.
citation: From the beginning of the world it has been ordained that certain signs must needs precede certain events. Book I, Chapter LII, section 118 Compare: "Often do the spirits / Of great events stride on before the events, / And in to-day alread

author: Cicero
text: Non enim omnis error stultitia est dicenda.
citation: We must not say that every mistake is a foolish one. Book II, Chapter LII, section 90

author: Cicero
text: Nihil tam absurde dici potest, quod non dicatur ab aliquo philosophorum.
citation: There is nothing so absurd that it has not been said by some philosopher. Book II, chapter LVIII, section 119 Cf. René Descartes' "On ne sauroit rien imaginer de si étranger et si peu croyable, qu'il n'ait été dit par quelqu'un des philosop

author: Cicero
text: Nec vero superstitione tollenda religio tollitur.
citation: We do not destroy religion by destroying superstition. Book II, chapter LXXII, sec. 148

author: Cicero
text: Maximas res publicas ab adulescentibus labefactatas, a senibus sustentatas et restitutas reperietis. ... temeritas est videlicet florentis aetatis, prudentia senescentis.
citation: The greatest states have been overthrown by the young and sustained and restored by the old. ... Rashness is the product of the budding-time of youth, prudence of the harvest-time of age. [http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseu

author: Cicero
text: Nemo enim est tam senex qui se annum non putet posse vivere.
citation: No one is so old as to think that he cannot live one more year. [http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Cic.+Sen.+24&fromdoc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2007.01.0039 section 24]

author: Cicero
text: Omnia autem quae secundum naturam fiunt sunt habenda in bonis.
citation: Whatever befalls in accordance with Nature should be accounted good. [http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A2007.01.0039%3Asection%3D71 section 71]

author: Cicero
text: Existunt etiam saepe iniuriae calumnia quadam et nimis callida sed malitiosa iuris interpretatione. Ex quo illud "summum ius summa iniuria" factum est iam tritum sermone proverbium.
citation: Injustice often arises also through chicanery, that is, through an over-subtle and even fraudulent construction of the law. This it is that gave rise to the now familiar saw, "More law, less justice." Book I, section 33; translation by Walt

author: Cicero
text: Non nobis solum nati sumus ortusque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici.
citation: We are not born for ourselves alone; a part of us is claimed by our nation, another part by our friends. Book I, section 22

author: Cicero
text: Nam cum sint duo genera decertandi, unum per disceptationem, alterum per vim, cumque illud proprium sit hominis, hoc beluarum, confugiendum est ad posterius, si uti non licet superiore.
citation: While there are two ways of contending, one by discussion, the other by force, the former belonging properly to man, the latter to beasts, recourse must be had to the latter if there be no opportunity for employing the former. Book I, secti

author: Cicero
text: In omnibus autem negotiis priusquam adgrediare, adhibenda est praeparatio diligens.
citation: Before entering any occupation, diligent preparation is to be undertaken. Book I, section 73

author: Cicero
text: Parvi enim sunt foris arma, nisi est consilium domi.
citation: Arms are of little value in the field unless there is wise counsel at home. Book I, section 76 (trans. Walter Miller)

author: Cicero
text: Cedant arma togae, concedat laurea laudi.
citation: Yield, ye arms, to the toga; to civic praise, ye laurels. Book I, section 77

author: Cicero
text: Ludo autem et ioco uti illo quidem licet, sed sicut somno et quietibus ceteris tum, cum gravibus seriisque rebus satis fecerimus.
citation: We may, indeed, indulge in sport and jest, but in the same way as we enjoy sleep or other relaxations, and only when we have satisfied the claims of our earnest, serious task. Book I, section 103

author: Cicero
text: Sed tamen ira procul absit, cum qua nihil recte fieri nec considerate potest.
citation: But still anger ought be far from us, for nothing is able to be done rightly nor judiciously with anger. Variant: In anger nothing right nor judicious can be done. Book I, section 136

author: Cicero
text: Illiberales autem et sordidi quaestus mercennariorum omnium, quorum operae, non quorum artes emuntur; est enim in illis ipsa merces auctoramentum servitutis.
citation: Unbecoming to a gentleman, too, and vulgar are the means of livelihood of all hired workmen whom we pay for mere manual labour, not for artistic skill; for in their case the very wage they receive is a pledge of their slavery. Book I, secti

author: Cicero
text: Omnium autem rerum, ex quibus aliquid adquiritur, nihil est agri cultura melius, nihil uberius, nihil dulcius, nihil homine libero dignius.
citation: For of all gainful professions, nothing is better, nothing more pleasing, nothing more delightful, nothing better becomes a well-bred man than agriculture. Book I, section 151. Translation by Cyrus R. Edmonds (1873), p. 73

author: Cicero
text: Omnium autem rerum nec aptius est quicquam ad opes tuendas ac tenendas quam diligi nec alienius quam timeri.
citation: But of all motives, none is better adapted to secure influence and hold it fast than love; nothing is more foreign to that end than fear. Book II, section 23; translation by Walter Miller

author: Cicero
text: Vera gloria radices agit atque etiam propagatur, ficta omnia celeriter tamquam flosculi decidunt nec simulatum potest quicquam esse diuturnum.
citation: True glory strikes root, and even extends itself; all false pretensions fall as do flowers, nor can anything feigned be lasting. Book II, section 43

author: Cicero
text: P. Scipionem [...] dicere solitum scripsit Cato [...] numquam se minus otiosum esse, quam cum otiosus; nec minus solum, quam cum solus esset.
citation: According to Cato the Elder, Scipio Africanus was wont to say that he was never less at leisure than when at leisure, nor less alone than when alone. Book III, section 1

author: Cicero
text: Ita duae res, quae languorem afferunt ceteris, illum acuebant; otium et solitudo.
citation: The two conditions that lead others to languor – i.e. leisure and solitude – him made sharper. Book III, section 1

author: Confucius
text: He that in his studies wholly applies himself to labour and exercise, and neglects meditation, loses his time, and he that only applies himself to meditation, and neglects labour and exercise, only wanders and loses himself.
citation: [http://books.google.pt/books?id=izgCAAAAQAAJ&printsec=frontcover&hl=pt-PT The Morals of Confucius], 2nd edition (London, 1724), Maxim X, p. 114

author: Confucius
text: Men do not stumble over mountains, but over molehills
citation: Reported in United States Congress House Committee on Agriculture (1973) Hearings Before the Committee on Agriculture, House of Representatives, Ninety-second Congress, p. 21

author: Confucius
text: Man has three ways of acting wisely. First, on meditation; that is the noblest. Secondly, on imitation; that is the easiest. Thirdly, on experience; that is the bitterest.
citation: The Analects, as reported in Chambers Dictionary of Quotations (1997), p. 279

author: Confucius
text: It is not truth that makes man great, but man that makes truth great.
citation: As quoted in The Importance of Living (1937) by Lin Yutang, p. v

author: Confucius
text: It is more shameful to distrust our friends than to be deceived by them.
citation: Reportedly in: United States. Congress. House. Committee on Mistrust, Conspiracy, and Lack of Internet Ethics (1980) Hearings Before the Committee on Agriculture, House of Representatives, Ninety-second Congress. p. 32

author: Confucius
text: The more man meditates upon good thoughts, the better will be his world and the world at large.
citation: Attributed to Confucius in Out of the Blue: Delight Comes Into Our Lives (1996) by Mark Victor Hansen, Barbara Nichols, and Patty Hansen, p. 93

author: Confucius
text: Follow the seasons of Ha, Ride in the state carriage of Yau, Wear the ceremonial cap of Chan, Let the music be the Shiu with its pantomimes.
citation: Quoted by T. W. Pearce, [https://archive.org/details/chroniclelondon00unkngoog/page/n322/mode/2up "Western Civilisation in Relation to Protestant Mission Work"], The Chronicle of the London Missionary Society (August 1890), p. 237

author: Confucius
text: I am not concerned that I have no place; I am concerned how I may fit myself for one. I am not concerned that I am not known; I seek to be worthy to be known.
citation: IV, xiv. Quoted from Will Durant, Our Oriental Heritage.

author: Confucius
text: To rank the effort above the prize may be called love.

author: Confucius
text: Cornered vessel without corners, strange cornered vessel, strange cornered vessel.
citation: 6.25 (sometimes cited as 6.23)

author: Confucius
text: A man's character is formed by the Odes, developed by the Rites and perfected by music.
citation: Quoted from Will Durant, Our Oriental Heritage.

author: Confucius
text: The man of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in his speech. When a man feels the difficulty of doing, can he be other than cautious and slow in speaking?
citation: III

author: Confucius
text: The superior man has neither anxiety nor fear. When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?
citation: IV

author: Confucius
text: If the people have no faith in their rulers, there is no standing for the state.
citation: VII

author: Confucius
text: By extensively studying all learning, and keeping himself under the restraint of the rules of propriety, one may thus likewise not err from what is right.
citation: XV

author: Confucius
text: The superior man loves his soul; the inferior man loves his property.
citation: Cited in Oriental Philosophy, p. 46

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: He who is in love is wise and is becoming wiser, sees newly every time he looks at the object beloved, drawing from it with his eyes and his mind those virtues which it possesses.
citation: The Method of Nature (1841), p. 25

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I fancy I need more than another to speak (rather than write), with such a formidable tendency to the lapidary style. I build my house of boulders.
citation: Letter to Thomas Carlyle (30 October 1841)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Yet a man may love a paradox, without losing either his wit or his honesty.
citation: "Walter Savage Landor", from The Dial, xii (1841)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Literature is the effort of man to indemnify himself for the wrongs of his condition.
citation: "Walter Savage Landor", from The Dial, xii (1841)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines.
citation: Self-Reliance (1841) [https://www.bartleby.com/lit-hub/familiar-quotations/6279-ralph-waldo-emerson-1803-1882-john-bartlett-2/ Bartleby]

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Self-reliance, the height and perfection of man, is reliance on God.
citation: The Fugitive Slave Law, a lecture in NYC (March 7, 1854)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Only the great generalizations survive. The sharp words of the Declaration of Independence, lampooned then and since as 'glittering generalities,' have turned out blazing ubiquities that will burn forever and ever.
citation: From a lecture on Books given in the Fraternity Course in Boston in 1864; the quoted phrase 'glittering generalities' had been used by Rufus Choate to describe the declaration of the rights of man in the Preamble to the Constitution

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A mollusk is a cheap edition [of man] with a suppression of the costlier illustrations, designed for dingy circulation, for shelving in an oyster-bank or among the seaweed.
citation: Power and Laws of Thought (c. 1870)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Poetry teaches the enormous force of a few words, and, in proportion to the inspiration, checks loquacity.
citation: Parnassus (1874) Preface

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: There are two classes of poets — the poets by education and practice, these we respect; and poets by nature, these we love.
citation: Parnassus (1874) Preface

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: What is a weed? A plant whose virtues have yet to be discovered.
citation: Fortune of the Republic (1878)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: We are never without a pilot. When we know not how to steer, and dare not hoist a sail, we can drift. The current knows the way, though we do not. The ship of heaven guides itself, and will not accept a wooden rudder.
citation: "The Sovereignty of Ethics", in The North America Review, no. 262 (May–June 1878) p. 407

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To different minds, the same world is a hell, and a heaven.
citation: December 20, 1822

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: When a whole nation is roaring Patriotism at the top of its voice, I am fain to explore the cleanness of its hands and purity of its heart.
citation: December 10, 1824

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The cup of life is not so shallow That we have drained the best That all the wine at once we swallow And lees make all the rest.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: There is a freemasonry among the dull by which they recognize and are sociable with the dull, as surely as a correspondent tact in men of genius.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A sect or party is an elegant incognito devised to save a man from the vexation of thinking.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Everything intercepts us from ourselves.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: No man can have society upon his own terms. If he seeks it, he must serve it too.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Four snakes gliding up and down a hollow for no purpose that I could see — not to eat, not for love, but only gliding.
citation: April 11, 1834

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: We are always getting ready to live, but never living.
citation: April 12, 1834

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Sometimes a scream is better than a thesis.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Let me never fall into the vulgar mistake of dreaming that I am persecuted whenever I am contradicted.
citation: November 8, 1838

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: I wish to write such rhymes as shall not suggest a restraint, but contrariwise the wildest freedom.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Man exists for his own sake and not to add a laborer to the state.
citation: November 15, 1839

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: He needs no library, for he has not done thinking; no church, for he is himself a prophet; no statute book, for he hath the Lawgiver; no money, for he is value itself; no road, for he is at home where he is.
citation: December 26, 1839

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The best effect of fine persons is felt after we have left their presence.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: How we hate this solemn Ego that accompanies the learned, like a double, wherever he goes.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: A good indignation brings out all one's powers.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: People do not deserve to have good writing, they are so pleased with bad.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: You shall have joy, or you shall have power, said God; you shall not have both.
citation: October 1842

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Do not be too timid and squeamish about your actions. All life is an experiment. The more experiments you make the better.
citation: November 11, 1842

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Poetry must be new as foam, and as old as the rock.
citation: March 1845

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: It is easy to live for others; everybody does. I call on you to live for yourselves.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Immortality. I notice that as soon as writers broach this question they begin to quote. I hate quotation. Tell me what you know.
citation: May 1849

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The word liberty in the mouth of Mr. Webster sounds like the word love in the mouth of a courtesan.
citation: February 12, 1851; cf. the remark of John Wilkes about Samuel Johnson, "Liberty is as ridiculous in his mouth as Religion in mine" (20 March 1778), quoted in Boswell's Life of Johnson (1791)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The blazing evidence of immortality is our dissatisfaction with any other solution.
citation: July 1855

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: All the thoughts of a turtle are turtle.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The book written against fame and learning has the author's name on the title-page.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: The believing we do something when we do nothing is the first illusion of tobacco.

author: Mark Twain
text: I haven't a particle of confidence in a man who has no redeeming petty vices whatsoever.
citation: "Answers to Correspondents", The Californian, 17 June 1865. Anthologized in [http://books.google.com/books?id=kqMDAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA35 The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County, and Other Sketches] (1867)

author: Mark Twain
text: I'll risk forty dollars that he can outjump any frog in Calaveras county.
citation: "The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County"; first published as "Jim Smiley and His Jumping Frog" in the New York Saturday Press, 18 November 1865; revised by the author and reprinted the following month in The Californian

author: Mark Twain
text: I don't see no p'ints about that frog that's any better'n any other frog.
citation: "The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County" (1865)

author: Mark Twain
text: He was ignorant of the commonest accomplishments of youth. He could not even lie.
citation: "Brief Biographical Sketch of George Washington", [http://books.google.com/books?id=kqMDAAAAQAAJ The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County, and Other Sketches] (1867), ed. John Paul Cited by: William E. Phipps, [https://books.google.n

author: Mark Twain
text: Soap and education are not as sudden as a massacre, but they are more deadly in the long run.
citation: "The Facts Concerning the Recent Resignation", described by the author as written about 1867, first published in [http://books.google.com/books?id=5LcIAAAAQAAJ Mark Twain's Sketches, New and Old]‎ (1875)

author: Mark Twain
text: Tomorrow night I appear for the first time before a Boston audience — 4000 critics.
citation: Letter to Pamela Clemens Moffet, 9 November 1869, in Albert Bigelow Paine, Mark Twain's Letters: Arranged with Comment (1917), Vol. 1, [http://books.google.com/books?id=Ia8hAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA168 p. 168]

author: Mark Twain
text: He is now fast rising from affluence to poverty.
citation: "Rev. Henry Ward Beecher's Farm" (1869 ), anthologized in [http://books.google.com/books?id=UwcCAAAAQAAJ Mark Twain's Sketches] (1872)

author: Mark Twain
text: Ah, it was worth ten years of a man’s life to be dead then! Everything was pleasant. I was in a good neighbourhood, for all the dead people that lived near me belonged to the best families in the city.
citation: "A Curious Dream", in Mark Twain’s Sketches, Selected and Revised by the Author (London: George Routledge & Sons, 1872) p. 308

author: Mark Twain
text: Barring that natural expression of villainy which we all have, the man looked honest enough.
citation: "A Mysterious Visit", Buffalo Express, 19 March 1870. Anthologized in [http://books.google.com/books?id=5LcIAAAAQAAJ Mark Twain's Sketches, New and Old‎] (1875)

author: Mark Twain
text: Formerly, if you killed a man, it was possible that you were insane—but now, if you, having friends and money, kill a man, it is evidence that you are a lunatic.
citation: "A New Crime", first published as "The New Crime" in the Buffalo Express, 16 April 1870. Anthologized in [http://books.google.com/books?id=5LcIAAAAQAAJ Mark Twain's Sketches, New and Old‎] (1875).

author: Mark Twain
text: A baby is an inestimable blessing and bother.
citation: Letter to Annie Moffett Webster (1 September 1876)

author: Mark Twain
text: We haven't all had the good fortune to be ladies; we haven't all been generals, or poets, or statesmen; but when the toast works down to the babies, we stand on common ground.
citation: Answering a toast, "To the Babies," at a banquet in honor of General U.S. Grant (November 14, 1879). The Writings of Mark Twain, Vol. 20 (1899), ed. Charles Dudley Warner, [http://books.google.com/books?id=mRARAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA397 p. 397]

author: Mark Twain
text: Among the three or four million cradles now rocking in the land are some which this nation would preserve for ages as sacred things, if we could know which ones they are.
citation: "To the Babies" (14 November 1879)

author: Mark Twain
text: Reader, suppose you were an idiot. And suppose you were a member of Congress. But I repeat myself.
citation: Draft manuscript (c.1881), quoted by Albert Bigelow Paine in Mark Twain: A Biography (1912), [http://books.google.com/books?id=2UYLAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA724#v=onepage&q&f=false p. 724]

author: Mark Twain
text: Be respectful to your superiors, if you have any.
citation: "Advice to Youth", speech to The Saturday Morning Club, Boston, 15 April 1882. Mark Twain Speaking (1976), ed. Paul Fatout, [http://books.google.com/books?id=mkFgXWvUkVoC&pg=PA169 p. 169]

author: Mark Twain
text: Loyalty to petrified opinions never yet broke a chain or freed a human soul in this world — and never will.
citation: "Consistency" (5 December 1887). This quote is engraved on Twain's bust in the National Hall of Fame

author: Mark Twain
text: He [George Washington Cable] has taught me to abhor and detest the Sabbath day and hunt up new and troublesome ways to dishonor it.
citation: Letter to William Dean Howells, 27 February 1885, in Albert Bigelow Paine, Mark Twain's letters: Arranged with Comment (1917), Vol. 2, [http://books.google.com/books?id=4KZhv9y8sMIC&pg=PA450&lpg=PA450 p. 450]

author: Mark Twain
text: An experienced, industrious, ambitious, and often quite picturesque liar.
citation: "The Private History of a Campaign That Failed", The Century, Vol. 31, No. 2, December 1885[http://books.google.com/books?id=-1UiAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA193]. Anthologized in [http://books.google.com/books?id=1T00Sc_cVYIC The American Claimant, and O

author: Mark Twain
text: As I slowly grow wise I briskly grow cautious.
citation: "English as She Is Taught", The Century, Vol. 33, No. 6, April 1887[http://books.google.com/books?id=EzGgAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA932]. A slightly abridged version was reprinted as [http://books.google.com/books?id=CxIuAAAAYAAJ&pg=PR11 Introduction] t

author: Mark Twain
text: A circle is a round straight line with a hole in the middle.
citation: Quoting a schoolchild in "English as She Is Taught"

author: Mark Twain
text: All you need in this life is ignorance and confidence, and then Success is sure.
citation: Mark Twain's Notebook, 1887 Letter to Cordelia Welsh Foote (Cincinnati), 2 December 1887. [http://www.twainquotes.com/Success.html Letter reprinted] in Benjamin De Casseres's [https://www.worldcat.org/title/when-huck-finn-went-highbrow/oclc

author: Mark Twain
text: The difference between the almost right word and the right word is really a large matter—'tis the difference between the lightning-bug and the lightning.
citation: Letter to George Bainton, 15 October 1888, solicited for and printed in George Bainton, The Art of Authorship: Literary Reminiscences, Methods of Work, and Advice to Young Beginners (1890), [http://books.google.com/books?id=XjBjzRN71_IC&pg=

author: Mark Twain
text: Weather is a literary specialty, and no untrained hand can turn out a good article on it.
citation: The American Claimant, foreword (1892)

author: Mark Twain
text: I am opposed to millionaires, but it would be dangerous to offer me the position.
citation: American Claimant (1892)

author: Mark Twain
text: If you tell the truth you don't have to remember anything.
citation: Notebook entry, January or February 1894, Mark Twain's Notebook, ed. Albert Bigelow Paine (1935), [http://books.google.com/books?id=DjBVlb7cBSIC&pg=PA240 p. 240]

author: Mark Twain
text: James Ross Clemens, a cousin of mine, was seriously ill two or three weeks ago in London, but is well now. The report of my illness grew out of his illness; the report of my death was an exaggeration.
citation: From a note Twain wrote in London on May 31, 1897 to reporter Frank Marshall White: [http://books.google.com/books?id=ms3tce7BgJsC&lpg=PA134&vq=%22the%20report%20of%20my%20death%20was%20an%20exaggeration%22&pg=PA134 Shelley Fisher Fishkin,

author: Mark Twain
text: A round man cannot be expected to fit in a square hole right away. He must have time to modify his shape.
citation: More Tramps Abroad (1897)

author: Mark Twain
text: Humor is the great thing, the saving thing. The minute it crops up, all our hardnesses yield, all our irritations and resentments flit away and a sunny spirit takes their place.
citation: "What Paul Bourget Thinks of Us?" (1897)

author: Mark Twain
text: Get your facts first, and then you can distort them as much as you please.
citation: As quoted in [https://web.archive.org/web/20181106220834/https://ebooks.adelaide.edu.au/k/kipling/rudyard/seatosea/chapter37.html "An Interview with Mark Twain"], From Sea to Sea: Letters of Travel (1899) by Rudyard Kipling, Ch. 37, p. 180

author: Mark Twain
text: I was sorry to have my name mentioned as one of the great authors, because they have a sad habit of dying off. Chaucer is dead, Spencer is dead, so is Milton, so is Shakespeare, and I'm not feeling so well myself.
citation: Speech to the Savage Club, 9 June 1899, in Mark Twain's Speeches (1910), ed. William Dean Howells, [http://books.google.com/books?id=7etXZ5Q17ngC&pg=PA277 pp. 277–278]. (Possibly fabricated from a paraphrase in Aaron Watson, The Savage Club

author: Mark Twain
text: He had only one vanity; he thought he could give advice better than any other person.
citation: "The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg", ch. I, in The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg and Other Stories and Essays (1900)

author: Mark Twain
text: There is nothing in the world like a persuasive speech to fuddle the mental apparatus and upset the convictions and debauch the emotions of an audience not practised in the tricks and delusions of oratory.
citation: "The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg", ch. III, in The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg and Other Stories and Essays (1900)

author: Mark Twain
text: Definition of a classic — something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.
citation: Quoting or paraphrasing a Professor Winchester in [http://etext.lib.virginia.edu/etcbin/toccer-new2?id=TwaSpee.sgm&images=images/modeng&data=/texts/english/modeng/parsed&tag=public&part=52&division=div1 "Disappearance of Literature"], speec

author: Mark Twain
text: We believe that out of the public school grows the greatness of a nation.
citation: Address at a meeting of the Berkeley Lyceum, New York, November 23, 1900. Quoted in Mark Twain's Speeches (1910), ed. William Dean Howells, [http://books.google.com/books?id=7etXZ5Q17ngC&pg=PA146 p. 146] (The speech is titled "Public Educat

author: Mark Twain
text: The silent colossal National Lie that is the support and confederate of all the tyrannies and shams and inequalities and unfairnesses that afflict the peoples — that is the one to throw bricks and sermons at.
citation: [http://www.mtwain.com/My_First_Lie,_And_How_I_Got_Out_Of_It/0.html "My First Lie, and How I Got Out of It"], in The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg and Other Stories and Essays (1900)

author: Mark Twain
text: Honesty is the best policy — when there is money in it.
citation: Speech to Eastman College (1901)

author: Mark Twain
text: Now what I contend is that my body is my own, at least I have always so regarded it. If I do harm through my experimenting with it, it is I who suffer, not the state.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=yxNgXs3TkJYC&pg=PT260&lpg=PT260&dq=%22Now+what+I+contend+is+that+my+body+is+my+own%2C+at+least+I+have+always+so+regarded+it.+If+I+do+harm+through+my+experimenting+with+it%2C+it+is+I+who+suffers%2C+not+the+s

author: Mark Twain
text: Always do right. This will gratify some people, and astonish the rest.
citation: To the Young People's Society, Greenpoint Presbyterian Church, Brooklyn (16 February 1901)

author: Mark Twain
text: To create man was a fine and original idea; but to add the sheep was a tautology.
citation: St. Louis Post-Dispatch (30 May 1902); also in Mark Twain : A Life, p. 611

author: Mark Twain
text: Belgium's royal palace is still what it has been for the last 14 years: a lair of a wild beast that for its money every year mutilates, murders and starves a half million helpless natives in the Congo Free State.
citation: Mark Twain about the infamous 1904 Casement report (detailing the abuses in the Congo Free State by Roger Casement) Quoted from the book "Zaïre, Ketens van Koper (translated: Zaire, Chains of Copper)" Chapter 2: From Leopold II to Bwana Kit

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: I am a parcel of vain strivings tied By a chance bond together, Dangling this way and that, their links Were made so loose and wide, Methinks, For milder weather.
citation: "Sic Vita", st. 1. The Dial (July 1841) p. 81

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: But now I see I was not plucked for naught, And after in life's vase Of glass set while I might survive, But by a kind hand brought Alive To a strange place.
citation: "Sic Vita", st. 6. The Dial (July 1841) p. 82

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Let us not underrate the value of a fact; it will one day flower in a truth.
citation: [https://archive.vcu.edu/english/engweb/transcendentalism/authors/thoreau/nathist.html "Natural History of Massachusetts"]. The Dial (July 1842) p. 39

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Great God, I ask thee for no meaner pelf Than that I may not disappoint myself, That in my action I may soar as high As I can now discern with this clear eye.
citation: "Prayer", st. 1. The Dial (July 1842) p. 79

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The life that I aspire to live No man proposeth me— No trade upon the street Wears its emblazonry.
citation: "The Black Knight" , l. 11. The Dial (October 1842) p. 180

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: My books I'd fain cast off, I cannot read, 'Twixt every page my thoughts go stray at large Down in the meadow, where is richer feed, And will not mind to hit their proper targe.
citation: "The Summer Rain", st. 1. The Dial (October 1842) p. 224

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Here while I lie beneath this walnut bough, What care I for the Greeks or for Troy town, If juster battles are enacted now Between the ants upon this hummock's crown?
citation: "The Summer Rain", st. 3. The Dial (October 1842) p. 224

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: When will the world learn that a million men are of no importance compared with one man?
citation: Letter to Ralph Waldo Emerson (8 June 1843)

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Talk of mysteries! — Think of our life in nature, — daily to be shown matter, to come in contact with it, — rocks, trees, wind on our cheeks! The solid earth! the actual world! the common sense! Contact! Contact! Who are we? where are we?
citation: The Maine Woods (1848) Ktaadn

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The law will never make men free; it is men who have got to make the law free.
citation: "Slavery in Massachusetts" (1854)

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
citation: Letter to Harrison Blake (November 16, 1857)

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: You ask particularly after my health. I suppose that I have not many months to live; but, of course, I know nothing about it. I may add that I am enjoying existence as much as ever, and regret nothing.
citation: Last letter, to Myron Benton (March 31, 1862) [http://www.walden.org/Institute/thoreau/writings/correspondence/1862_03_21_Benton.htm]

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Truth, Goodness, Beauty — those celestial thrins, Continually are born; e'en now the Universe, With thousand throats, and eke with greener smiles, Its joy confesses at their recent birth.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: That virtue we appreciate is as much ours as another's. We see so much only as we possess.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: On the death of a friend, we should consider that the fates through confidence have devolved on us the task of a double living, that we have henceforth to fulfill the promise of our friend's life also, in our own, to the world.
citation: February 28, 1840

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: An early morning walk is a blessing for the whole day.
citation: April 20, 1840

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Who looks in the sun will see no light else; but also he will see no shadow. Our life revolves unceasingly, but the centre is ever the same, and the wise will regard only the seasons of the soul.
citation: March 10, 1841

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: We are as much as we see. Faith is sight and knowledge. The hands only serve the eyes.
citation: April 9, 1841

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The Indian...stands free and unconstrained in Nature, is her inhabitant and not her guest, and wears her easily and gracefully. But the civilized man has the habits of the house. His house is a prison.
citation: April 26, 1841

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: A slight sound at evening lifts me up by the ears, and makes life seem inexpressibly serene and grand. It may be Uranus, or it may be in the shutter.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: One cannot too soon forget his errors and misdemeanors. To dwell long upon them is to add to the offense. Repentance and sorrow can only be displaced by something better, which is as free and original as if they had not been.
citation: January 9, 1842

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The most attractive sentences are not perhaps the wisest, but the surest and soundest.
citation: March 16, 1842

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: And the cost of a thing it will be remembered as the amount of life it requires to be exchanged for it.
citation: After December 6, 1845

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: For many years I was self-appointed inspector of snowstorms and rainstorms, and did my duty faithfully, though I never received one cent for it.
citation: After February 22, 1846

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Disobedience is the true foundation of liberty. The obedient must be slaves.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: And now, at half-past ten o'clock, I hear the cockerels crow in Hubbard's barns, and morning is already anticipated. It is the feathered, wakeful thought in us that anticipates the following day.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live.
citation: August 19, 1851

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Nothing is so much to be feared as fear. Atheism may comparatively be popular with God himself.
citation: September 7, 1851

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The bluebird carries the sky on his back.
citation: April 3, 1852

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The perception of beauty is a moral test.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The youth gets together his materials to build a bridge to the moon, or, perchance, a palace or temple on the earth, and, at length, the middle-aged man concludes to build a woodshed with them.

author: Henry David Thoreau
