text: Every poet has trembled on the verge of science.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Some circumstantial evidence is very strong, as when you find a trout in the milk.
citation: November 11, 1854 Referring to an 1849 dairyman's strike, during which there was suspicion of milk being watered down

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Nature is full of genius, full of the divinity; so that not a snowflake escapes its fashioning hand.
citation: January 5, 1856

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The same law that shapes the earth-star shapes the snow-star. As surely as the petals of a flower are fixed, each of these countless snow-stars comes whirling to earth...these glorious spangles, the sweeping of heaven's floor.
citation: January 5, 1856

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: That man is the richest whose pleasures are the cheapest.
citation: March 11, 1856

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: This bird sees the white man come and the Indian withdraw, but it withdraws not. Its untamed voice is still heard above the tinkling of the forge... It remains to remind us of aboriginal nature.
citation: March 23, 1856; of the crow

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: It is in vain to dream of a wildness distant from ourselves.
citation: August 30, 1856

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: You must love the crust of the earth on which you dwell more than the sweet crust of any bread or cake; you must be able to extract nutriment out of a sand heap.
citation: January 25, 1858

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The savage in man is never quite eradicated.
citation: September 26, 1859

author: Voltaire
text: On parle toujours mal quand on n'a rien à dire.
citation: One always speaks badly when one has nothing to say. "Commentaires sur Corneille", Oeuvres complètes de Voltaire (1827)

author: Voltaire
text: L'homme doit être content, dit-on; mais de quoi?
citation: Man ought to be content, it is said; but with what? Pensées, Remarques, et Observations de Voltaire; ouvrage posthume (1802) Posthumously published "Thoughts, remarks and observations" believed to be by Voltaire [http://www.voltaire-integra

author: Voltaire
text: Le public est une bête féroce: il faut l'enchaîner ou la fuir.
citation: The public is a ferocious beast: one must chain it up or flee from it. Letter to Mademoiselle Quinault, quoted in Charles Sainte-Beuve, "Lettres inédites de Voltaire," Causeries de Lundi (20 October 1856) [http://www.voltaire-integral.com/G

author: Voltaire
text: If I had had more time, this letter would have been shorter.
citation: Written by Voltaire in an over-long letter to a friend, quoted to A. P. Martinich in Philosophical Writing: An Introduction, Note to the Second Edition (1996)

author: Voltaire
text: On doit des égards aux vivants; on ne doit aux morts que la vérité.
citation: We should be considerate to the living; to the dead we owe only the truth. Critique de l'Œdipe. Première lettre à M. de Genonville. Footnote to second edition. Tr. Harbottle and Dalbiac, Dictionary of Quotations: French and Italian, 2nd ed.

author: Voltaire
text: C'est un poids bien pesant qu'un nom trop tôt fameux.
citation: Quite a heavy weight, a name too quickly famous. La Henriade, song 3, l. 41 (1722)

author: Voltaire
text: L'homme est libre au moment qu'il veut l'être.
citation: Man is free at the instant he wants to be. Brutus, act II, scene I (1730)

author: Voltaire
text: Les mortels sont égaux; ce n'est pas la naissance, C'est la seule vertu qui fait la différence.
citation: All mortals are equal; it is not their birth, But virtue itself that makes the difference. Ériphyle, Act II, scene I (1732); these lines were also later used in Voltaire's Mahomet, Act I, scene IV (1741) Variant translations: Men are equal;

author: Voltaire
text: Les anciens Romains élevaient des prodiges d'architecture pour faire combattre des bêtes.
citation: The ancient Romans built their greatest masterpieces of architecture for wild beasts to fight in. Letter addressed to "un premier commis" [name unknown] (20 June 1733), from Oeuvres Complètes de Voltaire: Correspondance [Garnier frères, Par

author: Voltaire
text: If there were only one religion in England there would be danger of despotism, if there were two they would cut each other's throats, but there are thirty, and they live in peace and happiness.
citation: Letters on England, letter 6, "On the Presbyterians", trans. Leonard Tancock (Penguin Books, 1980) p. 41, published first in English in 1733

author: Voltaire
text: Tous les genres sont bons, hors le genre ennuyeux.
citation: All styles are good except the boring kind. L'Enfant prodigue: comédie en vers dissillabes (1736), Preface

author: Voltaire
text: Tout homme sensé, tout homme de bien, doit avoir la secte chrétienne en horreur.
citation: Every sensible man, every honorable man, must hold the Christian sect in horror. [http://www.worldcat.org/title/examen-important-de-milord-bolingbroke-ecrit-sur-la-fin-de-1736-accompagne-des-notes-de-mr-m-editeur-de-ses-ouvrages/oclc/110073

author: Voltaire
text: Aime la vérité, mais pardonne à l'erreur.
citation: Love truth, but pardon error. "Deuxième discours: de la liberté," Sept Discours en Vers sur l'Homme (1738)

author: Voltaire
text: Le secret d'ennuyer est celui de tout dire.
citation: The secret of being a bore is to tell everything. "Sixième discours: sur la nature de l'homme", Sept Discours en Vers sur l'Homme (1738)

author: Voltaire
text: Une seule partie de la physique occupe la vie de plusieurs hommes, et les laisse souvent mourir dans l'incertitude.
citation: A single part of physics occupies the lives of many men, and often leaves them dying in uncertainty. "A Madame la Marquise du Châtelet, Avant-Propos", Eléments de Philosophie de Newton (1738)

author: Voltaire
text: Ne peut-on pas remonter jusqu'à ces anciens scélérats, fondateurs illustres de la superstition et du fanatisme, qui, les premiers, ont pris le couteau sur l'autel pour faire des victimes de ceux qui refusaient d'etre leurs disciples?
citation: May we not return to those scoundrels of old, the illustrious founders of superstition and fanaticism, who first took the knife from the altar to make victims of those who refused to be their disciples? Letter to Frederick II of Prussia (De

author: Voltaire
text: Les habiles tyrans ne sont jamais punis.
citation: Clever tyrants are never punished. Mérope, act V, scene V (1743)

author: Voltaire
text: Il vaut mieux hasarder de sauver un coupable que de condamner un innocent.
citation: It is better to risk sparing a guilty person than to condemn an innocent one. Zadig (1747)

author: Voltaire
text: C'est le privilège du vrai génie, et surtout du génie qui ouvre une carrière, de faire impunément de grandes fautes.
citation: It is the privilege of true genius, and certainly of the genius that opens a new road, to make without punishment great mistakes. "Siècle de Louis XIV", ch. 32 (1751), qtd. in Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation (1818)

author: Voltaire
text: The king [Frederic] has sent me some of his dirty linen to wash; I will wash yours another time.
citation: Reply to General Manstein. Voltaire writes to his niece Dennis, July 24, 1752, "Voilà le roi qui m'envoie son linge à blanchir"; reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

author: Voltaire
text: C'est une des superstitions de l'esprit humain d'avoir imaginé que la virginité pouvait être une vertu.
citation: It is one of the superstitions of the human mind to have imagined that virginity could be a virtue. Notebooks (c.1735-c.1750) Note: This quotation and the three that follow directly below are from the so-called Leningrad Notebook, also know

author: Voltaire
text: Prier Dieu c'est se flatter qu'avec des paroles on changera toute la nature.
citation: To pray to God is to flatter oneself that with words one can alter nature. Notebooks (c.1735-c.1750)

author: Voltaire
text: Si Dieu nous a faits à son image, nous le lui avons bien rendu.
citation: If God has made us in his image, we have returned him the favor. Notebooks (c.1735-c.1750)

author: Voltaire
text: Un peuple qui trafique de ses enfants est encore plus condamnable que l'acheteur: ce négoce démontre notre supériorité; ce qui se donne un maître était né pour en avoir.
citation: A people that sells its own children is more condemnable than the buyer; this commerce demonstrates our superiority; he who gives himself a master was born to have one. Essai sur les Moeurs et l'Espit des Nations (1753), ch. CXCVII: Résumé

author: Voltaire
text: Ce corps qui s'appelait et qui s'appelle encore le saint empire romain n'était en aucune manière ni saint, ni romain, ni empire.
citation: This body which called itself and which still calls itself the Holy Roman Empire was in no way holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. Essai sur l'histoire générale et sur les mœurs et l'esprit des nations, Chapter 70 (1756)

author: Voltaire
text: En aimant tant la gloire, comment pouvez-vous vous obstiner à un projet qui vous la fera perdre?
citation: While loving glory so much how can you persist in a plan which will cause you to lose it? Letters of Voltaire and Frederick the Great (New York: Brentano's, 1927), transl. Richard Aldington, letter 130 from Voltaire to Frederick II of Pruss

author: Voltaire
text: Les opinions ont plus causé de maux sur ce petit globe que la peste et les tremblements de terre.
citation: Opinions have caused more ills than the plague or earthquakes on this little globe of ours. Letter to Élie Bertrand (5 January 1759)

author: Voltaire
text: Il faut toujours en fait de nouvelles attendre le sacrement de la confirmation.
citation: When we hear news, we should always wait for the sacrament of confirmation. Letter to Charles-Augustin Ferriol, comte d'Argental (28 August 1760]])

author: Voltaire
text: Quand il s'agit d'argent, tout le monde est de la même religion.
citation: When it is a question of money, everybody is of the same religion. Letter to Mme. d'Épinal, Ferney (26 December 1760) from Oeuvres Complètes de Voltaire: Correspondance (Garnier frères, Paris, 1881), vol. IX, letter # 4390 (p. 124)

author: Voltaire
text: Il y a des vérités qui ne sont pas pour tous les hommes et pour tous les temps.
citation: There are truths which are not for all men, nor for all times. Letter to François-Joachim de Pierre, cardinal de Bernis (23 April 1764)

author: Voltaire
text: Les hommes seront toujours fous; et ceux qui croient les guérir sont les plus fous de la bande.
citation: Men will always be mad, and those who think they can cure them are the maddest of all. Letter to Louise Dorothea of Meiningen, duchess of Saxe-Gotha Madame (30 January 1762)

author: Voltaire
text: La superstition est à la religion ce que l'astrologie est à l'astronomie, la fille très folle d'une mère très sage. Ces deux filles ont longtemps subjugué toute la terre.
citation: Superstition is to religion what astrology is to astronomy, the mad daughter of a wise mother. These daughters have too long dominated the earth. "Whether it is useful to maintain the people in superstition," Treatise on Toleration (1763)

author: Voltaire
text: Ils ne se servent de la pensée que pour autoriser leurs injustices, et n'emploient les paroles que pour déguiser leurs pensées.
citation: Men use thought only to justify their wrongdoings, and speech only to conceal their thoughts. Dialogue 14, Le Chapon et la Poularde (1766); reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

author: Voltaire
text: A false science makes atheists, a true science prostrates men before the Deity
citation: <small>[http://books.google.es/books?id=aItKAAAAcAAJ&printsec=frontcover&hl=es#v=onepage&q&f=false The critical review, or annals of literature, Volume XXVI], by A Society of Gentlemen (1768) p. 450</small>

author: Voltaire
text: Religion may be purified. This great work was begun two hundred years ago: but men can only bear light to come in upon them by degrees.
citation: <small>[http://books.google.es/books?id=aItKAAAAcAAJ&printsec=frontcover&hl=es#v=onepage&q&f=false The critical review, or annals of literature, Volume XXVI], by A Society of Gentlemen (1768) p. 450</small>

author: Voltaire
text: J'ai toujours fait une prière à Dieu, qui est fort courte. La voici: Mon Dieu, rendez nos ennemis bien ridicules! Dieu m'a exaucé.
citation: I always made one prayer to God, a very short one. Here it is: "O Lord, make our enemies quite ridiculous!" God granted it. Letter to Étienne Noël Damilaville (16 May 1767)

author: Voltaire
text: En effet, l'histoire n'est que le tableau des crimes et des malheurs.
citation: Indeed, history is nothing more than a tableau of crimes and misfortunes. L'Ingénu, ch.10 (1767) Quoted in The End, part 13 of A Series of Unfortunate Events

author: Voltaire
text: Il est bien malaisé (puisqu'il faut enfin m'expliquer) d'ôter à des insensés des chaînes qu'ils révèrent.
citation: It is difficult to free fools from the chains they revere. Le dîner du comte de Boulainvilliers (1767): Troisième Entretien

author: Voltaire
text: La vie est hérissée de ces épines, et je n'y sais d'autre remède que de cultiver son jardin.
citation: Life is bristling with thorns, and I know no other remedy than to cultivate one's garden. Letter to Pierre-Joseph Luneau de Boisjermain (21 October 1769), from Oeuvres Complètes de Voltaire: Correspondance [Garnier frères, Paris, 1882], vol

author: Voltaire
text: On dit que Dieu est toujours pour les gros bataillons.
citation: It is said that God is always on the side of the big battalions. Letter to François-Louis-Henri Leriche (6 February 1770) Note: In his Notebooks (c.1735-c.1750), Voltaire wrote: God is not on the side of the big battalions, but on the side

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The hero of my tale, whom I love with all the power of my soul, whom I have tried to portray in all his beauty, who has been, is, and will be beautiful, is Truth.
citation: Sevastopol in May (1855), Ch. 16

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I know that my unity with all people cannot be destroyed by national boundaries and government orders.
citation: My Religion (1884), as translated in The Human Experience : Contemporary American and Soviet Fiction and Poetry (1989) by the Quaker US/USSR Committee

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: A man can live and be healthy without killing animals for food; therefore, if he eats meat, he participates in taking animal life merely for the sake of his appetite. And to act so is immoral.
citation: Writings on Civil Disobedience and Nonviolence (1886)

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: I sit on a man's back, choking him, and making him carry me, and yet assure myself and others that I am very sorry for him and wish to ease his lot by any means possible, except getting off his back.
citation: Writings on Civil Disobedience and Nonviolence (1886)

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Six feet of land was all that he needed.
citation: How Much Land Does a Man Need? (1886)

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The happiness of men consists in life. And life is in labor.
citation: What Is To Be Done? (1886) Chap. XXXVIII, as translated in The Novels and Other Works of Lyof N. Tolstoï (1902) edited by Nathan Haskell Dole, p. 259

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The vocation of every man and woman is to serve other people.
citation: What Is To Be Done? (1886) Chap. XL, as translated in The Novels and Other Works of Lyof N. Tolstoï (1902) edited by Nathan Haskell Dole, p. 281

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The more is given the less the people will work for themselves, and the less they work the more their poverty will increase.
citation: Help for the Starving, Pt. III (January 1892)

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Condemn me if you choose — I do that myself, — but condemn me, and not the path which I am following, and which I point out to those who ask me where, in my opinion, the path is.
citation: "Letter to N.N.," quoted by Havelock Ellis in [http://books.google.com/books?id=xCp6OIGcojMC& "The New Spirit"] (1892) p. 226

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Government is violence, Christianity is meekness, non-resistance, love. And, therefore, government cannot be Christian, and a man who wishes to be a Christian must not serve government.
citation: [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Letter_to_Dr._Eugen_Heinrich_Schmitt Letter to Dr. Eugen Heinrich Schmitt] (October 12, 1896), translated by [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Nathan_Haskell_Dole Nathan Haskell Dole]

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: All violence consists in some people forcing others, under threat of suffering or death, to do what they do not want to do.
citation: [http://www.calebjohnson.org/lawoflove.pdf The Law of Love and the Law of Violence (1908)]

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The truth is that the State is a conspiracy designed not only to exploit, but above all to corrupt its citizens ... Henceforth, I shall never serve any government anywhere.
citation: As quoted in Tolstoy (1988) by A. N. Wilson, p. 146

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Science is meaningless because it gives no answer to our question, the only question important for us: 'what shall we do and how shall we live
citation: Quoted by Max Weber in his lecture "Science as a Vocation"; in Lynda Walsh (2013), Scientists as Prophets: A Rhetorical Genealogy (2013), Oxford University Press, p. 90

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: There is only one enduring happiness in life—to live for others.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=eWU4AAAAYAAJ&q=%22there+is+only+one+enduring+happiness+in+life+to+live+for+others%22&pg=PA22#v=onepage Part 1, chapter 2]

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Now about your family. Do you know that since your daughter came out everyone has been enraptured by her? They say she is amazingly beautiful.
citation: Bk. I, Ch. I

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly. It is the one thing we are interested in here.
citation: Book IV, Ch. 11

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: You will die — and it will all be over. You will die and find out everything — or cease asking.
citation: Bk. V, Ch. 1

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The only thing that we know is that we know nothing — and that is the highest flight of human wisdom.
citation: Book V, Ch. I

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Everything comes in time to him who knows how to wait.
citation: Bk. X, ch. 16

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The strongest of all warriors are these two — Time and Patience.
citation: Bk. X, ch. 16

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: He did not, and could not, understand the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the manifestation of an activity unknown to him, which was his life.
citation: About Platon Karataev in Bk. XII, ch. 13

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: To love life is to love God. Harder and more blessed than all else is to love this life in one's sufferings, in undeserved sufferings.
citation: Bk. XIV, ch. 15

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: For us, with the rule of right and wrong given us by Christ, there is nothing for which we have no standard. And there is no greatness where there is not simplicity, goodness, and truth.
citation: Bk. XIV, ch. 18

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Pure and complete sorrow is as impossible as pure and complete joy.
citation: Bk. XV, ch. 1

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Despite the fact that the doctors treated him, bled him, and gave him medicines to drink, he recovered. [sometimes quoted as "Though the doctors treated him, let his blood, and gave him medications to drink, he nevertheless recovered."]
citation: Bk. XV, ch. 12

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: History is the life of nations and of humanity. To seize and put into words, to describe directly the life of humanity or even of a single nation, appears impossible.
citation: [http://www.classicreader.com/book/92/354/ Epilogue II, ch. 1]

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Stephan Arkadievich chose neither his attitudes nor his opinions, no, the attitudes and opinions came to him on their own, just as he chose neither the style of his hat nor of his coats but got what people were wearing.
citation: Part 1, Chapter 3

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: He knew she was there by the joy and fear that overwhelmed his heart.
citation: Pt. I, ch. 9

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: He stepped down, trying not to look long at her, as if she were the sun, yet he saw her, like the sun, even without looking.
citation: Pt. I, ch. 9

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: One can insult an honest man or an honest woman, but to tell a thief that he is a thief is merely la constation d'un fait [The establishing of a fact.]
citation: Pt. IV, ch. 4

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Respect was invented to cover the empty place where love should be.
citation: (voice of Anna) C. Garnett, trans. (New York: 2003), Part 7, Chapter 24 p. 685

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: There is one evident, indubitable manifestation of the Divinity, and that is the laws of right which are made known to the world through Revelation.
citation: Pt. VIII, ch. 19

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Go — take the mother's soul, and learn three truths: Learn What dwells in man, What is not given to man, and What men live by. When thou hast learnt these things, thou shalt return to heaven.
citation: Ch. IV

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Then I remembered the first lesson God had set me: "Learn what dwells in man." And I understood that in man dwells Love! I was glad that God had already begun to show me what He had promised, and I smiled for the first time.
citation: Ch. XI

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: When the woman showed her love for the children that were not her own, and wept over them, I saw in her the living God, and understood What men live by.
citation: Ch. XI

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Quite often a man goes on for years imagining that the religious teaching that had been imparted to him since childhood is still intact, while all the time there is not a trace of it left in him.
citation: Pt. I, ch. 1

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: One can only live while one is intoxicated with life; as soon as one is sober it is impossible not to see that it is all a mere fraud and a stupid fraud!
citation: Ch. 4 Variant: It is possible to live only as long as life intoxicates us; once we are sober we cannot help seeing that it is all a delusion, a stupid delusion.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The only absolute knowledge attainable by man is that life is meaningless.
citation: Ch. 5, translated by David Patterson, 1983

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: For man to be able to live he must either not see the infinite, or have such an explanation of the meaning of life as will connect the finite with the infinite.
citation: Ch. 9

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Ivan Ilych's life had been most simple and most ordinary and therefore most terrible.
citation: Ch. II

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: By God, if you try anything like that, I'll kick you, I'll bite you, I'll kick you in the balls. I'll do anything to you — you'd better leave me alone.
citation: 1881, to "Big John" McManus, a Tammany Hall politician in the New York State Assembly, about a plan to humiliate Roosevelt by tossing him in a blanket. Quoted in "I Rose Like a Rocket: The Political Education of Theodore Roosevelt" (2007) b

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: No candid observer will deny that whatever of good there may be in our American civilization is the product of Christianity.
citation: “Our Nation, A Product of Christianity,” Springfield Republican, 1884, editorial.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: The most vicious cowboy has more moral principle than the average Indian.
citation: January 1886, in a campaign speech given in New York https://www.history.com/news/teddy-roosevelt-race-imperialism-national-parks

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I don’t go so far as to think that the only good Indian is the dead Indian, but I believe nine out of every ten are, and I shouldn’t like to inquire too closely into the case of the tenth.
citation: Ibid, January 1886 https://www.history.com/news/teddy-roosevelt-race-imperialism-national-parks

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: There is much talk about "jingoism". If by "jingoism" they mean a policy in pursuance of which Americans will with resolution and common sense insist upon our rights being respected by foreign powers, then we are "jingoes".
citation: In [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1895/10/24/106070065.pdf "For An Honest Election"]. New York Times. 23 Oct 1895. The reference is found halfway down the article.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: The worst lesson that can be taught a man is to rely upon others and to whine over his sufferings.
citation: [https://books.google.com/books?id=J2FAAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA39 "How Not To Better Social Conditions" in Review of Reviews (January 1897), p. 39] · [http://www.theodore-roosevelt.com/images/research/speeches/trhnthopb.pdf Full text online (with at

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is both foolish and wicked to teach the average man who is not well off that some wrong or injustice has been done him, and that he should hope for redress elsewhere than in his own industry, honesty and intelligence.
citation: "How Not To Better Social Conditions" in Review of Reviews (January 1897), p. 39

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: To sit home, read one's favorite paper, and scoff at the misdeeds of the men who do things is easy, but it is markedly ineffective. It is what evil men count upon the good men's doing.
citation: "The Higher Life of American Cities", in The Outlook (21 December 1895), p. 1083-1085

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: To borrow a simile from the football field, we believe that men must play fair, but that there must be no shirking, and that the success can only come to the player who hits the line hard.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay, NY] (October 1897)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Don't let anyone impose on you. Don't be quarrelsome, but stand up for your rights. If you've got to fight, fight hard and well. To my mind, a coward is the only thing meaner than a liar.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Talk to schoolchildren in Oyster Bay, Christmastime (1898)], as quoted in The Bully Pulpit : A Teddy Roosevelt Book of Quotations (2002) by H. Paul Jeffers, p. 22

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I have always been fond of the West African proverb "Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far.
citation: [http://www.lcweb.loc.gov/exhibits/treasures/trm139.html Letter to Henry L. Sprague] (26 January 1900); this is the first known use of this phrase, which became a signature motto of Roosevelt's after he used it in a speech as vice president

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Death is always and under all circumstances a tragedy, for if it is not, then it means that life itself has become one.
citation: Letter to Cecil Spring-Rice (12 March 1900)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: In short, in life, as in a football game, the principle to follow is: Hit the line hard; don't foul and don't shirk, but hit the line hard!
citation: "The American Boy", published in St. Nicholas 27, no. 7 (May 1900), p. 574

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I'm as strong as a bull moose and you can use me to the limit.
citation: Letter to Mark Hannah (27 June 1900)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is a dreadful thing to come into the Presidency in this way; but it would be far worse to be morbid about it. Here is the task, and I have got to do it to the best of my ability.
citation: Probably 1901. [https://www.nps.gov/thri/learn/historyculture/index.htm Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historical Site -- National Park Service]

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I can be President of the United States, or I can control Alice. I cannot possibly do both.
citation: Response when a dignitary asked if he could better control his daughter, as quoted in Hail to the Chiefs : My Life and Times with Six Presidents (1970) by Ruth Shick Montgomery, and [http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,950286,0

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I don't pity any man who does hard work worth doing. I admire him. I pity the creature who does not work, at whichever end of the social scale he may regard himself as being.
citation: [https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/remarks-the-brotherhood-locomotive-firemen-chattanooga-tennessee Remarks to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen in Chattanooga, Tennessee (8 September 1902).] [http://books.google.de/books?id=7_3

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: The government is us; we are the government, you and I.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=kfYEAAAAYAAJ&q=%22The+government+is+us+we+are+the+government+you+and+I%22&pg=PA521#v=onepage Speech] at Asheville, North Carolina (9 September 1902)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Let us speak courteously, deal fairly, and keep ourselves armed and ready.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Address in San Francisco, California (13 May 1903)]

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: A man who is good enough to shed his blood for his country is good enough to be given a square deal afterwards. More than that no man is entitled to, and less than that no man shall have.
citation: Speech at Springfield, Illinois (4 July 1903)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is no use to preach to [children] if you do not act decently yourself.
citation: [https://web.archive.org/web/20130210023816/http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Speech to Holy Name Society, Oyster Bay, August 16, 1903]

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: No man is above the law and no man is below it; nor do we ask any man's permission when we require him to obey it. Obedience to the law is demanded as a right; not asked as a favor.
citation: Third State of the Union Address (7 December 1903)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: The only man who makes no mistakes is the man who never does anything.
citation: As quoted by Jacob A. Riis in Theodore Roosevelt, the Citizen (1904), [http://www.bartleby.com/206/16.html chapter XVI A Young Men's Hero]

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: We face the future with our past and our present as guarantors of our promises; and we are content to stand or to fall by the record which we have made and are making.
citation: [http://www.theodore-roosevelt.com/images/research/txtspeeches/104.txt Address at Oyster Bay, New York (27 July 1904)], in response to the committee appointed to notify him of his nomination for the Presidency.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: This country has nothing to fear from the crooked man who fails. We put him in jail. It is the crooked man who succeeds who is a threat to this country.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Address in Memphis, Tennessee (25 October 1905)]

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: You tell me that saccharin is injurious to health? Dr. Rixey gives it to me every day. Anybody who says saccharin is injurious to health is an idiot.
citation: Response when Harvey W. Wiley opposed the use of saccharin because it is injurious to health, as quoted in The History of a Crime Against the Food Law (1929) by Harvey W. Wiley

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I suppose my critics will call that preaching, but I have got such a bully pulpit!
citation: As quoted by Lyman Abbott, in The Outlook (27 February 1909); repeated in the New York Times (6 March 1909); "Bully" in this sense was common slang adjective for "admirable", "excellent".

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I don't think any President ever enjoyed himself more than I did. Moreover, I don't think any ex-President ever enjoyed himself more.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly University of Cambridge, England] (26 May 1910)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: The nation behaves well if it treats the natural resources as assets which it must turn over to the next generation increased, and not impaired, in value.
citation: Speech before the Colorado Live Stock Association, Denver, Colorado (August 29, 1910); in The New Nationalism (1910), p. 52; also inscribed on Cox Corridor II, a first floor House corridor, U.S. Capitol.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I have never in my life envied a human being who led an easy life; I have envied a great many people who led difficult lives and led them well.
citation: Address in Des Moines, Iowa (4 November 1910)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is true of the Nation, as of the individual, that the greatest doer must also be a great dreamer.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Berkeley, CA] (1911)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: We stand at Armageddon and we battle for the Lord.
citation: [http://www.theodore-roosevelt.com/images/research/speeches/trreactionaires.pdf Speech at Progressive Party Convention, Chicago] (17 June 1912)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: This country will not be a permanently good place for any of us to live in unless we make it a reasonably good place for all of us to live in.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Chicago, IL] (17 June 1912)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: There can be no greater issue than that of conservation in this country.
citation: [http://www.bartleby.com/55/5.html Confession of Faith Speech, Progressive National Convention, Chicago] (6 August 1912)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: We propose to make the process of constitutional amendment far easier, speedier, and simpler than at present.
citation: [https://books.google.com/books?id=1LpOAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA589 "Democratic Ideals" in The Outlook (15 November 1913)]

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: If I must choose between righteousness and peace I choose righteousness.
citation: America and the World War (1915)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: If a man does not have an ideal and try to live up to it, then he becomes a mean, base, and sordid creature, no matter how successful.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Letter to his son, Kermit, quoted in Theodore Roosevelt by Joseph Bucklin Bishop] (1915)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: You could no more make an agreement with them than you could nail currant jelly to a wall - and the failure to nail current jelly to a wall is not due to the nail; it is due to the currant jelly.
citation: Letter to William Roscoe Thayer (2 July 1915)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I have a perfect horror of words that are not backed up by deeds.
citation: [http://www.trsite.org/content/pages/speaking-loudly Oyster Bay, NY] (7 July 1915)

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I have already lived and enjoyed as much life as any nine other men I have known.
citation: As quoted in "Roosevelt The Greatest Outdoor Man" by Arthur K. Willyoung in Outing Vol. 74, No. 6 (September 1919), p. 353

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: If all printers were determined not to print anything till they were sure it would offend nobody, there would be very little printed.
citation: "Apology for Printers" (1730); later in Benjamin Franklin's Autobiographical Writings (1945) edited by Carl Van Doren

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Ambition has its disappointments to sour us, but never the good fortune to satisfy us.
citation: "On True Happiness", Pennsylvania Gazette (20 November 1735).

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: If you would keep your Secret from an enemy, tell it not to a friend. Up, Sluggard, and waste not life; in the grave will be sleeping enough.
citation: September 1741. [https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-02-02-0066 “Poor Richard, 1741,”] Founders Online, National Archives, accessed 27 May 2020. [Original source: The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, vol. 2, January 1, 1735, thr

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety.
citation: This was first used by Franklin for the Pennsylvania Assembly in its "Reply to the Governor" (November 11, 1755) [https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-06-02-0107 Reply to the Governor] [https://founders.archives.gov/documents

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: He has paid dear, very dear, for his whistle.
citation: The Whistle (November, 1779); reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: The first man put at the helm will be a good one. No body knows what sort may come afterwards. The Executive will be always increasing here, as elsewhere, till it ends in a Monarchy.
citation: Records of the Federal Convention (which resulted in the United States Constitution), [https://press-pubs.uchicago.edu/founders/documents/a1_7_2-3s4.html June 4, 1787]

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Do not anticipate trouble, or worry about what may never happen. Keep in the sunlight.
citation: As quoted in Dictionary of Thoughts (1908) by Tryon Edwards, p. 22

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: God grant, that not only the Love of Liberty, but a thorough Knowledge of the Rights of Man, may pervade all the Nations of the Earth, so that a Philosopher may set his Foot anywhere on its Surface, and say, 'This is my Country.'
citation: Letter to David Hartley (December 4, 1789); reported in Albert H. Smyth, ed., The Writings of Benjamin Franklin (1907), Volume 10, p. 72; often quoted as, "Where liberty dwells, there is my country".

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Three may keep a secret, if two of them are dead.
citation: Quoted by Gerald Gawalt in "[https://www.loc.gov/loc/lcib/0601/franklin.html In His Own Words: Library Exhibition Celebrates Tercentenary of Benjamin Franklin's Birth]"

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Distrust & caution are the parents of security.
citation: Poor Richard's Almanack (1733)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: If you desire many things, many things will seem but a few.
citation: [http://www.rarebookroom.org/Control/frapos/index.html Poor Richard's Almanack (1736),] November

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Let all Men know thee, but no man know thee thoroughly: Men freely ford that see the shallows.
citation: Poor Richard's Almanack (1743)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Love your Enemies, for they tell you your Faults.
citation: Poor Richard's Almanack (1756); this has also been quoted in a paraphrased form used by Bill Clinton in [[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/asia-pacific/122320.stm 1998 address to Beijing University], as "Our critics are our friends, they show us

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: It would be thought a hard Government that should tax its People one-tenth Part of their Time, to be employed in its Service.
citation: Poor Richard's Almanack (1758), “The Way to Wealth”

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: From a Child I was fond of Reading, and all the little Money that came into my Hands was ever laid out in Books.
citation: Part I, p. 9

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: These Names of Virtues with their Precepts were
citation: 1. TEMPERANCE. Eat not to Dulness. Drink not to Elevation. 2. SILENCE. Speak not but what may benefit others or your self. Avoid trifling Conversation. 3. ORDER. Let all your Things have their Places. Let each part of your Business have its

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Human Felicity is produc'd not so much by great Pieces of good Fortune that seldom happen, as by little Advantages that occur every Day.
citation: Part III, p. 108

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: I think opinions should be judged of by their influences and effects; and if a man holds none that tend to make him less virtuous or more vicious, it may be concluded that he holds none that are dangerous, which I hope is the case with me.
citation: Letter to his father, 13 April 1738, printed in Memoirs of Benjamin Franklin (Philadelphia, 1834), volume 1, p. 233; also quoted in Benjamin Franklin: An American Life (2003) by Walter Isaacson

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: We are a kind of posterity in respect to them.
citation: Letter to William Strahan (1745); reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: But I must own that I am much in the Dark about Light. I am not satisfy'd with the doctrine that supposes particles of matter call'd light continually driven off from the Sun's Surface, with a Swiftness so prodigious!
citation: Letter to Cadwallader Colden (23 April 1752)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Every Body cries, a Union is absolutely necessary, but when they come to the Manner and Form of the Union, their weak Noddles are perfectly distracted.
citation: Letter to Peter Collinson (29 December 1754); published in The Writings of Benjamin Franklin (1905), edited by Albert Henry Smyth, Vol. III, p. 242; also misquoted using "Noodles" for "Noddles".

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Idleness and Pride Tax with a heavier Hand than Kings and Parliaments; If we can get rid of the former we may easily bear the Latter.
citation: Letter to Charles Thomson, 11 July 1765; also quoted in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919). The last sentence is sometimes misquoted as "If we can get rid of the former, we can get rid of the latter".

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: In 200 years will people remember us as traitors or heros? That is the question we must ask.
citation: Letter to Thomas Jefferson (March 16th, 1775)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: You and I were long friends: you are now my enemy, and I am yours.
citation: Letter to William Strahan (5 July 1775); reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)thumb|We hear of the conversion of water into wine at the [[w:Marriage_at_Cana|marriage in Cana as of a miracle. But this conversion is, thr

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Here you would know and enjoy what posterity will say of Washington. For a thousand leagues have nearly the same effect with a thousand years.
citation: Letter to Washington (5 March 1780); reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: There never was a good war or a bad peace.
citation: Letter to Josiah Quincy (11 September 1783)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Let me add, that only a virtuous people are capable of freedom. As nations become corrupt and vicious, they have more need of masters.
citation: letter to the Abbés Chalut and Arnaud (17 April 1787)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: That it is better 100 guilty Persons should escape than that one innocent Person should suffer, is a maxim that has been long and generally approved; never, that I know of, controverted.
citation: [https://books.google.de/books?id=d3UPAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA166&dq=maxim Letter to Benjamin Vaughan], on Blackstone's Ratio (14 March 1785)

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Our new Constitution is now established, and has an appearance that promises permanency; but in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes!
citation: Letter to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy (13 November 1789), quoting a popular phrase dated back to the 1716 play The Cobbler of Preston, written by Christopher Bullock (actor). {{cite web |url=https://www.mentalfloss.com/history/famous-quotes-everyo

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Freier Wille ohne Fatum ist ebenso wenig denkbar, wie Geist ohne Reelles, Gutes ohne Böses.
citation: Free will without fate is no more conceivable than spirit without matter, good without evil. "Fatum und Geschichte," April 1862

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Here the ways of men part: if you wish to strive for peace of soul and pleasure, then believe; if you wish to be a devotee of truth, then inquire.
citation: Letter to Elisabeth Nietzsche, Bonn, 1865-06-11,{{fix cite }} quoted as epigraph in Walter Kaufmann, The Faith of a Heretic (1961)

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: May I really say it! All truths are bloody truths to me—take a look at my previous writings.
citation: Notebooks (Summer 1880) 4[271]

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Style ought to prove that one believes in an idea; not only that one thinks it but also feels it.
citation: Letter to Lou Andreas-Salomé (August 1881), in Salomé's biography of Nietzsche, tr. Siegfried Mandel (1988)

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Against that positivism which stops before phenomena, saying "there are only facts," I should say: no, it is precisely facts that do not exist, only interpretations.
citation: Notebooks (Late 1886 – Spring 1887) [http://www.nietzschesource.org/eKGWB/NF-1886,7[60&#x5D] Popular usage: "There are no facts, only interpretations."

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Is Wagner a human being at all? Is he not rather a disease? He contaminates everything he touches - he has made music sick.
citation: Der Fall Wagner (1888)

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Der philosophische Mensch hat sogar das Vorgefühl, dass auch unter dieser Wirklichkeit, in der wir leben und sind, eine zweite ganz andre verborgen liege...
citation: Underneath this reality in which we live and have our being, another and altogether different reality lies concealed... p. 23, William Haussmann translation

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Darum hat Lessing, der ehrlichste theoretische Mensch, es auszusprechen gewagt, dass ihm mehr am Suchen der Wahrheit als an ihr selbst gelegen sei...
citation: Lessing, the most honest of theoretical men, dared to say that he took greater delight in the quest for truth than in the truth itself. p. 73

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Today as always, men fall into two groups: slaves and free men. Whoever does not have two-thirds of his day for himself, is a slave, whatever he may be: a statesman, a businessman, an official, or a scholar.
citation: Aphorism 283, tr. Marion Faber and Stephen Lehmann

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: He who thinks a great deal is not suited to be a party man: he thinks his way through the party and out the other side too soon.
citation: Aphorism 579, tr. R. J. Hollingdale

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Merchant and pirate...for a long period are one and the same person...Even to-day mercantile morality is really nothing but a refinement on piratical morality.
citation: Aphorism 22, tr. Paul V. Cohn

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: A witticism is an epigram on the death of a feeling.
citation: Aphorism 202, tr. R. J. Hollingdale

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: On the heights it is warmer than people in the valleys suppose, especially in winter. The thinker recognises the full import of this simile.
citation: Aphorism 335, tr. Paul V. Cohn

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Christianity has succeeded in transforming Eros and Aphrodite—great powers capable of idealisation—into diabolical kobolds and phantoms.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: The surest way to corrupt a youth is to instruct him to hold in higher esteem those who think alike than those who think differently.

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Gott ist tot! aber so wie die Art der Menschen ist, wird es vielleicht noch Jahrtausende lang Höhlen geben, in denen man seinen Schatten zeigt. — Und wir — Wir müssen auch noch seinen Schatten besiegen.
citation: God is dead; but given the way of men, there may still be caves for thousands of years in which his shadow will be shown. — And we — we still have to vanquish his shadow, too. Sec. 108

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: To what extent can truth endure incorporation? That is the question; that is the experiment.
citation: Sec. 110

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Morality is herd instinct in the individual.
citation: Sec. 116

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Gott ist tot! Gott bleibt tot! Und wir haben ihn getötet.
citation: God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him. How shall we comfort ourselves, the murderers of all murderers? What was holiest and mightiest of all that the world has yet owned has bled to death under our knives: who will wipe this

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Thoughts are the shadows of our feelings — always darker, emptier, simpler.
citation: Sec. 179

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed. What have ye done to surpass man?
citation: Prologue, § 3, tr. Thomas Common

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not a goal.
citation: Prologue, § 4, tr. Thomas Common

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: I tell you: one must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star.
citation: Prologue, § 5

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: There is more wisdom in your body than in your deepest philosophy.
citation: Part I, Chapter 4

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Of all that is written, I love only what a man has written with his own blood.
citation: Part I, Chapter 7

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: There is always some madness in love. But there is also always some reason in madness.
citation: Part I, Chapter 7

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Brave, unconcerned, mocking, violent—thus wisdom wants us: she is a woman, and loves only a warrior.
citation: Part I, Chapter 7

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: In the mountains, the shortest way is from peak to peak: but for that, you need long legs. Aphorisms should be peaks: and those to whom they are spoken, big and tall.
citation: Part I, Chapter 7

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: The state lieth in all languages of good and evil; and whatever it saith it lieth; and whatever it hath it hath stolen.
citation: Part I, Chapter 11, Thomas Common translation

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: The true man wants two things: danger and play. For that reason he wants woman, as the most dangerous toy.
citation: Part I, Chapter 18

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Man should be trained for war and woman for the recreation of the warrior: all else is folly.
citation: p. 91, tr. R.J. Hollingdale

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Man is for woman a means; the end is always the child.
citation: Part I, Chapter 18

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Everything in woman is a riddle, and everything in woman hath one solution—it is called pregnancy.
citation: Part II, Chapter 18

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: I have often laughed at the weaklings who thought themselves good because they had no claws.
citation: Part II, Chapter 13

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: They are not clean enough for me, either: they all disturb their waters so that they may seem deep.
citation: Part II, Chapter 39, tr. Walter Kaufmann

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Whence come the highest mountains? I once asked. Then I learned that they came out of the sea. The evidence is written in their rocks and in the walls of their peaks. It is out of the deepest depth that the highest must come to its height.
citation: Part III, Chapter 45

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Christianity is Platonism for the "people".
citation: Prelude

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Gradually it has become clear to me what every great philosophy has been: namely, the personal confession of its author and a kind of involuntary and unconscious memoir.
citation: Chapter I, aphorism 6, tr. Walter Kaufmann

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: Independence is for the very few; it is a privilege of the strong.
citation: Chapter II, aphorism 29, tr. Walter Kaufmann

author: Friedrich Nietzsche
text: So long as thou feelest the stars as an ‘above thee’, thou lackest the eye of the discerning one.
citation: Chapter IV, aphorism 71, tr. Helen Zimmern

author: Galileo Galilei
text: I would say here something that was heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree [probably Caesar Baronius]: "The intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes.
citation: Variant translation: I would say here something that was heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree: "That the intention of the Holy Spirit is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go."

author: Victor Hugo
text: Ces deux moitiés de Dieu, le pape et l'empereur!
citation: These two halves of God, the Pope and the emperor. Hernani (1830), [http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Hernani#ACTE_4 Act IV, Scene II]

author: Victor Hugo
text: Dieu s'est fait homme; soit. Le diable s'est fait femme!
citation: God became a man, granted. The devil became a woman. Ruy Blas (1838), [http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Ruy_Blas#ACTE_2_SCENE_5 Act II, Scene V]

author: Victor Hugo
text: La raison, c'est l'intelligence en exercice; l'imagination c'est l'intelligence en érection
citation: Reason is intelligence taking exercise; imagination is intelligence with an erection. Unpublished notebook from 1845-50. Published in Seebacher (ed.), Oeuvres Complètes, vol. 10, p. 158 (Laffont, 1989). English translation from Robb, Victor

author: Victor Hugo
text: Vous tenez à l’exemple [de la peine de mort]. Pourquoi? Pour ce qu’il enseigne. Que voulez-vous enseigner avec votre exemple? Qu’il ne faut pas tuer. Et comment enseignez-vous qu’il ne faut pas tuer? En tuant.
citation: You insist on the example [of the death penalty]. Why? For what it teaches. What do you want to teach with your example? That thou shalt not kill. And how do you teach thou shalt not kill? By killing. [http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Plaidoye

author: Victor Hugo
text: One can no more pray too much than love too much.
citation: Les Misérables (1862), page 55, as translated by Charles Wilbour and provided by A.L. Bert Publishers. Source: Shawn Thomas (June 24, 2013): Quotes & Illustrations From Victor Hugo’s Les Miserables. [https://web.archive.org/web/202303111510

author: Victor Hugo
text: Happy, even in anguish, is he to whom God has given a soul worthy of love and of grief!
citation: Les Misérables (1862), page 746, as translated by Charles Wilbour and provided by A.L. Bert Publishers. Source: Shawn Thomas (June 24, 2013): Quotes & Illustrations From Victor Hugo’s Les Miserables. [https://web.archive.org/web/20230311151

author: Victor Hugo
text: The best way to worship God is to love your wife.
citation: Les Misérables (1862), page 1190, as translated by Charles Wilbour and provided by A.L. Bert Publishers. Source: Shawn Thomas (June 24, 2013): Quotes & Illustrations From Victor Hugo’s Les Miserables. [https://web.archive.org/web/2023031115

author: Victor Hugo
text: To love or to have loved, that is enough. Ask nothing further. There is no other pearl to be found in the dark folds of life. To love is a consummation.
citation: Les Misérables (1862), page 1190, as translated by Charles Wilbour and provided by A.L. Bert Publishers. Source: Shawn Thomas (June 24, 2013): Quotes & Illustrations From Victor Hugo’s Les Miserables. [https://web.archive.org/web/2023031115

author: Victor Hugo
text: Il y a maintenant en France dans chaque village un flambeau allumé, le maître d'école, et une bouche qui souffle dessus, le curé.
citation: Histoire d'un crime. Déposition d'un témoin (1877), Deuxième Journée. La lutte, ch. III: La barricade Saint-Antoine Translation: There is now, in France, in each village, a lighted torch—the schoolmaster—and a mouth which blows upon it—the

author: Victor Hugo
text: Je n'entre qu'à moitié dans la guerre civile. Je veux bien y mourir, je ne veux pas y tuer.
citation: I only take a half share in the civil war; I am willing to die, I am not willing to kill. Histoire d'un crime (The History of a Crime) [written 1852, published 1877], Quatrième journée. La victoire, ch. II: Les Faits de la nuit. Quartier de

author: Victor Hugo
text: On résiste à l'invasion des armées; on ne résiste pas à l'invasion des idées.
citation: Literal translations: One resists the invasion of armies; one does not resist the invasion of ideas. One withstands the invasion of armies; one does not withstand the invasion of ideas. Histoire d'un Crime (The History of a Crime) [written

author: Victor Hugo
text: Waterloo! Waterloo! Waterloo! Morne plaine!
citation: Waterloo! Waterloo! Waterloo! Dismal plain! [http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/L%27Expiation L'Expiation], from Les Châtiments (1853), Book V

author: Victor Hugo
text: Jésus a pleuré, Voltaire a souri; c’est de cette larme divine et de ce sourire humain qu’est faite la douceur de la civilisation actuelle.
citation: Jesus wept; Voltaire smiled. Of that divine tear and that human smile is composed the sweetness of the present civilization. Speech, [http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Actes_et_paroles_-_Depuis_l%E2%80%99exil_-_1878#II_LE_CENTENAIRE_DE_VOLTAIRE

author: Victor Hugo
text: Change your opinions, keep to your principles; change your leaves, keep intact your roots.
citation: "Thoughts," Postscriptum de ma vie, in Victor Hugo's Intellectual Autobiography, Funk and Wagnalls (1907) as translated by Lorenzo O'Rourke

author: Victor Hugo
text: C'est ici le combat du jour et de la nuit... Je vois de la lumière noire.
citation: This is the battle between day and night... I see black light. Last words (1885-05-22); quoted in Olympio, ou la vie de Victor Hugo by André Maurois (1954)

author: Victor Hugo
text: Lever à six, coucher à dix, Dîner à dix, souper à six, Font vivre l'homme dix fois dix.
citation: To rise at six, to sleep at ten, To sup at ten, to dine at six, Make a man live for ten times ten. Inscription in Hugo's dining room, quoted in Gustave Larroumet, La maison de Victor Hugo: Impressions de Guernesey (1895), Chapter III

author: Victor Hugo
text: Ce besoin de l’immatériel est le plus vivace de tous. Il faut du pain; mais avant le pain, il faut l’idéal.
citation: The need of the immaterial is the most deeply rooted of all needs. One must have bread; but before bread, one must have the ideal. "[http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Proses_philosophiques_-_Les_Fleurs#IV Les fleurs]," (ca. 1860 - 1865), from O

author: Victor Hugo
text: To divinise is human, to humanise is divine.
citation: Les feuilles d'automne (1831)

author: Victor Hugo
text: Homère est un des génies qui résolvent ce beau problème de l’art, le plus beau de tous peut-être, la peinture vraie de l’humanité obtenue par le grandissement de l’homme, c’est-à-dire la génération du réel dans l’idéal.
citation: Homer is one of the men of genius who solve that fine problem of art — the finest of all, perhaps — truly to depict humanity by the enlargement of man: that is, to generate the real in the ideal. Part I, Book II, Chapter II, Section I

author: Victor Hugo
text: Que l'avenir soit un orient au lieu d'être un couchant, c'est la consolation de l'homme.
citation: It is man's consolation that the future is to be a sunrise instead of a sunset. Part I, Book II, Chapter II, Section V

author: Victor Hugo
text: La musique...est la vapeur de l’art. Elle est à la poésie ce que la rêverie est à la pensée, ce que le fluide est au liquide, ce que l’océan des nuées est à l’océan des ondes.
citation: Music...is the vapour of art. It is to poetry what revery is to thought, what the fluid is to the liquid, what the ocean of clouds is to the ocean of waves. Part I, Book II, Chapter IV

author: Victor Hugo
text: Ce qu’on ne peut dire et ce qu’on ne peut taire, la musique l’exprime.
citation: Music expresses that which cannot be said and on which it is impossible to be silent. Part I, Book II, Chapter IV

author: Victor Hugo
text: Mettre tout en équilibre, c'est bien; mettre tout en harmonie, c'est mieux.
citation: To put everything in balance is good, to put everything in harmony is better. Quatre-vingt-treize (Ninety-Three) (1874), [http://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Quatre-vingt-treize_-_III%2C_7#V_LE_CACHOT Book VII, Chapter V]

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Her reverence for the divine, her generosity, her inability not only to do wrong but even to conceive of doing it. And the simple way she lived—not in the least like the rich. (Hays translation)

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called [Eupatridas Gk.], i.e. nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void of natural affection.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not to display anger or other emotions. To be free of passion and yet full of love. (Hays translation)

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Self-control and resistance to distractions. Optimism in adversity—especially illness. (Hays translation)

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He was a man who looked at what ought to be done, not to the reputation which is got by a man's acts.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatever this is that I am, it is flesh and a little spirit and an intelligence. (Hays translation)
citation: This that I am, whatever it be, is mere flesh and a little breathe and the ruling Reason (Haines translation) This Being of mine, whatever it really is, consists of a little flesh, a little breath, and the part which governs. A little flesh

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is divine is full of Providence. Even chance is not divorced from nature, from the inweaving and enfolding of things governed by Providence. Everything proceeds from it. (Hays translation)
citation: All that is from the gods is full of Providence. II, 3

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is a limit to the time assigned you, and if you don't use it to free yourself it will be gone and never return. (Hays translation)
citation: II, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Concentrate every minute like a Roman—like a man—on doing what's in front of you with precise and genuine seriousness, tenderly, willingly, with justice. And on freeing yourself from all other distractions. (Hays translation)
citation: II, 5

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: You see how few things you have to do to live a satisfying and reverent life? If you can manage this, that's all even the gods can ask of you. (Hays translation)
citation: Thou seest how few be the things, the which if a man has at his command his life flows gently on and is divine. II, 5

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around.
citation: II, 7

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This thou must always bear in mind, what is the nature of the whole...
citation: Τούτων ἀεὶ μεμνῆσθαι, τίς ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις II, 9

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think. (Hays translation)
citation: II, 11

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Yet living and dying, honour and dishonour, pain and pleasure, riches and poverty, and so forth are equally the lot of good men and bad. Things like these neither elevate nor degrade; and therefore they are no more good than they are evil.
citation: II, 11

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The longest-lived and the shortest-lived man, when they come to die, lose one and the same thing.
citation: II, 14

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No state sorrier than that of the man who keeps up a continual round, and pries into "the secrets of the nether world," as saith the poet, and is curious in conjecture of what is in his neighbour's heart.
citation: II, 13

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Though thou be destined to live three thousand years and as many myriads besides, yet remember that no man loseth other life than that which he liveth, nor liveth other than that which he loseth.
citation: II, 14

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As for life, it is a battle and a sojourning in a strange land; but the fame that comes after is oblivion.
citation: II, 17

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Waste not the remnant of thy life in those imaginations touching other folk, whereby thou contributest not to the common weal.
citation: III, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The lot assigned to every man is suited to him, and suits him to itself.
citation: III, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: For we carry our fate with us — and it carries us. (Hays translation)
citation: III, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be not unwilling in what thou doest, neither selfish nor unadvised nor obstinate; let not over-refinement deck out thy thought; be not wordy nor a busybody.
citation: III, 5

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A man should be upright, not kept upright.
citation: III, 5

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Choose what's best.—Best is what benefits me. (Hays translation)
citation: III, 6

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Never esteem anything as of advantage to you that will make you break your word or lose your self-respect.
citation: III, 7

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Respect the faculty that forms thy judgments.
citation: III, 9

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that man lives only in the present, in this fleeting instant; all the rest of his life is either past and gone, or not yet revealed. Short, therefore, is man's life, and narrow is the corner of the earth wherein he dwells.
citation: III, 10

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Each of us lives only now, this brief instant. (Hays translation)
citation: III, 10

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The span we live is small—small as the corner of the earth in which we live it. Small as even the greatest renown, passed from mouth to mouth by short-lived stick figures, ignorant alike of themselves and those long dead. (Hays translation)
citation: III, 10

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nothing has such power to broaden the mind as the ability to investigate systematically and truly all that comes under thy observation in life.
citation: III, 11

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nothing earthly succeeds by ignoring heaven, nothing heavenly by ignoring the earth. (Hays translation)
citation: III, 14

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The ruling power within, when it is in its natural state, is so related to outer circumstances that it easily changes to accord with what can be done and what is given it to do.
citation: IV, 1

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let no act be done at haphazard, nor otherwise than according to the finished rules that govern its kind.
citation: IV, 2

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: By a tranquil mind I mean nothing else than a mind well ordered.
citation: IV, 3

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Think on this doctrine,—that reasoning beings were created for one another's sake; that to be patient is a branch of justice, and that men sin without intending it.
citation: IV, 3

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The abyss of endless time that swallows it all. The emptiness of all those applauding hands. The people who praise us—how capricious they are, how arbitrary. And the tiny region in which it all takes place. (Hays translation)
citation: IV, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be straightforward. Look at things like a man, like a human being, like a citizen, like a mortal. (Hays translation)
citation: IV, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Disturbance comes only from within—from our own perceptions. (Hays translation)
citation: IV, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The world is nothing but change. Our life is only perception.” (Hays translation)
citation: IV, 4

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nothing can come out of nothing, any more than a thing can go back to nothing.
citation: IV, 4

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Kaffirs are as a rule uncivilised—the convicts even more so. They are troublesome, very dirty and live almost like animals.
citation: "My Experience in Gaol", Indian Opinion (7 March 1908). Also: Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, op cit., Vol. 8, p. 199.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: One of the objects of a newspaper is to understand popular feeling and to give expression to it; another is to arouse among the people certain desirable sentiments; and the third is fearlessly to expose popular defects.
citation: Sect. 1

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: We who seek justice will have to do justice to others.
citation: Sect. 1

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: The only real, dignified, human doctrine is the greatest good of all, and this can only be achieved by uttermost self-sacrifice.
citation: Adapted from Hind Swaraj, 1909, Chapter 17: Summary, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 10, pp. 83–84.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: We but mirror the world. All the tendencies present in the outer world are to be found in the world of our body. If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change.
citation: From an article on dealing with snake bites, published in Indian Opinion dated [https://archive.org/details/HindSwaraj.IndianOpinion.1.vol11/page/n517/mode/1up?view=theater August 9th, 1913], in the Gujarti language edition, English transla

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Victory attained by violence is tantamount to a defeat, for it is momentary.
citation: Satyagraha Leaflet No. 13 (3 May 1919)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: In matters of conscience, the law of majority has no place.
citation: Young India (4 August 1920)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: When there is only a choice between cowardice and violence, I would advise violence… I would rather have India resort to arms in order to defend her honour than to remain a helpless witness to her own dishonour.
citation: Young India, 11 August 1920, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 21, p. 133.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Cowardice is impotence worse than violence. The coward desires revenge but being afraid to die, he looks to others… to do the work of defense for him.
citation: Young India, 11 August 1920, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 21, p. 133.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Complete civil disobedience is a state of peaceful revolution, a refusal to obey every single state-made law.
citation: As quoted in Mahatma: Life of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1920-1929), D.G. Tendulkar, Vol. 2, (1920-1929), 2nd edition, Publications Division (1960), p 52

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: I have learnt through bitter experience the one supreme lesson to conserve my anger, and as heat conserved is transmuted into energy, even so our anger controlled can be transmuted into a power which can move the world.
citation: Young India (15 September 1920), reprinted in Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 21 (electronic edition), p. 252.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: There are many causes that I am prepared to die for but no causes that I am prepared to kill for.
citation: Young India, 15 November 1920, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 22, p. 169.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: If India adopted the doctrine of love as an active part of her religion and introduced it in her politics. Swaraj would descend upon India from heaven. But I am painfully aware that that event is far off as yet.
citation: "A Word of Explanation" in Young India (January 1921)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: It has always been easier to destroy than to create.
citation: Young India, 8 September 1921, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 25, p. 224.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: I claim that in losing the spinning wheel we lost our left lung. We are, therefore, suffering from galloping consumption. The restoration of the wheel arrests the progress of the fell disease.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=6XRDAAAAYAAJ&q=galloping The Great Sentinel] in Young India 13 October 1921

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: There is no such thing as slow freedom. Freedom is like a birth. Till we are fully free we are slaves.
citation: Young India (15 December 1921)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: There is a higher court than courts of justice and that is the court of conscience. It supersedes all other courts.
citation: Young India (15 December 1921)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: I hold the opinion firmly that Civil Disobedience is the purest type of constitutional agitation. Of course, it becomes degrading and despicable if its civil, i.e. non-violent character is a mere camouflage.
citation: Young India (15 December 1921)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: A man is but the product of his thoughts. What he thinks, he becomes.
citation: In Ethical Religion, (Madras: S. Ganesan, 1922), [http://hdl.handle.net/2027/mdp.39015002732066?urlappend=%3Bseq=66 p. 62], [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044018862300&q1=%22A+man+is+but+the+product+of%22&seq=128 Scan from Ha

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Any action that is dictated by fear or by coercion of any kind ceases to be moral.
citation: Ethical Religion, S. Ganesan, Madras (1922) p. 8

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: No action which is not voluntary can be called moral.
citation: Ethical Religion, S. Ganesan, Madras (1922) p. 8

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Satan's successes are the greatest when he appears with the name of God on his lips.
citation: "The Inwardness of Non-Co-operation". Quoted in Freedom's Battle: Being a Comprehensive Collection of Writings and Speeches (1922), [https://books.google.com/books?id=ZRXCAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA144 p. 144].

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: The only tyrant I accept in this world is the "still small voice" within me. And even though I have to face the prospect of being a minority of one, I humbly believe I have the courage to be in such a hopeless minority.
citation: In Young India (2 March 1922). Quoted in The Essential Gandhi: An Anthology of His Writings on His Life, Work, and Ideas edited by Louis Fischer (2002), [http://books.google.com/books?id=gz6l-vCVgxQC&lpg=PP1&pg=PA160#v=onepage&q&f=false p.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Under democracy individual liberty of opinion and action is jealously guarded.
citation: Young India (2 March 1922)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: If one has no affection for a person or a system, one should feel free to give the fullest expression to his disaffection so long as he does not contemplate, promote, or incite violence.
citation: Statement during his trial for "exciting disaffection toward His Majesty's Government as established by law in India" (18 March 1922) {{fix cite}}

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Nonviolence is the first article of my faith. It is also the last article of my creed.
citation: Opening words of his defense speech at his trial Young India (23 March 1922)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Non-cooperation with evil is as much a duty as is cooperation with good.
citation: [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015027778375;view=1up;seq=43 Written statement] in trial for sedition, March 1922

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Always believe in your dreams, because if you don't, you'll still have hope.
citation: Young India (23 March 1924)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Man becomes great exactly in the degree in which he works for the welfare of his fellow-men. The best way to find yourself is to lose yourself in the service of others.
citation: Young India, 5 March 1925, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 31, p. 105.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: One of the objects of a newspaper is to understand popular feeling and to give expression to it; another is to arouse among the people certain desirable sentiments; and the third is fearlessly to expose popular defects.
citation: Young India, 2 July 1925, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 27, p. 326.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Seven social sins: politics without principles , wealth without work, pleasure without conscience, knowledge without character, commerce without morality, science without humanity, and worship without sacrifice.
citation: A list closing an article in Young India (22 October 1925); Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi [http://www.gandhiserve.org/cwmg/VOL033.PDF Vol. 33 (PDF) p. 135] Variant: The seven blunders that human society commits and cause all the violenc

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Politics without principle, wealth without work, pleasure without conscience, knowledge without character, commerce without morality, science without humanity, and worship without sacrifice — are the seven social sins.
citation: Originally published in Young India, 22 October 1925, in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Vol. 33, p. 135.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Disobedience is a right that belongs to every human being, and it becomes a sacred duty when it springs from civility.
citation: Young India (4 January 1926)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Our sages have taught us to learn one thing; `As in the Self, so in the Universe.' It is not possible to scan the universe as it is to scan the self. Know the self and you know the universe.
citation: Young India (8 April 1926)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Now when we talk of brotherhood of men, we stop there and feel that all other life is there for man to exploit for his own purposes. But Hinduism excludes all exploitation.
citation: Young India (26 December 1926)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: I do regard Islam to be a religion of peace in the same sense as Christianity, Buddhism and Hinduism are.
citation: Young India, January 20, 1927, in [https://archive.org/details/HindSwaraj-CWMG-032/page/588/mode/2up Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi], vol. 32, p. 588.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: An error does not become truth by reason of multiplied propagation, nor does truth become error because nobody sees it. Truth stands, even if there be no public support. It is self sustained.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: I'm a lover of my own liberty, and so I would do nothing to restrict yours. I simply want to please my own conscience, which is God.
citation: Young India (21 January 1927)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: For one man cannot do right in one department of life whilst he is occupied in doing wrong in any other department. Life is one indivisible whole.
citation: Young India (27 January 1927)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: My ambition is much higher than independence. Through the deliverance of India, I seek to deliver the so-called weaker races of the Earth from the crushing heels of Western exploitation in which England is the greatest partner.
citation: Young India (12 January 1928). Quoted in The Essential Writings of Gandhi, edited by Judith Brown. Oxford University Press, 2008, (p. 153).

author: Jane Austen
text: Here I am once more in this scene of dissipation and vice, and I begin already to find my morals corrupted.
citation: Letter (August 1796) on arriving in London [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: What dreadful hot weather we have! It keeps one in a continual state of inelegance.
citation: Letter (1796-09-18) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: Next week I shall begin my operations on my hat, on which you know my principal hopes of happiness depend.
citation: Letter (1798-10-27) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1798-12-24) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: You deserve a longer letter than this; but it is my unhappy fate seldom to treat people so well as they deserve.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1798-12-24) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I had a very pleasant evening, however, though you will probably find out that there was no particular reason for it; but I do not think it worth while to wait for enjoyment until there is some real opportunity for it.
citation: Letter (1799-01-21) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: She would tell you herself that she has a very dreadful cold in her head at present; but I have not much compassion for colds in the head without fever or sore throat.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1799-01-21) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I am rather impatient to know the fate of my best gown.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1799-05-17) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I cannot help thinking that it is more natural to have flowers grow out of the head than fruit.
