citation: Letter to Cassandra (1799-06-11) on decorating her hat [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I can recollect nothing more to say at present; perhaps breakfast may assist my ideas. I was deceived — my breakfast supplied only two ideas — that the rolls were good and the butter bad.
citation: Letter (1799-06-19) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I believe I drank too much wine last night at Hurstbourne; I know not how else to account for the shaking of my hand today. You will kindly make allowance therefore for any indistinctness of writing, by attributing it to this venial error.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1800-11-20) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: The General has got the gout, and Mrs. Maitland the jaundice. Miss Debary, Susan, and Sally, all in black, but without any stature, made their appearance, and I was as civil to them as their bad breath would allow me.
citation: Letter (1800-11-20) on people she met at a ball [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: We have been exceedingly busy ever since you went away. In the first place we have had to rejoice two or three times everyday at your having such very delightful weather for the whole of your journey...
citation: Letter (1800-11-25) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I have now attained the true art of letter-writing, which we are always told, is to express on paper exactly what one would say to the same person by word of mouth.
citation: Letter (1801-01-03) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: Another stupid party last night; perhaps if larger they might be less intolerable, but here there were only just enough to make one card-table, with six people to look on and talk nonsense to each other.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1801-05-12) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: We are to have a tiny party here tonight. I hate tiny parties, they force one into constant exertion.
citation: Letter (1801-05-21) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: You will have a great deal of unreserved discourse with Mrs. K., I dare say, upon this subject, as well as upon many other of our family matters. Abuse everybody but me.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1807-01-07) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: You know how interesting the purchase of a sponge-cake is to me.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1808-06-15) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: The pleasures of friendship, of unreserved conversation, of similarity of taste and opinions will make good amends for orange wine.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1808-06-20) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I am sorry to tell you that I am getting very extravagant, and spending all my money, and, what is worse for you, I have been spending yours too.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1811-04-18) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I give you joy of our new nephew, and hope if he ever comes to be hanged it will not be till we are too old to care about it.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1811-04-25) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: How horrible it is to have so many people killed! And what a blessing that one cares for none of them!
citation: Letter (1811-05-31) referring to the Peninsular War [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I will not say that your mulberry-trees are dead, but I am afraid they are not alive.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1811-05-31) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: Mr. Digweed has used us basely. Handsome is as handsome does; he is therefore a very ill-looking man.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1813-01-24) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: Let me know when you begin the new tea, and the new white wine. My present elegancies have not yet made me indifferent to such matters. I am still a cat if I see a mouse.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1813-09-23) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: He seems a very harmless sort of young man, nothing to like or dislike in him — goes out shooting or hunting with the two others all the morning, and plays at whist and makes queer faces in the evening.
citation: Letter to Cassandra (1813-09-23) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: By the bye, as I must leave off being young, I find many douceurs in being a sort of chaperon, for I am put on the sofa near the fire and can drink as much wine as I like.
citation: Letter (1813-11-06) on ageing [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I cannot help hoping that many will feel themselves obliged to buy it. I shall not mind imagining it a disagreeable duty to them, so as they do it.
citation: Letter (1813-11-06) on the reprint of Sense and Sensibility [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: I would recommend to her and Mr. D. the simple regimen of separate rooms.
citation: Letter (1817-02-20) on Mrs. Deedes having an eighteenth child [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: Single women have a dreadful propensity for being poor, which is one very strong argument in favour of matrimony.
citation: Letter to Fanny Knight (1817-03-13) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

author: Jane Austen
text: There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends. I have no notion of loving people by halves, it is not my nature.
citation: Northanger Abbey

author: Isaac Newton
text: Amicus Plato — amicus Aristoteles — magis amica veritas
citation: Plato is my friend — Aristotle is my friend — but my greatest friend is truth. These are notes in Latin that Newton wrote to himself that he titled: Quaestiones Quaedam Philosophicae [Certain Philosophical Questions] (c. 1664) Variant trans

author: Isaac Newton
text: If I have seen further it is by standing on ye sholders of Giants.
citation: Letter to Robert Hooke (15 February 1676) <small> [dated as 5 February 1675 using the Julian calendar with March 25th rather than January 1st as New Years Day, equivalent to 15 February 1676 by Gregorian reckonings.] A facsimile of the orig

author: Isaac Newton
text: Bullialdus wrote that all force respecting the Sun as its center & depending on matter must be reciprocally in a duplicate ratio of the distance from the center.
citation: Letter to Edmund Halley (June 20, 1686) quoted in I. Bernard Cohen and George E. Smith, ed.s, The Cambridge Companion to Newton (2002) p. 204

author: Isaac Newton
text: I keep the subject constantly before me, and wait 'till the first dawnings open slowly, by little and little, into a full and clear light.
citation: Reply upon being asked how he made his discoveries, as quoted in "[http://books.google.es/books?id=rYhDAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA3241&dq=I+keep+the+subject+constantly+before+me+and+wait+till+the+first+dawnings+open+little+by+little+into+the+full+light.

author: Isaac Newton
text: I have studied these things — you have not.
citation: Reported as Newton's response, whenever Edmond Halley would say anything disrespectful of religion, by Sir David Brewster in The Life of Sir Isaac Newton (1831). This has often been quoted in recent years as having been a statement specific

author: Isaac Newton
text: We account the Scriptures of God to be the most sublime philosophy. I find more sure remarks of authenticity in the Bible than in any profane history whatever.
citation: Anecdote reported by Dr. Robert Smith, late Master of Trinity College, to his student Richard Watson, as something that Newton expressed when he was writing his Commentary On Daniel. In Watson's Apology for the Bible. London 8vo. (1806), p.

author: Isaac Newton
text: Oh, Diamond! Diamond! thou little knowest what mischief thou hast done!
citation: This is from an anecdote found in [http://www.gutenberg.org/files/15331/15331-h/15331-h.htm St. Nicholas magazine, Vol. 5, No. 4, (February 1878)] :

author: Isaac Newton
text: Truth is ever to be found in simplicity, and not in the multiplicity and confusion of things.
citation: Cited in Rules for methodizing the Apocalypse, Rule 9, from a manuscript published in The Religion of Isaac Newton (1974) by Frank E. Manuel, p. 120, as quoted in Socinianism And Arminianism : Antitrinitarians, Calvinists, And Cultural Exch

author: Isaac Newton
text: God created everything by number, weight and measure.
citation: As quoted in Symmetry in Plants (1998) by Roger V. Jean and Denis Barabé, p. xxxvii, a translation of a Latin phrase he wrote in a student's notebook, elsewhere given as Numero pondere et mensura Deus omnia condidit. This is similar to Lati

author: Isaac Newton
text: Whence are you certain that ye Ancient of Days is Christ? Does Christ anywhere sit upon ye Throne?
citation: He wrote in discussing with John Locke the passage of Daniel 7:9. The Correspondence of Isaac Newton, Vol. III, Letter 362. Cited in The Watchtower magazine, 1977, 4/15, article: Isaac Newton’s Search for God.

author: Isaac Newton
text: One [method] is by a Watch to keep time exactly. But, by reason of the motion of the Ship, the Variation of Heat and Cold, Wet and Dry, and the Difference of Gravity in different Latitudes, such a watch hath not yet been made.
citation: Written in remarks to the 1714 Longitude committee; quoted in Longitude (1995) by Dava Sobel, p. 52 (i998 edition) <small>{{ISBN|1-85702-571-7}}</small>)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Instruction does much, but encouragement everything.
citation: Letter to A. F. Oeser (9 November 1768), Early and miscellaneous letters of J. W. Goethe, including letters to his mother. With notes and a short biography (1884) Alternative translation: "Correction does much, but encouragement does more."

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Wo viel Licht ist, ist starker Schatten.
citation: There is strong shadow where there is much light. Götz von Berlichingen, Act I (1773)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: I hold to faith in the divine love — which, so many years ago for a brief moment in a little corner of the earth, walked about as a man bearing the name of Jesus Christ — as the foundation on which alone my happiness rests.
citation: (1773), translated by Albert Schweizer in [http://archive.is/tOo5z Goethe: Five Studies] (1961), Beacon Press, p. 53

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Getting along with women, Knocking around with men, Having more credit than money, Thus one goes through the world.
citation: Claudine von Villa Bella (1776)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: When young, one is confident to be able to build palaces for mankind, but when the time comes one has one's hands full just to be able to remove their trash.
citation: Letter to Johann Kaspar Lavatar (6 March 1780)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Noble be man, Helpful and good! For that alone Sets hims apart From every other creature On earth.
citation: Das Göttliche (The Divine) (1783)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: As great, everlasting, Adamantine laws Dictate, we must all Complete the cycles Of our existence.
citation: Das Göttliche (The Divine) (1783)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Only mankind Can do the impossible: He can distinguish, He chooses and judges, He can give permanence To the moment.
citation: Das Göttliche (The Divine) (1783)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Let the noble man Be generous and good, Tirelessly achieving What is just and useful: Let him be a model For those beings whom he surmises.
citation: Das Göttliche (The Divine) (1783)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: A noble person attracts noble people, and knows how to hold on to them.
citation: Torquato Tasso, Act I, sc. i (1790)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: A talent is formed in stillness, a character in the world's torrent.
citation: Torquato Tasso, Act I, sc. ii (1790)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Untersuchen was ist, und nicht was behagt
citation: Investigate what is, and not what pleases. Der Versuch als Vermittler von Objekt und Subjekt (The Attempt as Mediator of Object and Subject) (1792)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: Die Liebe herrscht nicht, aber sie bildet; und das ist mehr!
citation: Love does not dominate, it cultivates. And that is more. Das Märchen (1795), as translated by Hermann J. Weigand in Wisdom and Experience (1949); also translated elsewhere as The Fairy-Tale, The Green Snake and the Beautiful Lily, and simpl

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: We can't form our children on our own concepts; we must take them and love them as God gives them to us.
citation: Hermann und Dorothea (1797)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: The spirits that I summoned up I now can't rid myself of.
citation: Der Zauberlehrling (The Sorcerer's Apprentice) (1797)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: One of the most striking signs of the decay of art is the intermixing of different genres.
citation: Propylaea (1798) Introduction

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: The true, prescriptive artist strives after artistic truth; the lawless artist, following blind instinct, after an appearance of naturalness. The one leads to the highest peaks of art, the other to its lowest depths.
citation: Propylaea (1798) Introduction

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: In limitations he first shows himself the master, And the law can only bring us freedom.
citation: Was Wir Bringen (1802)

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
text: One never goes so far as when one doesn't know where one is going.
citation: Letter to Carl Friedrich Zelter (3 December 1812)

author: Stephen Hawking
text: I am discounting reports of UFOs. Why would they appear only to cranks and weirdos?
citation: As quoted in a TED talk, "[http://www.ted.com/talks/view/id/242 Asking Big Questions about the Universe]"

author: Stephen Hawking
text: My expectations were reduced to zero when I was 21. Everything since then has been a bonus.
citation: As quoted in "The Science of Second-Guessing", The New York Times (12 December 2004) Unsourced variant: "When one's expectations are reduced to zero, one really appreciates everything one does have."

author: Stephen Hawking
text: The life we have on Earth must have spontaneously generated itself. It must therefore be possible for life to generate spontaneously elsewhere in the universe.
citation: From an appearance in the Discovery Channel program Alien Planet (14 May 2005)

author: Stephen Hawking
text: Evolution has ensured that our brains just aren't equipped to visualise 11 dimensions directly. However, from a purely mathematical point of view it's just as easy to think in 11 dimensions, as it is to think in three or four.
citation: As quoted in [http://books.guardian.co.uk/departments/scienceandnature/story/0,6000,1579384,00.html "Return of the time lord" in The Guardian] (27 September 2005)

author: Stephen Hawking
text: I think that it's important for scientists to explain their work, particularly in cosmology. This now answers many questions once asked of religion.
citation: As quoted in "Return of the time lord" in The Guardian (27 September 2005)

author: Stephen Hawking
text: It is a waste of time to be angry about my disability. One has to get on with life and I haven't done badly. People won't have time for you if you are always angry or complaining.
citation: As quoted in "Return of the time lord" in The Guardian (27 September 2005)

author: Stephen Hawking
text: Equations are just the boring part of mathematics. I attempt to see things in terms of geometry.
citation: As quoted in Stephen Hawking: A Biography (2005) by Kristine Larsen, p. 43

author: Stephen Hawking
text: The victim should have the right to end his life, if he wants. But I think it would be a great mistake. However bad life may seem, there is always something you can do, and succeed at. While there's life, there is hope.
citation: On voluntary euthanasia as quoted in [http://english.people.com.cn/200606/14/eng20060614_273839.html People's Daily Online (14 June 2006)]

citation: Interview on Israeli television, as quoted in [http://www.startrek.com/startrek/view/news/article/37695.html "Happy 65th Birthday to Prof. Stephen Hawking!" at StarTrek.com (8 January 2007)]

author: Stephen Hawking
text: I'm not religious in the normal sense. I believe the universe is governed by the laws of science. The laws may have been decreed by God, but God does not intervene to break the laws.

text: The zero-G part was wonderful and the higher-G part was no problem. I could have gone on and on. Space, here I come!

author: Stephen Hawking

author: Stephen Hawking
text: The whole history of science has been the gradual realization that events do not happen in an arbitrary manner, but that they reflect a certain underlying order, which may or may not be divinely inspired.

text: One could say: "The boundary condition of the universe is that it has no boundary." The universe would be completely self-contained and not affected by anything outside itself. It would neither be created nor destroyed. It would just BE.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: If a person is stupid, we excuse him by saying that he cannot help it; but if we attempted to excuse in precisely the same way the person who is bad, we should be laughed at.
citation: E. Payne, trans., vol. 2, p. 230

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: All religions promise a reward for excellences of the will or heart, but none for excellences of the head or understanding.
citation: E. Payne, trans., vol. 2, p. 230

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Philosophy … is a science, and as such has no articles of faith; accordingly, in it nothing can be assumed as existing except what is either positively given empirically, or demonstrated through indubitable conclusions.
citation: Vol I

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Philosophy of religion … really amounts to … philosophizing on certain favorite assumptions that are not confirmed at all.
citation: E. Payne, trans. (1974) Vol. 1, p. 143

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: No doubt, when modesty was made a virtue, it was a very advantageous thing for the fools, for everybody is expected to speak of himself as if he were one.
citation: Vol. 1, Ch. 3, Section 2: Pride

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Rascals are always sociable — more’s the pity! and the chief sign that a man has any nobility in his character is the little pleasure he takes in others’ company.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: National character is only another name for the particular form which the littleness, perversity and baseness of mankind take in every country. Every nation mocks at other nations, and all are right.
citation: Variant translation: Every nation criticizes every other one — and they are all correct. As quoted by Wolfgang Pauli in a letter to Abraham Pais (17 August 1950) published in The Genius of Science (2000) by Abraham Pais, p. 242

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Im allgemeinen freilich haben die Weisen aller Zeiten immer dasselbe gesagt, und die Toren, d.h. die unermessliche Majorität aller Zeiten, haben immer dasselbe, nämlich das Gegenteil getan; und so wird es denn auch ferner bleiben.
citation: In general admittedly the Wise of all times have always said the same thing, and the fools, that is to say the vast majority of all times, have always done the same thing, i.e. the opposite; and so it will remain in the future.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Die Gegenwart eines Gedankens ist wie die Gegenwart einer Geliebten.
citation: The presence of a thought is like the presence of a lover.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Die Erinnerung wirkt wie das Sammlungsglas in der Camera obscura: Sie zieht alles zusammen und bringt dadurch ein viel schöneres Bild hervor, als sein Original ist.
citation: Memory works like the collection glass in the Camera obscura: it gathers everything together and therewith produces a far more beautiful picture than was present originally.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Alles, alles kann einer vergessen, nur nicht sich selbst, sein eigenes Wesen.
citation: One can forget everything, everything, only not oneself, one's own being.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Zu unserer Besserung bedürfen wir eines Spiegels.
citation: For our improvement we need a mirror.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Meistens belehrt uns erst der Verlust über den Wert der Dinge.
citation: Mostly it is loss which teaches us about the worth of things.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Je weniger einer, in Folge objektiver oder subjektiver Bedingungen, nötig hat, mit den Menschen in Berührung zu kommen, desto besser ist er daran.
citation: The less one, as a result of objective or subjective conditions, has to come into contact with people, the better off one is for it.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Was nun andrerseits die Menschen gesellig macht, ist ihre Unfähigkeit, die Einsamkeit und in dieser sich selbst zu ertragen.
citation: What now on the other hand makes people sociable is their incapacity to endure solitude and thus themselves.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: A great affliction of all Philistines is that idealities afford them no entertainment, but to escape from boredom they are always in need of realities.
citation: E. Payne, trans. (1974) Vol. 1, p. 345

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: It is difficult, if not impossible, to define the limit of our reasonable desires in respect of possessions.
citation: E. Payne, trans. (1974) Vol. 1, p. 346

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Wealth is like sea-water; the more we drink, the thirstier we become.
citation: E. Payne, trans. (1974) Vol. 1, p. 347

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: For the purpose of acquiring gain, everything else is pushed aside or thrown overboard, for example, as is philosophy by the professors of philosophy.
citation: E. Payne, trans. (1974) Vol. 1, p. 347

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Means at our disposal should be regarded as a bulwark against the many evils and misfortunes that can occur. We should not regard such wealth as a permission or even an obligation to procure for ourselves the pleasures of the world.
citation: E. Payne, trans. (1974) Vol. 1, p. 348

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: The fundament upon which all our knowledge and learning rests is the inexplicable.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: All the cruelty and torment of which the world is full is in fact merely the necessary result of the totality of the forms under which the will to live is objectified.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: The discovery of truth is prevented more effectively, not by the false appearance things present and which mislead into error, not directly by weakness of the reasoning powers, but by preconceived opinion, by prejudice.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: If you feel irritated by the absurd remarks of two people whose conversation you happen to overhear, you should imagine that you are listening to a dialogue of two fools in a comedy.
citation: T. B. Saunders, trans., § 38

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Newspapers are the second hand of history. This hand, however, is usually not only of inferior metal to the other hands, it also seldom works properly.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Great minds are related to the brief span of time during which they live as great buildings are to a little square in which they stand: you cannot see them in all their magnitude because you are standing too close to them.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Patriotism, when it wants to make itself felt in the domain of learning, is a dirty fellow who should be thrown out of doors.

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Je veux qu'on me voit en ma façon simple, naturelle, et ordinaire, sans étude et artifice; car c'est moi que je peins...Je suis moi-même la matière de mon livre.
citation: I want to be seen here in my simple, natural, ordinary fashion, without straining or artifice; for it is myself that I portray...I am myself the matter of my book. To the Reader (tr. Donald M. Frame, 1957)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Certes, c'est un subject merveilleusement vain, divers, et ondoyant, que l'homme. Il est malaisé d'y fonder jugement constant et uniforme.
citation: Truly man is a marvellously vain, diverse, and undulating object. It is hard to found any constant and uniform judgement on him. Ch. 1. That Men by various Ways arrive at the same End (tr. Donald M. Frame) Man in sooth is a marvellous, vain

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: All passions that suffer themselves to be relished and digested are but moderate.
citation: Ch. 2. Of Sorrow (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: A strong memory is commonly coupled with infirm judgment.
citation: Ch. 9. Of Liars (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: It is not without good reason said, that he who has not a good memory should never take upon him the trade of lying.
citation: Ch. 9. Of Liars (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: I live from day to day, and content myself with having enough to meet my present and ordinary needs; for the extraordinary, all the provision in the world could not suffice.
citation: Ch. 14

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Every rich man is avaricious, in my opinion.
citation: Ch. 14

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Things are not so painful and difficult of themselves, but our weakness or cowardice makes them so.
citation: Ch. 14 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: We are, I know not how, double in ourselves, which is the cause that what we believe we do not believe, and cannot disengage ourselves from what we condemn.
citation: Ch. 16. Of Glory (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: C'est ce de quoi j'ai le plus de peur que la peur.
citation: The thing I fear most is fear. Ch. 18. That Men are not to judge of our Happiness till after Death (tr. Donald M. Frame)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: He who should teach men to die would at the same time teach them to live.
citation: Ch. 18. That Men are not to judge of our Happiness till after Death (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Whatever can be done another day can be done today.
citation: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Donald M. Frame)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Je veux que la mort me trouve plantant mes choux.
citation: I want death to find me planting my cabbages. Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Donald M. Frame)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: All the opinions of the world agree in this, that pleasure is our end.
citation: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: He who would teach men to die would teach them to live.
citation: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Donald M. Frame)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: The day of your birth is one day’s advance towards the grave.
citation: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877) <small>Cf. Dávid Baróti Szabó, Nem kímíl meg senkit halál (wr. 1786; ed. 1914)</small>

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Live as long as you please, you will strike nothing off the time you will have to spend dead.
citation: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: All of the days go toward death and the last one arrives there.
citation: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: The laws of conscience, which we pretend to be derived from nature, proceed from custom.
citation: Ch. 22. Of Custom (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: We must not attach knowledge to the mind, we have to incorporate it there.
citation: Ch. 25

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Every other knowledge is harmful to him who does not have knowledge of goodness.
citation: Ch. 25

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Un peu de chaque chose, et rien du tout, a la française.
citation: A little of all things, but nothing of everything, after the French manner. Chapter 26 . Of the Education of Children

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Je ne dis les autres, sinon pour d'autant plus me dire.
citation: I do not speak the minds of others except to speak my own mind better. Ch. 26. On the Education of Children Variant: I quote others only in order the better to express myself.

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Since I would rather make of him an able man than a learned man, I would also urge that care be taken to choose a guide with a well-made rather than a well-filled head.
citation: Ch. 26. On the Education of Children

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Accustom him to every thing, that he may not be a Sir Paris, a carpet-knight, but a sinewy, hardy, and vigorous young man.
citation: Ch. 26 . Of the Education of Children (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Combien de choses nous servoyent hier d’articles de foy, qui nous sont fables aujourd’huy?
citation: How many things served us yesterday for articles of faith, which today are fables for us? Ch. 27. Of Friendship

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: We were halves throughout, and to that degree that, methinks, by outliving him I defraud him of his part.
citation: Ch. 27. Of Friendship (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Si on me presse de dire pourquoi je l'aimais, je sens que cela ne se peut exprimer qu'en répondant: parce que c'était lui; parce que c'était moi.
citation: If you press me to say why I loved him, I can say no more than it was because he was he, and I was I. Variants: If a man urge me to tell wherefore I loved him, I feel it cannot be expressed but by answering: Because it was he, because it wa

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: There are some defeats more triumphant than victories.
citation: Ch. 30. Of Cannibals (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: A wise man never loses anything, if he has himself.
citation: Ch. 38. Of Solitude (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: L'homme d'entendement n'a rien perdu, s'il a soi-même.
citation: A man of understanding has lost nothing, if he has himself. Ch. 39

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: La plus grande chose du monde, c'est de savoir être à soi.
citation: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself. Ch. 39

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Even opinion is of force enough to make itself to be espoused at the expense of life.
citation: Book I, Ch. 40. Of Good and Evil (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: He who does not give himself leisure to be thirsty cannot take pleasure in drinking.
citation: Ch. 42

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Les rois et les philosophes fientent, et les dames aussi.
citation: Kings and philosophers shit, and so do ladies. Ch. 42, English translation from Hartle, Ann (2003), Michel de Montaigne: Accidental Philosopher, Cambridge University Press.

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: There is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others.
citation: Ch. 1. Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: It is the part of cowardice, not of courage, to go and crouch in a hole under a massive tomb, to avoid the blows of fortune.
citation: Ch. 3. A Usage of the Island of Cea (tr. George B. Ives, 1925)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: C'est une épineuse entreprise, et plus qu'il ne semble, de suivre une allure si vagabonde que celle de nôtre esprit; de pénétrer les profondeurs opaques de ses replis internes; de choisir et arrêter tant de menus de ses agitations.
citation: It is a thorny undertaking, and more so than it seems, to follow a movement so wandering as that of our mind, to penetrate the opaque depths of its innermost folds, to pick out and immobilize the innumerable flutterings that agitate it. Ch.

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Virtue refuses facility for her companion ... the easy, gentle, and sloping path that guides the footsteps of a good natural disposition is not the path of true virtue. It demands a rough and thorny road.
citation: Ch. 11. Of Cruelty (tr. Donald M. Frame)

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: For my own part, I cannot without grief see so much as an innocent beast pursued and killed that has no defence, and from which we have received no offence at all.
citation: Ch. 11 (tr. Cotton, 1685)

author: Thomas Edison
text: To Monsieur Eiffel the Engineer, the brave builder of so gigantic and original a specimen of modern Engineering from one who has the greatest respect and admiration for all Engineers including the Great Engineer the Bon Dieu.
citation: When Thomas Edison visited the Eiffel Tower during the 1889 World's Fair, he signed the guestbook with this message, as quoted in The Tallest Tower by Joseph Harris, p. 95

author: Thomas Edison
text: The doctor of the future will give no medicine, but will instruct his patient in the care of the human frame, in diet and in the cause and prevention of disease.
citation: This has been reprinted many times with slight variations on the wording; it is part of a much larger quote directly from Edison published in 1903:

author: Thomas Edison
text: X-rays ... I am afraid of them. I stopped experimenting with them two years ago, when I came near to losing my eyesight and Dally, my assistant practically lost the use of both of his arms.
citation: Quoted in 'Edison Fears Hidden Perils of the X-Rays', New York World (3 Aug 1903), 1

author: Thomas Edison
text: Hell! There ain't no rules around here! We are tryin' to accomplish somep'n!
citation: Response received (after Edison spat on the floor and before he walked off) when M. A. Rosanoff joined the West Orange, New Jersey team in 1903 and humbly asked: “Mr. Edison, please tell me what laboratory rules you want me to observe.” M.

author: Thomas Edison
text: Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration.
citation: Edison claimed authorship of this statement in a 1927 letter: "it is quite true I once made the statement that genius is one percent inspiration and 99 percent perspiration, and I am still of the same opinion". {{cite journal |journal=Argus

author: Thomas Edison
text: My mind is incapable of conceiving such a thing as a soul. I may be in error, and man may have a soul; but I simply do not believe it. What a soul may be is beyond my understanding.
citation: "Do We Live Again?" an interview with Edison, as quoted in Mr. Edison's New Argument from Design" in The Illustrated London News (3 May 1924)

author: Thomas Edison
text: I believe in the existence of a Supreme Intelligence pervading the Universe.
citation: As quoted in Thomas A. Edison, Benefactor of Mankind : The Romantic Life Story of the World's Greatest Inventor (1931) by Francis Trevelyan Miller, Ch. 25 : Edison's Views on Life — His Philosophy and Religion, p. 293

author: Thomas Edison
text: We don't know a millionth of one percent about anything.
citation: As quoted in Golden Book (April 1931), according to Stevenson's Book of Quotations (Cassell 3rd edition 1938) by Burton Egbert Stevenson.

author: Thomas Edison
text: Restlessness is discontent — and discontent is the first necessity of progress. Show me a thoroughly satisfied man — and I will show you a failure.
citation: The Diary and Sundry Observations of Thomas Alva Edison (1948), p. 110

author: Thomas Edison
text: So far as the religion of the day is concerned, it is a damned fake … Religion is all bunk.
citation: As quoted in What on Earth is an Atheist! (1972) by Madalyn Murray O'Hair, p. 251

author: Thomas Edison
text: Opportunity is missed by most people because it is dressed in overalls and looks like work.
citation: As quoted in An Enemy Called Average (1990) by John L. Mason, p. 55

author: Thomas Edison
text: If we did all the things we are capable of doing, we would literally astound ourselves.
citation: As quoted in Motivating Humans : Goals, Emotions, and Personal Agency Beliefs (1992) by Martin E. Ford, p. 17

author: Thomas Edison
text: To invent, you need a good imagination and a pile of junk.
citation: As quoted in Behavior-Based Robotics (1998) by Ronald C. Arkin. p. 8

author: Thomas Edison
text: Everyone steals in commerce and industry. I've stolen a lot, myself. But I know how to steal! They don't know how to steal!
citation: As quoted in Tesla : The Modern Sorcerer (1999) by Daniel Blair Stewart, p. 411 Variant: Everyone steals in commerce and industry. I have stolen a lot myself. But at least I know how to steal.

author: Thomas Edison
text: I find out what the world needs. Then, I go ahead and invent it.
citation: As quoted in American Greats (1999) Edited by Robert A. Wilson and Stanley Marcus, p. 70

author: Thomas Edison
text: Just because something doesn't do what you planned it to do doesn't mean it's useless.
citation: As quoted in Artifacts : An Archaeologist's Year in Silicon Valley (2001) by Christine Finn. p. 90

author: Thomas Edison
text: I never did a day's work in my life, it was all fun.
citation: As quoted in Edison & Ford Quote Book (2003) edited by Edison & Ford Winter Estates

author: Thomas Edison
text: Our greatest weakness lies in giving up. The most certain way to succeed is always to try just one more time.
citation: As quoted in Edison & Ford Quote Book (2003) edited by Edison & Ford Winter Estates

author: Thomas Edison
text: I have never seen the slightest scientific proof of the religious ideas of heaven and hell, of future life for individuals, or of a personal God.
citation: As quoted in Jesus : Myth Or Reality? (2006) by Ian Curtis, p. 289

author: Thomas Edison
text: I do not believe in the God of the theologians; but that there is a Supreme Intelligence I do not doubt
citation: The Freethinker (1970), G.W. Foote & Company, Volume 90, p. 147

author: Thomas Edison
text: I owe my success to the fact that I never had a clock in my workroom. Seventy-five of us worked twenty hours every day and slept only four hours — and thrived on it.
citation: Diary entry, as quoted in Defending and Parenting Children Who Learn Differently : Lessons from Edison's Mother (2007) by Scott Teel, p. 12

author: Charles Darwin
text: Through the principle of associated habit, the same movements of the face and eyes are practised, and can, indeed, hardly be avoided, whenever we know or believe that others are blaming, or too strongly praising, our moral conduct.
citation: chapter XIII: "Self-attention — Shame — Shyness — Modesty: Blushing", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=375&itemID=F1142&viewtype=image page 347]

author: Charles Darwin
text: Even insects express anger, terror, jealousy, and love by their stridulation.
citation: chapter XIV: "Concluding Remarks and Summary", page 350

author: Charles Darwin
text: The subject may appear an insignificant one, but we shall see that it possesses some interest; and the maxim "de minimis lex non curat," does not apply to science.
citation: Introduction, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=17&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 2.] de minimis non curat lex - The law does not concern itself with trifles.

author: Charles Darwin
text: As I was led to keep in my study during many months worms in pots filled with earth, I became interested in them, and wished to learn how far they acted consciously, and how much mental power they displayed.
citation: Introduction, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=17&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 2-3.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: Earth-worms abound in England in many different stations. Their castings may be seen in extraordinary numbers on commons and chalk-downs, so as almost to cover the whole surface, where the soil is poor and the grass short and thin.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=24&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 9.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: M. Perrier found that their exposure to the dry air of a room for only a single night was fatal to them. On the other hand he kept several large worms alive for nearly four months, completely submerged in water.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=27&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image pp. 12-13].

author: Charles Darwin
text: Every morning during certain seasons of the year, the thrushes and blackbirds on all the lawns throughout the country draw out of their holes an astonishing number of worms; and this they could not do, unless they lay close to the surface.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=31&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 16.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: As it is certain that worms swallow many little stones, independently of those swallowed while excavating their burrows, it is probable that they serve, like mill-stones, to triturate their food.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=33&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 18.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: When a worm is suddenly illuminated and dashes like a rabbit into its burrow—to use the expression employed by a friend—we are at first led to look at the action as a reflex one.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=38&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 23.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: When the pots containing two worms which had remained quite indifferent to the sound of the piano, were placed on this instrument, and the note C in the bass clef was struck, both instantly retreated into their burrows.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=43&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 28.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: It may be presumed that all animals which feed on various substances possess the sense of taste, and this is certainly the case with worms.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=47&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 32.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: But some degree of intelligence appears, as we shall see in the next chapter, to be exhibited in this work,—a result which has surprised me more than anything else in regard to worms.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=50&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 35.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: With respect to the function of the calciferous glands, it is probable that they primarily serve as organs of excretion, and secondarily as an aid to digestion.
citation: Chapter 1: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=64&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 49.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: Worms seize leaves and other objects, not only to serve as food, but for plugging up the mouths of their burrows; and this is one of their strongest instincts.
citation: Chapter 2: Habits of Worms, [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=73&itemID=F1357&viewtype=image p. 58.]

author: Charles Darwin
text: I have deeply regretted that I did not proceed far enough at least to understand something of the great leading principles of mathematics, for men thus endowed seem to have an extra sense.
citation: volume I, chapter II: "Autobiography", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=64&itemID=F1452.1&viewtype=image page 46]

author: Charles Darwin
text: A man who dares to waste one hour of time has not discovered the value of life.
citation: volume I, chapter VI: "The Voyage", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=284&itemID=F1452.1&viewtype=image page 266]; letter to sister Susan Elizabeth Darwin (4 August 1836)

author: Charles Darwin
text: As for a future life, every man must judge for himself between conflicting vague probabilities.
citation: volume I, chapter VIII: "Religion", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=325&itemID=F1452.1&viewtype=image page 307]; letter to an unidentified German student (1879)

author: Charles Darwin
text: I cannot pretend to throw the least light on such abstruse problems. The mystery of the beginning of all things is insoluble by us; and I for one must be content to remain an Agnostic.
citation: volume I, chapter VIII: "Religion", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=331&itemID=F1452.1&viewtype=image page 313]

author: Charles Darwin
text: I hate a Barnacle as no man ever did before, not even a Sailor in a slow-sailing ship.
citation: volume I, chapter IX: "Life at Down", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=405&itemID=F1452.1&viewtype=image page 385]; [http://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/entry-1489 letter] to William Darwin Fox (24 October 1852) quoted in At

author: Charles Darwin
text: I am almost convinced (quite contrary to opinion I started with) that species are not (it is like confessing a murder) immutable.
citation: volume II, chapter II: "The Growth of the 'Origin of Species' — 1843-1856", [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?pageseq=39&itemID=F1452.2&viewtype=image page 23]; [http://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/letter/entry-729 letter] to J.D. Ho

author: Charles Darwin
text: The time is always ripe for the re-interpretation of theories in the light of new vision and of new facts. This is the very province of science.
citation: page 13

author: Charles Darwin
text: To my mind there are no advantages and many disadvantages in lectures compared with reading.
citation: page 47

author: Charles Darwin
text: Science consists in grouping facts so that general laws or conclusions may be drawn from them.
citation: page 70

author: Charles Darwin
text: This leads me to remark that I have almost always been treated honestly by my reviewers, passing over those without scientific knowledge as not worthy of notice.
citation: page 125

author: Charles Darwin
text: I hope that I may die before my mind fails to a sensible extent.
citation: page 136

author: Charles Darwin
text: Though the theory is worthless without the well-observed facts, the facts are useless without the frame of the theory to receive them.
citation: page 158

author: Charles Darwin
text: Animals whom we have made our slaves we do not like to consider our equals. — Do not slave holders wish to make the black man other kind? — animals with affections, imitation, fear of death, pain, sorrow for the dead. — respect.

citation: What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily?

author: Seneca the Younger
text: In hoc enim fallimur, quod mortem prospicimus: magna pars eius iam praeterit; quidquid aetatis retro est mors tenet.
citation: For we are mistaken when we look forward to death; the major portion of death has already passed. Whatever years be behind us are in death's hands.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Nusquam est qui ubique est. Vitam in peregrinatione exigentibus hoc evenit, ut multa hospitia habeant, nullas amicitias.
citation: Who is everywhere is nowhere. When a person spends all his time in foreign travel, he ends by having many acquaintances, but no friends. Line 2.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est.
citation: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor. Line 6.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Nam illa tumultu gaudens non est industria sed exagitatae mentis concursatio.
citation: For love of bustle is not industry – it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind. Line 5.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Nulli potest secura vita contingere qui de producenda nimis cogitat.
citation: No man can have a peaceful life who thinks too much about lengthening it. Line 4.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Plus tamen tibi et viva vox et convictus quam oratio proderit; in rem praesentem venias oportet, primum quia homines amplius oculis quam auribus credunt, deinde quia longum iter est per praecepta, breve et efficax per exempla.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind.
citation: Seneca is quoting Hecato.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Recede in te ipse quantum potes; cum his versare qui te meliorem facturi sunt, illos admitte quos tu potes facere meliores. Mutuo ista fiunt, et homines dum docent discunt.
citation: Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach. Line 8.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Plura sunt, Lucili, quae nos terrent quam quae premunt, et saepius opinione quam re laboramus.
citation: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Mos antiquis fuit, usque ad meam servatus aetatem, primis epistulae verbis adicere 'si vales bene est, ego valeo'. Recte nos dicimus 'si philosopharis, bene est'. Valere enim hoc demum est. Sine hoc aeger est animus.
citation: The old Romans had a custom which survived even into my lifetime. They would add to the opening words of a letter: "If you are well, it is well; I also am well." Persons like ourselves would do well to say. "If you are studying philosophy,

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Leve aes alienum debitorem facit, grave inimicum.
citation: A trifling debt makes a man your debtor; a large one makes him an enemy. Line 11.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Nemo quam bene vivat sed quam diu curat, cum omnibus possit contingere ut bene vivant, ut diu nulli.
citation: Men do not care how nobly they live, but only how long, although it is within the reach of every man to live nobly, but within no man's power to live long. Line 17.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Illud autem ante omnia memento, demere rebus tumultum ac videre quid in quaque re sit: scies nihil esse in istis terribile nisi ipsum timorem.
citation: Remember, however, before all else, to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom; you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear. Line 12 Alternate translation: You

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Sola virtus praestat gaudium perpetuum, securum; etiam si quid obstat, nubium modo intervenit, quae infra feruntur nec umquam diem vincunt.
citation: Virtue alone affords everlasting and peace-giving joy; even if some obstacle arise, it is but like an intervening cloud, which floats beneath the sun but never prevails against it.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Nam qui peccare se nescit, corrigi non vult.
citation: If one doesn't know his mistakes, he won't want to correct them. Line 9

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Magnus gubernator et scisso navigat velo.
citation: A great pilot can sail even when his canvas is rent. Line 3.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Praeterea qui alium sequitur nihil invenit, immo nec quaerit.
citation: Besides, he who follows another not only discovers nothing but is not even investigating.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Amicitia semper prodest, amor aliquando etiam nocet
citation: Friendship is always helpful, but love sometimes even does harm

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Non refert quam multos sed quam bonos habeas.
citation: It is quality rather than quantity that matters. Line 1

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Vis tu cogitare istum quem servum tuum vocas ex isdem seminibus ortum eodem frui caelo, aeque spirare, aeque vivere, aeque mori! tam tu illum videre ingenuum potes quam ille te servum.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Quae sit libertas, quaeris? Nulli rei servire, nulli necissitati, nullis casibus, fortunam in aequum deducere.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Quidni mallet, quisquis vir est, somnum suum classico quam symphonia rumpi?
citation: Would not anyone who is a man have his slumbers broken by a war-trumpet rather than by a chorus of serenaders? Line 13.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Ante senectutem curavi ut bene viverem, in senectute ut bene moriar; bene autem mori est libenter mori.
citation: Before I became old I tried to live well; now that I am old, I shall try to die well; but dying well means dying gladly. Line 2.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Brevissima ad divitias per contemptum divitiarum via est.
citation: The shortest way to wealth is through the contempt of wealth.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Nulla res citius in odium venit quam dolor, qui recens consolatorem invenit et aliquos ad se adducit, inveteratus vero deridetur, nec inmerito.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Sapiens vivit quantum debet, non quantum potest.
citation: The wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can. Line 4.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Tamdiu, discendum est, quemadmodum vivas, quamdiu vivas.
citation: As long as you live, keep learning how to live.

author: Seneca the Younger
text: Saepe debemus mori nec volumus, morimur nec volumus.
citation: There are times when we ought to die and are unwilling; sometimes we die and are unwilling. 7

author: Seneca the Younger

author: Charles Dickens
text: To conceal anything from those to whom I am attached, is not in my nature. I can never close my lips where I have opened my heart.

author: Charles Dickens
text: I am quite serious when I say that I do not believe there are, on the whole earth besides, so many intensified bores as in these United States. No man can form an adequate idea of the real meaning of the word, without coming here.
citation: Comment while on an American tour (March 1842), as quoted in Dickens (1949) by Hesketh Pearson, Ch. 8

author: Charles Dickens
text: O let us love our occupations, Bless the squire and his relations, Live upon our daily rations, And always know our proper stations.

author: Thomas Jefferson

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: The two principles on which our conduct towards the Indians should be founded, are justice and fear. After the injuries we have done them, they cannot love us....
citation: Letter to Benjamin Hawkins (13 August 1786) Lipscomb & Bergh ed. 5:390

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: The policy of American government is to leave its citizens free, neither restraining them nor aiding them in their pursuits.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: Experience declares that man is the only animal which devours his own kind; for I can apply no milder term to the governments of Europe, and to the general prey of the rich on the poor.
citation: Letter to Colonel Edward Carrington (16 January 1787)

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: I am convinced that those societies (as the Indians) which live without government enjoy in their general mass an infinitely greater degree of happiness than those who live under the European governments.
citation: Letter to Colonel Edward Carrington, Paris, (16 January 1787)

author: Thomas Jefferson

author: Thomas Jefferson

author: Thomas Jefferson
