citation: Return to Tipasa (1954) Variant translation: In the depths of winter, I finally learned that within me there lay an invincible summer. As translated in Lyrical and Critical Essays (1968), p. 169; also in The Unquiet Vision : Mirrors of Man

author: Albert Camus
text: A living man can be enslaved and reduced to the historic condition of an object. But if he dies in refusing to be enslaved, he reaffirms the existence of another kind of human nature which refuses to be classified as an object.
citation: quoted in Existentialism Versus Marxism : Conflicting Views on Humanism (1966, New York, Dell Pub. Co., p.234, available on [https://archive.org/details/existentialismve0000unse archive.org]), an essay edited by George Edward Novack; this e

author: Albert Camus
text: There is not love of life without despair about life.
citation: Preface, Lyrical and Critical Essays (1970)

author: Albert Camus
text: Accepting the absurdity of everything around us is one step, a necessary experience: it should not become a dead end. It arouses a revolt that can become fruitful.
citation: "Three Interviews" in Lyrical and Critical Essays (1970)

author: Albert Camus
text: Knowing that certain nights whose sweetness lingers will keep returning to the earth and sea after we are gone, yes, this helps us to die.
citation: "The Sea Close By" in Lyrical and Critical Essays (1970)

author: Albert Camus
text: Autumn is a second Spring when every leaf is a flower.
citation: As quoted in Visions from Earth (2004) by James R. Miller, p. 126

author: Albert Camus
text: Ce que, finalement, je sais de plus sûr sur la morale et les obligations des hommes, c'est au football que je le dois.
citation: "Ce que je sais de plus sûr à propos de la moralité et des obligations des hommes, c'est au sport que je le dois", sentence parfois modifiée en : "C'est au football que je le dois !" All I know most surely about morality and obligations, I

author: Albert Camus
text: If there is a sin against life, it consists perhaps not so much in despairing of life as in hoping for another life and in eluding the implacable grandeur of this life.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=N0bNUqDVKJgC&q=%22If+there+is+a+sin+against+life+it+consists+perhaps+not+so+much+in+despairing+of+life+as+in+hoping+for+another+life+and+in+eluding+the+implacable+grandeur+of+this+life%22&pg=PA153#v=onepage

author: Albert Camus
text: Seulement, il faut du temps pour être heureux. Beaucoup de temps. Le bonheur lui aussi est une longue patience.
citation: Only it takes time to be happy. A lot of time. Happiness, too, is a long patience.

author: Albert Camus
text: Avoir de l'argent c'est se libérer de l'argent.
citation: Having money is a way of being free of money.

author: Albert Camus
text: Aujourd'hui maman est morte. Ou peut-être hier, je ne sais pas.
citation: Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday; I can't be sure. First sentences of the book; some translations retain the original Maman.

author: Albert Camus
text: Those who need myths are indeed poor. Here the gods serve as beds or resting places as the day races across the sky.
citation: "Noces à Tipasa"

author: Albert Camus
text: Nothing is harder to understand than a symbolic work. A symbol always transcends the one who makes use of it and makes him say in reality more than he is aware of expressing.
citation: "Hope and the Absurd in the work of Franz Kafka"

author: Albert Camus
text: What must be remembered in any case is that secret complicity that joins the logical and the everyday to the tragic.
citation: "Hope and the Absurd in the work of Franz Kafka"

author: Albert Camus
text: With the exception of professional rationalists, today people despair of true knowledge. If the only significant history of human thought were to be written, it would have to be history of its successive regrets and impotences.
citation: Absurd Walls

author: Albert Camus
text: A man is more a man through the things he keeps to himself than through those he says.
citation: Conquest

author: Albert Camus
text: To become god is merely to be free on this earth, not to serve an immortal being.
citation: Kirilov

author: Albert Camus
text: Existence is illusory and it is eternal.
citation: Kirilov

author: Albert Camus
text: There is no mystery in humans creation. Will performs this miracle. But at least there is no true creation without a secret.
citation: Kirilov

author: Albert Camus
text: Il y a toujours une philosophie pour le manque de courage.
citation: There is always a philosophy for lack of courage.

author: Albert Camus
text: Pauvre et libre plutôt que riche et asservi. Bien entendu les hommes veulent être et riches et libres et c'est ce qui les conduit quelquefois à être pauvres et esclaves.
citation: Poor and free rather than rich and enslaved. Of course, men want to be both rich and free, and this is what leads them at times to be poor and enslaved.

author: Albert Camus
text: Absolute freedom mocks at justice. Absolute justice denies freedom. To be fruitful, the two ideas must find their limits in each other.
citation: "Historical Murder", as translated by Anthony Bower

author: Albert Camus
text: Every revolutionary ends as an oppressor or a heretic.
citation: Variant translation: Every revolutionary ends by becoming either an oppressor or a heretic.

author: Albert Camus
text: Man is the only creature who refuses to be what he is.
citation: Introduction

author: Albert Camus
text: The most elementary form of rebellion, paradoxically, expresses an aspiration for order.
citation: Part 2: Metaphysical Rebellion

author: Albert Camus
text: Real fulfillment, for the man who allows absolutely free rein to his desires, and who much dominate everything, lies in hatred.
citation: Part 2: Metaphysical Rebellion

author: Albert Camus
text: A nihilist is not one who believes in nothing, but one who does not believe in what exists.
citation: Part 2: Metaphysical Rebellion

author: Albert Camus
text: The ancients, even though they believed in destiny, believed primarily in nature, in which they participated wholeheartedly. To rebel against nature amounted to rebelling against oneself. It was butting one's head against a wall.
citation: Part 2: Metaphysical Rebellion

author: Albert Camus
text: A character is never the author who created him. It is quite likely, however, that an author may be all his characters simultaneously.
citation: Part 2: Metaphysical Rebellion; also quoted in Albert Camus : The Invincible Summer (1958) by Albert Maquet, p. 86; a remark made about the Marquis de Sade

author: Albert Camus
text: Art is the activity that exalts and denies simultaneously. "No artist tolerates reality," says Nietzsche.
citation: Part 4: Rebellion and Art

author: Albert Camus
text: The artist reconstructs the world to his plan.
citation: Part 4: Rebellion and Art

author: Albert Camus
text: Artistic creation is a demand for unity and a rejection of the world.
citation: Part 4: Rebellion and Art

author: Albert Camus
text: In every rebellion is to be found the metaphysical demand for unity, the impossibility of capturing it, and the construction of a substitute universe.
citation: Part 4: Rebellion and Art

author: Albert Camus
text: The contradiction is this: man rejects the world as it is, without accepting the necessity of escaping it. In fact, men cling to the world and by far the majority do not want to abandon it.
citation: Part 4: Rebellion and Art

author: Samuel Johnson
text: By Numbers here from Shame or Censure free, All Crimes are safe, but hated Poverty. This, only this, the rigid Law persues, This, only this, provokes the snarling Muse.
citation: [http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~jlynch/Texts/london2.html London: A Poem (1738)], lines 158–161

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Of all the Griefs that harrass the Distrest, Sure the most bitter is a scornful Jest
citation: [http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~jlynch/Texts/london2.html London: A Poem (1738)], lines 166–167

author: Samuel Johnson
text: This mournful truth is ev'rywhere confessed — Slow rises worth, by poverty depressed.
citation: [http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~jlynch/Texts/london2.html London: A Poem (1738)], lines 176–177

author: Samuel Johnson
text: A thousand horrid Prodigies foretold it. A feeble government, eluded Laws, A factious Populace, luxurious Nobles, And all the maladies of stinking states.
citation: The Tragedy of Irene (1749), Act I, Sc. 1

author: Samuel Johnson
text: There Poetry shall tune her sacred voice, And wake from ignorance the Western World.
citation: The Tragedy of Irene (1749), Act IV, Sc. 1

author: Samuel Johnson
text: To neglect at any time preparation for death, is to sleep on our post at a siege, but to omit it in old age, is to sleep at an attack.
citation: [http://www.yalejohnson.com/frontend/sda_viewer?n=106855 The Rambler, No. 78 (Sat 15 December 1750).] See also The Yale Book of Quotations, Samuel Johnson 2 (2006)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: It is always observable that silence propagates itself, and that the longer talk has been suspended, the more difficult it is to find any thing to say.
citation: [http://www.gutenberg.org/etext/12050 The Adventurer, # 84 (25 August 1753)]

author: Samuel Johnson
text: The reciprocal civility of authors is one of the most risible scenes in the farce of life.
citation: [http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~jlynch/Texts/browne.html The Life of Sir Thomas Browne (1756)]

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Liberty is, to the lowest rank of every nation, little more than the choice of working or starving.
citation: "The Bravery of the English Common Soldiers", in The British Magazine (January 1760) Note: This essay was "added to some editions of [http://books.google.co.uk/books?id=5L9GAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA306&dq=%22Liberty+is%22&hl=pt-PT&sa=X&ei=QMMqU_f7MMPM

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Nature has given women so much power that the law has very wisely given them little.
citation: Letter from Johnson to John Taylor, 18 August 1763. The Yale Book of Quotations edited by Fred R. Shapiro, p. 400.

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Resolve to spend a certain number of hours every day amongst your books.
citation: Letter to James Boswell (8 Dec 1763)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: I have always suspected that the reading is right, which requires many words to prove it wrong; and the emendation wrong, that cannot without so much labour appear to be right.
citation: The Plays of William Shakespeare, Vol. I (1765), Preface

author: Samuel Johnson
text: The only end of writing is to enable the readers better to enjoy life, or better to endure it.
citation: A [http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~jlynch/Texts/jenyns.html Review] of Soame Jenyns' A Free Enquiry into the Nature and Origin of Evil, published in the first volume of Miscellaneous and Fugitive Pieces (London, 1774), p. 23

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Whatever withdraws us from the power of our senses; whatever makes the past, the distant, or the future predominate over the present, advances us in the dignity of thinking beings.
citation: A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775), Inch Kenneth

author: Samuel Johnson
text: That man is little to be envied whose patriotism would not gain force upon the plain of Marathon, or whose piety would not grow warmer among the ruins of Iona.
citation: A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775), Inch Kenneth

author: Samuel Johnson
text: There will always be a part, and always a very large part of every community, that have no care but for themselves, and whose care for themselves reaches little further than impatience of immediate pain, and eagerness for the nearest good.
citation: [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Taxation_No_Tyranny Taxation No Tyranny] (1775)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: There is no wisdom in useless and hopeless sorrow; but there is something in it so like virtue, that he who is wholly without it cannot be loved.
citation: Letter to Hester Thrale (12 April 1781) [http://books.google.com/books?id=184WAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA736]

author: Samuel Johnson
text: I am inclined to believe that few attacks either of ridicule or invective make much noise, but by the help of those they provoke.
citation: Letter to Hester Thrale (5 July 1783) [http://books.google.com/books?id=8JuiYLGldcsC&pg=PA169&lpg=PA169&dq=%22samuel+johnson%22+few+attacks+ridicule+invective+noise+provoke&source=web&ots=HMST_SM18L&sig=xovCcC2lKiTX9V0p61QvIC_yHW0&hl=en&sa=

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Every man naturally persuades himself that he can keep his resolutions, nor is he convinced of his imbecility but by length of time and frequency of experiment.
citation: Prayers and Meditations, No. 1770 (1785)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Here closed in death th' attentive eyes That saw the manners in the face.
citation: Epitaph on Hogarth (1786)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Catch then, O! catch the transient hour, Improve each moment as it flies; Life's a short Summer — man a flower, He dies — alas! how soon he dies!
citation: Winter, An Ode. The works of Samuel Johnson, LL.D. (1787), p. 355

author: Samuel Johnson
text: He who praises everybody praises nobody.
citation: Johnson's Works (1787), vol. XI, p. 216; This set included the Life of Samuel Johnson by Sir John Hawkins

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Books that you may carry to the fire, and hold readily in your hand, are the most useful after all.
citation: From Sir John Hawkins's Life of Johnson, Apothegms (1787)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Fly fishing may be a very pleasant amusement; but angling or float fishing I can only compare to a stick and a string, with a worm at one end and a fool at the other.
citation: Attributed in Instructions to Young Sportsmen (1824) by Colonel Peter Hawker

author: Samuel Johnson
text: I never desire to converse with a man who has written more than he has read.
citation: Quoted in the "Apophthegms, Sentiments, Opinions and Occasional Reflections" of Sir John Hawkins (1787-1789) in Johnsonian Miscellanies (1897), vol. II, p. 6, edited by George Birkbeck Hill

author: Samuel Johnson
text: A man is in general better pleased when he has a good dinner upon his table, than when his wife talks Greek.
citation: Quoted in the "Apophthegms, Sentiments, Opinions and Occasional Reflections" of Sir John Hawkins (1787-1789) in Johnsonian Miscellanies (1897), vol. II, p. 11, edited by George Birkbeck Hill

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Abstinence is as easy to me as temperance would be difficult.
citation: Quoted in Anecdotes of Johnson by Hannah More in Johnsonian Miscellanies (1897), vol. II, p. 197, edited by George Birkbeck Hill. More had quoted this remark in a letter to her sister (April 1782)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Ignorance in other men may be censured as idleness, in an academick it must be abhorred as treachery.
citation: "[https://cs.nyu.edu/~davise/personal/JohnsonAcademick.pdf On the Character and Duty of an Academick]", pub. 1793.

author: Samuel Johnson
text: He who makes a beast of himself gets rid of the pain of being a man.
citation: Quoted in "Anecdotes of the Revd. Percival Stockdale" (1809) in Johnsonian Miscellanies (1897), vol. II, p. 333, edited by George Birkbeck Hill; also quoted in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas by Hunter S. Thompson, in the Avenged Sevenfold s

author: Samuel Johnson
text: From Thee, great God: we spring, to Thee we tend, Path, motive, guide, original, and end.
citation: Reported in Josiah Hotchkiss Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 257

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Let me rejoice in the light which Thou hast imparted; let me serve Thee with active zeal, humbled confidence, and wait with patient expectation for the time in which the soul which Thou receivest shall be satisfied with knowledge.
citation: Reported in Josiah Hotchkiss Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 613

author: Samuel Johnson
text: A desire for knowledge is the natural feeling of mankind; and every human being, whose mind is not debauched, will be willing to give all he has to get knowledge.
citation: Dr. Johnson's Table Talk (London: 1807), p. 64

author: Samuel Johnson
text: It is more from carelessness about truth than from intentional lying, that there is so much falsehood in the world.
citation: Dr. Johnson's Table Talk (London: 1807), p. 67

author: Samuel Johnson
text: The richest author that ever grazed the common of literature.
citation: Of John Campbell, as quoted by Joseph Wharton; reported in "John Campbell", Encyclopedia Britannica (1911)

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Let observation with extensive view Survey mankind, from China to Peru.
citation: Line 1; comparable to: "All human race, from China to Peru, Pleasure, howe'er disguis'd by art, pursue", Thomas Warton, Universal Love of Pleasure

author: Samuel Johnson
text: But, scarce observ'd, the knowing and the bold Fall in the gen'ral massacre of gold.
citation: Line 21

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Deign on the passing world to turn thine eyes, And pause a while from learning to be wise. There mark what ills the scholar's life assail — Toil, envy, want, the patron, and the jail.
citation: Line 157

author: Samuel Johnson
text: A frame of adamant, a soul of fire, No dangers fright him, and no labors tire.
citation: Line 193

author: Samuel Johnson
text: He left the name at which the world grew pale, To point a moral, or adorn a tale.
citation: Line 221

author: Samuel Johnson
text: Enlarge my life with multitude of days!" In health, in sickness, thus the suppliant prays: Hides from himself his state, and shuns to know That life protracted is protracted woe.
citation: Line 255

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Variation does not mean evolution. If an artist varies his mode of expression this only means that he has changed his manner of thinking, and in changing, it might be for the better or it might be for the worse.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: The smell of opium is the least stupid smell in the world.
citation: Quote, attributed to Picasso in: Jean Cocteau (1932), Opium: The Diary of an Addict. p. 63

author: Pablo Picasso
text: It is my misfortune - and probably my delight - to use things as my passions tell me. What a miserable fate for a painter who adores blondes to have to stop himself putting them into a picture because they don't go with the basket of fruit!
citation: Herschel Browning Chip (1968, p. 267). (another and longer version:) What a sad fate for a painter who loves blondes, but who refrains from putting them in his picture because they don’t go with the basket of fruit! What misery for a painte

author: Pablo Picasso
text: I would like to manage to prevent people from ever seeing how a picture of mine has been done. What can it possibly matter? What I want is that the only thing emanating from my pictures should be emotion. [Boisgeloup, winter 1934].
citation: Richard Friendenthal (1963, p. 256).

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Abstract art is only painting. What about drama? There is no abstract art. You always start with something. Afterward you can remove all traces of reality.
citation: Herschel Browning Chip (1968, p. 270). Other translation: Abstract art is only painting. And what's so dramatic about that? There is no abstract art. One must always begin with something. Afterwards one can remove all semblance of reality.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Art is not made to decorate rooms. It is an offensive weapon in the defence against the enemy.
citation: La peinture n'est pas faite pour décorer des appartements. C'est un instrument de guerre offensive et défensive contre l'ennemi. La pintura no se ha inventado para adornar las habitaciones. La pintura es un arma ofensiva, en la defensa cont

author: Pablo Picasso
text: When I was a child my mother said to me, 'If you are a soldier, you will become a general. If you are a monk, you will become the Pope.' Instead, I was a painter, and became Picasso.
citation: As quoted in Life with Picasso, by François Gilot, 1964, p. 60

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Les gloires, les trompettes, les palmes... et les bas-reliefs,... tout cela fait un monument.
citation: Translation: The glories, trumpets, palms... and low reliefs,... all that makes a monument. Picasso (1952). Quoted in: Michael D. Garval (2004), "A Dream of Stone": Fame, Vision, and Monumentality in Nineteenth-century French Literary Cultu

author: Pablo Picasso
text: When Matisse died, he left me his Odalisques 'as a legacy', he proclaimed.
citation: after the death of Matisse (1954); as quoted in Matisse & Picasso, By Paul Trachtman, Smithsonian Magazine, February 2003, p. 7

author: Pablo Picasso
text: On August 2, 1914, I took Braque and Derain to the Gare d'Avignon [drafted as a soldier for World war 1.] I never saw them again [not literally a fact, but the close relation between Picasso and Braque ended].
citation: Quote in My Galleries and Painters, Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler, New York Viking Press, 1971, p. 46 Picasso in a talk c. 1955, with Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Accidents, try to change them - it's impossible. The accidental reveals man.
citation: Quote in Vogue, 1 November 1956.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: There are painters who transform the sun into a yellow spot but there are others who with the help of their art and their intelligence transform a yellow spot into a sun.
citation: In: Sergei Eisenstein (1957), Film form [and]: The film sense, p. 127.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Even the signature of Kodra is a work of art.
citation: Repubblica, 2006 La Provincia, 2006

author: Pablo Picasso
text: L'art n'est pas chaste [...], on devrait l’interdire aux ignorants innocents, ne jamais mettre en contact avec lui ceux qui y sont insuffisamment préparés. Oui, l'art est dangereux. Ou s'il est chaste, ce n'est pas de l'art.
citation: Art is never chaste. It ought to be forbidden to ignorant innocents, never allowed into contact with those not sufficiently prepared. Yes, art is dangerous. Where it is chaste, it is not art. Quote by Antonina Vallentin (1963 [1957]), Picas

author: Pablo Picasso
text: It's like God's. God is really only another artist. He invented the giraffe, the elephant, and the cat. He has no real style. He just goes on trying other things.
citation: Picasso quoted in 'TIME'; quoted in: The Atlantic, Vol. 214 (1964), p. 97. Picasso commented on his ambiguous style, or use of multiple styles.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: You have got to be able to picture side by side everything Matisse and I were doing at that time. No one has ever looked at Matisse's painting more carefully than I; and no one has looked at mine more carefully than he.
citation: Quote by old Picasso (1960's); as quoted in 'Matisse & Picasso', Paul Trachtman, Smithsonian Magazine, February 2003, p 1

author: Pablo Picasso
text: It means nothing to me. I have no opinion about it, and I don't care.
citation: On the first moon landing, quoted in The New York Times (1969-07-21).

author: Pablo Picasso
text: For me, there are two kinds of women — goddesses and doormats.
citation: Quoted in: Briton Hadden, ‎Henry Robinson Luce (1969), Time, Vol. 93. p. 66.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: I was thinking about Casagemas's death that started me painting in blue.
citation: Original: C’est en passant que Casagemas était mort que je me suis mis à piendre en bleu Quoted in Pierre Daix, La Vie de Peintre de Pablo Picasso, Paris: Editions du Seuil, 1977. Picasso explained his friend Pierre Daix (around 1965), why

author: Pablo Picasso
text: To contradict. To show one eye full face and one in profile. Nature does many things the way I do, but she hides them! My painting is a series of non-sequiturs. ...
citation: Quoted in: Pierre Cabanne (1977), Pablo Picasso: His Life and Times, p. 268.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Success is dangerous. One begins to copy oneself and to copy oneself is more dangerous than to copy others.
citation: Quoted in: The Artist, Vol. 93 (1978) p. 5.

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Drink to me. Drink to my health. You know I can't drink any more.
citation: Quoted in: Scott Slater, ‎Alec Solomita (1980), Exits: stories of dying moments & parting words. p. 8. Slater & Solomita (1980) explained: "It was a spirited dinner and Picasso a cheerful, genial host. After the meal, while pouring wine int

author: John Stuart Mill
text: It is not because men's desires are strong that they act ill; it is because their consciences are weak.
citation: On Liberty (1859)

author: John Stuart Mill
text: How can great minds be produced in a country where the test of a great mind is agreeing in the opinions of small minds?
citation: As quoted in Egoists: A Book of Supermen (1909) by James Huneker, p. 367

author: John Stuart Mill
text: It might be plausibly maintained, that in almost every one of the leading controversies, past or present, in social philosophy, both sides were in the right in what they affirmed, though wrong in what they denied.
citation: J. S. Mill, [http://books.google.gr/books?id=FyfPAAAAMAAJ&dq= Dissertations and discussions: political, philosophical, and historical, Volume 2], H. Holt, 1864, p. 11.

author: John Stuart Mill
text: France has done more for even English history than England has.
citation: John Stuart Mill. Michelet.On the writing of English history. Complete Works Vol 20. Page 221.http://files.libertyfund.org/pll/pdf/Mill_0223-20_EBk_v7.0.pdf

author: John Stuart Mill
text: I regard utility as the ultimate appeal on all ethical questions; but it must be utility in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being.
citation: Ch. 1: Introductory

author: John Stuart Mill
text: The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.
citation: Ch. 1: Introductory

author: John Stuart Mill
text: The great writers to whom the world owes what religious liberty it possesses, have mostly asserted freedom of conscience as an indefeasible right, and denied absolutely that a human being is accountable to others for his religious belief.
citation: Ch. 1: Introductory

author: John Stuart Mill
text: If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.
citation: Ch. II: Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Truth gains more even by the errors of one who, with due study and preparation, thinks for himself, than by the true opinions of those who only hold them because they do not suffer themselves to think.
citation: Ch. II: Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Whatever crushes individuality is despotism, by whatever name it may be called, and whether it professes to be enforcing the will of God or the injunctions of men.
citation: Ch. III: Of Individuality, As One of the Elements of Well-Being

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Persons of genius, it is true, are, and are always likely to be, a small minority; but in order to have them, it is necessary to preserve the soil in which they grow. Genius can only breathe freely in an atmosphere of freedom.
citation: Ch. III: Of Individuality, As One of the Elements of Well-Being

author: John Stuart Mill
text: A bureaucracy always tends to become a pedantocracy.
citation: Ch. VI: Of the Infirmities and Dangers to Which Representative Government Is Liable (p. 234)

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Among a people without fellow-feeling, especially if they read and speak different languages, the united public opinion, necessary to the working of the representative government, cannot exist.
citation: Ch. XVI: Of Nationality, As Connected with Representative Government (p. 382)

author: John Stuart Mill
text: The utilitarian doctrine is, that happiness is desirable, and the only thing desirable, as an end; all other things being only desirable as means to that end.
citation: Ch. 4

author: John Stuart Mill
text: For the apotheosis of Reason we have substituted that of Instinct; and we call everything instinct which we find in ourselves and for which we cannot trace any rational foundation.
citation: Ch. 1

author: John Stuart Mill
text: The best state for human nature is that in which, while no one is poor, no one desires to be richer, nor has any reason to fear being thrust back by the efforts of others to push themselves forward.
citation: Book IV, Chapter VI, §2

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Landlords... grow richer, as it were in their sleep, without working, risking, or economizing.
citation: Book V, Chapter 1, Section 5

author: John Stuart Mill
text: The reasons for legal intervention in favour of children, apply not less strongly to the case of those unfortunate slaves and victims of the most brutal part of mankind, the lower animals.
citation: Book V, Chapter 11, Section 9

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Since the state must necessarily provide subsistence for the criminal poor while undergoing punishment, not to do the same for the poor who have not offended is to give a premium on crime.
citation: Book V, Chapter XI, §13

author: John Stuart Mill
text: It is also a study peculiarly adapted to an early stage in the education of philosophical students, since it does not presuppose the slow process of acquiring, by experience and reflection, valuable thoughts of their own.
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/19/mode/1up pp. 19-20])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: A pupil from whom nothing is ever demanded which he cannot do never does all he can.
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/32/mode/1up p. 32])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: In my education, as in that of everyone, the moral influences, which are so much more important than all others, are also the most complicated, and the most difficult to specify with any approach to completeness.
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/38/mode/1up p. 38])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: I am thus one of the very few examples, in this country, of one who has, not thrown off religious belief, but never had it...
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/43/mode/1up p. 43])

author: John Stuart Mill

citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/45/mode/1up p. 45])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Nothing contributes more to nourish elevation of sentiments in a people, than the large and free character of their habitations.
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/55/mode/1up p. 55])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: I frequently asked myself, if I could, or if I was bound to go on living, when life must be passed in this manner. I generally answered to myself, that I did not think I could possibly bear it beyond a year.
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/140/mode/1up p. 140])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: I well knew that to propose something which would be called extreme, was the true way not to impede but to facilitate a more moderate experiment.
citation: ([https://archive.org/details/autobiography01mill/page/294/mode/1up p. 294])

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Wisdom and contrivance are shown in overcoming difficulties, so there is no place for them in a Being for whom no difficulties exist
citation: pages 176-177; Early Modern Texts page 16

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Where in the hell have you guys been? I've been at this bus stop for a whole week now.

text: If more politicians knew poetry, and more poets knew politics, I am convinced the world would be a little better place in which to live.

text: I have just received the following wire from my generous daddy: "Dear Jack – Don’t buy a single vote more than necessary – I’ll be damned if I am going to pay for a landslide.

text: In the Chinese language, the word "crisis" is composed of two characters, one representing danger and the other, opportunity.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx Remarks at the United Negro College Fund, Indianapolis, Indiana (12 April 1959)]; Box 902, Senate Speech Files, Pre-Presidential Papers, John F. Kennedy P

citation: Source: Profiles in Courage Excerpts. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library & Museum. [https://web.archive.org/web/20250817100527/https://www.jfklibrary.org/learn/education/profile-in-courage-essay-contest/teacher-information-and-curriculum-

author: John F. Kennedy
text: The voters selected us, in short, because they had confidence in our judgement and our ability to exercise that judgement from a position where we could determine what were their own best interest, as a part of the nation's interest.

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Only the very courageous will be able to keep alive the spirit of individualism and dissent which gave birth to this nation, nourished it as an infant, and carried it through its severest tests upon the attainment of its maturity.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=JVEHpHb-VKQC&printsec=frontcover&dq=Pro%EF%AC%81les+in+Courage&hl=en&sa=X&ei=aZntUeC6CpOMyAG2_ICgAw&ved=0CDQQ6AEwAA#v=snippet&q=individualism%20&f=false Profiles in Courage (1956), p. 17]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Dick Nixon is the victim of the worst press that ever hit a politician in this country. What they did to him in the Helen Gahagan Douglas race was disgusting.
citation: As quoted in Kennedy and Nixon (1996) by Christopher Matthews, p.123

author: John F. Kennedy
text: We celebrate the past to awaken the future.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Remarks at the 25th Anniversary of the Signing of the Social Security Act," Hyde Park, New York (14 August 1960)]; Box 910, Senate Speech Files, John F.

author: John F. Kennedy
text: That requires only one kind of defense policy, a policy summed up in a single word "first." I do not mean "first, if," I do not mean "first, but," I do not mean "first, when," but I mean "First, period.
citation: Speech at Civic Auditorium, Seattle, Washington (6 September 1960)

author: John F. Kennedy
text: My call is not to those who believe they belong to the past. My call is to those who believe in the future.
citation: Speech at Civic Auditorium, Seattle, Washington (6 September 1960)

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Their platform, made up of left-over Democratic planks, has the courage of our old convictions. Their pledge is a pledge to the status quo — and today there can be no status quo.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx Address Accepting the Democratic Party Nomination for the Presidency of the United States — Memorial Coliseum, Los Angeles (15 July 1960)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: We have all seen these circus elephants complete with tusks, ivory in their head and thick skins, who move around the circus ring and grab the tail of the elephant ahead of them.
citation: Comments on members of the Republican party, in [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx Remarks at the Cow Palace, San Francisco, California (2 November 1960)]; Box 914, Senate Speech Files, Joh

author: John F. Kennedy
text: I can assure you that every degree of mind and spirit that I possess will be devoted to the long-range interests of the United States and to the cause of freedom around the world.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Ready-Reference/JFK-Speeches/Acceptance-Speech-by-John-F-Kennedy-Hyannis-Armory-Hyannis-Massachusetts-November-9-1960.aspx Acceptance speech (9 November 1960)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: The Federal Budget can and should be made an instrument of prosperity and stability, not a deterrent to recovery.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Special message to Congress: Program for Economic Recovery and Growth (17)", (2 February 1961)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: For I can assure you that we love our country, not for what it was, though it has always been great — not for what it is, though of this we are deeply proud — but for what it someday can, and, through the efforts of us all, someday will be.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Address at a Luncheon Meeting of the National Industrial Conference Board (33)", (13 February 1961)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: The great revolution in the history of man, past, present and future, is the revolution of those determined to be free.
citation: Message to Chairman Khrushchev Concerning the Meaning of Events in Cuba (18 April 1961) .

author: John F. Kennedy
text: There's an old saying that victory has a hundred fathers and defeat is an orphan.... I'm the responsible officer of the Government.
citation: State Department press conference (21 April 1961), following the Bay of Pigs Invasion, as quoted in A Thousand Days : John F. Kennedy in the White House (1965, 2002 edition), by Arthur Schlesinger, p. 262; also in [http://books.google.com/b

author: John F. Kennedy
text: If all of you had voted the other way — there's about 5500 of you here tonight — I would not be the President of the United States.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Address in Chicago at a dinner of the Democratic Party of Cook County (155)," (28 April 1961)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Geography has made us neighbors. History has made us friends. Economics has made us partners. And necessity has made us allies. Those whom nature hath so joined together, let no man put asunder.
citation: Address to the Canadian Parliament (17 May 1961)

author: John F. Kennedy
text: There is danger that totalitarian governments, not subject to vigorous popular debate, will underestimate the will and unity of democratic societies where vital interests are concerned.
citation: President Kennedy's 13th News Conferences on June 28, 1961 John Source: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/Press-Conferences/News-Conference-13.aspx F. Kennedy Presidential Library & Museum]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Freedom is not merely a word or an abstract theory, but the most effective instrument for advancing the welfare of man.
citation: [http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/?pid=8271 Message to the Inter-American Economic and Social Conference at Punta del Este, Uruguay (5 August 1961)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Somebody once said that Washington was a city of Northern charm and Southern efficiency.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Asset-Viewer/Archives/JFKPOF-036-014.aspx Speech] to the Trustees and Advisory Committee of the National Cultural Center in the White House Movie Theater, 14 November 1961

author: John F. Kennedy
text: We have become more and more not a nation of athletes but a nation of spectators.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Remarks at National Football Foundation and Hall of Fame Banquet (496)," December 5 1961. Public Papers of the Presidents: John F. Kennedy, 1961.]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: We must use time as a tool, not as a couch.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Address in New York City to the National Association of Manufacturers (496)," December 5, 1961, Public Papers of the Presidents: John F. Kennedy, 1961.]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: I wonder how it is with you, Harold? If I don't have a woman for three days, I get terrible headaches.
citation: Conversation with Harold Macmillan, in Bermuda (1961) as recounted by Richard Reeves in his book President Kennedy: Profile of Power (1994)

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Let every nation know, whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe to assure the survival and the success of liberty.
citation: This is one of seven quotes inscribed on the walls at the gravesite of John F. Kennedy at Arlington National Cemetery.

author: John F. Kennedy
text: For one true measure of a nation is its success in fulfilling the promise of a better life for each of its members. Let this be the measure of our nation.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx Special message to the Congress on National Health Needs (65)" (27 February 1962)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: Those who make peaceful revolution impossible will make violent revolution inevitable.
citation: Address on the First Anniversary of the Alliance for Progress at the White House (13 March 1962)

author: John F. Kennedy
text: I think this is the most extraordinary collection of talent, of human knowledge, that has ever been gathered together at the White House, with the possible exception of when Thomas Jefferson dined alone.
citation: Address at a White House dinner honoring Nobel Prize winners (29 April 1962), quoted in [http://www.jfklibrary.org/white%20house%20diary/1962/April/29 The White House Diary, at the JFK Library]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: While geography has made us neighbors, tradition has made us friends. Economics has made us partners. And necessity has made us allies — in a vast Alianza para el Progreso. Those whom nature has so joined together, let no man put asunder.
citation: [http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=8741&st=&st1= Address by the President at a Luncheon Given in His Honor by President Lopez Matcos (29 June 1962)]

author: John F. Kennedy
text: It's only when they join together in a forward movement that this country moves ahead...
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Remarks at Los Banos, CA at the Groundbreaking Ceremonies for the San Luis Dam (337)" (18 August 1962)]

text: Bullfight critics row on row Fill the enormous Plaza de toros But only one is there who knows And he is the one who fights the bull.

text: I am certain that after the dust of centuries has passed over our cities, we, too, will be remembered not for victories or defeats in battle or in politics, but for our contribution to the human spirit.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "Remarks at a Closed-circuit Television Broadcast on Behalf of the National Cultural Center (527)" (29 November 1962)]

text: To further the appreciation of culture among all the people, to increase respect for the creative individual, to widen participation by all the processes and fulfillments of art — this is one of the fascinating challenges of these days.
citation: "The Arts in America" in LOOK magazine (18 December 1962), p. 110; also published in [https://books.google.com/books?id=kbA3MUsJS-cC&pg=PA907&dq=%22this+is+one+of+the+fascinating+challenges+of+these+days%22&hl=en&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&sa=

author: John F. Kennedy
text: The life of the arts, far from being an interruption, a distraction, in the life of a nation, is very close to the center of a nation's purpose...and is a test of the quality of a nation's civilization.
citation: [http://www.jfklibrary.org/Research/Research-Aids/Ready-Reference/JFK-Quotations.aspx "LOOK Magazine Article 'The Arts in America' (552)" (18 December 1962)] ; also inscribed at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington

text: One can never consent to creep when one feels an impulse to soar.
citation: [http://www.afb.org/mylife/book.asp?ch=P3Ch4 Address to the American Association to Promote the Teaching of Speech to the Deaf at Mt. Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (8 July 1896)], quoted in supplement to The Story of My Life

text: The bulk of the world's knowledge is an imaginary construction.
