author: Helen Keller
text: We differ, blind and seeing, one from another, not in our senses, but in the use we make of them, in the imagination and courage with which we seek wisdom beyond the senses.
citation: The Five-sensed World (1910)

author: Helen Keller
text: Our puny sentimentalism has caused us to forget that a human life is sacred only when it may be of some use to itself and to the world.
citation: Quoted in, The Black Stork: Eugenics and the Death of "Defective" Babies in American Medicine and Motion Pictures since 1915, (1996), Martin S. Pernick, Oxford University Press, New York, NY., {{ISBN|0195135393}} {{ISBN|9780195135398 }}Part

author: Helen Keller
text: It is the possibility of happiness, intelligence and power that give life its sanctity, and they are absent in the case of a poor, misshapen, paralyzed, unthinking creature.
citation: "Physicians", The New Republic (18 December 1915) [http://www.uffl.org/vol16/gerdtz06.pdf]

author: Helen Keller
text: When one door of happiness closes, another opens; but often we look so long at the closed door that we do not see the one which has been opened for us.
citation: We Bereaved (1929)

author: Helen Keller
text: Believe, when you are most unhappy, that there is something for you to do in the world. So long as you can sweeten another's pain, life is not in vain.
citation: We Bereaved (1929)

author: Helen Keller
text: Many persons have a wrong of idea of what constitutes true happiness. It is not attained through self-gratification but through fidelity to a worthy purpose.
citation: Helen Keller's Journal: 1936-1937 (1938), p. 57

author: Helen Keller
text: No doubt the reason is that character cannot be developed in ease and quiet. Only through experience of trial and suffering can the soul be strengthened, vision cleared, ambition inspired, and success achieved.
citation: Helen Keller's Journal: 1936-1937 (1938), p. 60

author: Helen Keller
text: Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. The fearful are caught as often as the bold.
citation: Let Us Have Faith (1940)

author: Helen Keller
text: Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it. Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing.
citation: The Open Door (1957) This quotation is often contracted into: Security is mostly a superstition... Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing. or paraphrased: Life is either a daring adventure or nothing at all.

author: Helen Keller
text: I do not want the peace that passeth understanding. I want the understanding which bringeth peace.
citation: Quoted in Henry More: The Rational Theology of a Cambridge Plattonist (1962) by Rabbi Aharon Lichtenstein, page 100

author: Helen Keller
text: Some people do not like to think. If one thinks, one must reach conclusions; and conclusions are not always pleasant. They are a thorn in the spirit. But I consider it a priceless gift and a deep responsibility to think.
citation: Helen Keller: Her Socialist Years (1967)

author: Helen Keller
text: Alone we can do so little. Together we can do so much.
citation: [http://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/04/21/together/ "Helen and Teacher: The Story of Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan Macy", Joseph P. Lash (1980)]

author: Helen Keller
text: I would rather walk with a friend in the dark than walk alone in the light.
citation: [https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/05/10/walk-with-friend/ "Helen and Teacher: The Story of Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan Macy", Joseph P. Lash (1980)]

author: Helen Keller
text: Tyranny cannot defeat the power of ideas.
citation: As quoted in the [http://www.ushmm.org/museum/press/archives/detail.php?category=10-publicprograms&content=2003-04-13 Fighting the Fires of Hate: America and the Nazi Book Burnings exhibit at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (13

author: Helen Keller
text: Now, so far as I can judge, self-love is the root of all evil
citation: Ch. 21

author: Helen Keller
text: Virgil is serene and lovely like a marble Apollo in the moonlight; Homer is a beautiful, animated youth in the full sunlight with the wind in his hair.
citation: Ch. 21

author: Helen Keller
text: The Bible gives me a deep, comforting sense that "things seen are temporal and things unseen are eternal.
citation: Ch. 21

author: Helen Keller
text: I do not remember a time since I have been capable of loving books that I have not loved Shakespeare.
citation: Ch. 21

author: Helen Keller
text: There are moments when I feel that the Shylocks, the Judases, and even the Devil, are broken spokes in the great wheel of good which shall in due time be made whole.
citation: Ch. 21

author: Helen Keller
text: If it is true that the violin is the most perfect of musical instruments, then Greek is the violin of human thought.
citation: Part II: Letters (1887 - 1901) TO MRS. LAURENCE HUTTON Wrentham, February 20, 1898.

author: Helen Keller
text: Toleration ... is the greatest gift of the mind; it requires the same effort of the brain that it takes to balance oneself on a bicycle.
citation: Part III, Ch. 2: [http://books.google.com/books?id=zev1dMhB7C4C&q=Toleration+"is+the+greatest+gift+of+the+mind+it+requires+the+same+effort+of+the+brain+that+it+takes+to+balance+oneself+on+a+bicycle"&pg=PA295#v=onepage Personality]

author: Helen Keller
text: It is wonderful how much time good people spend fighting the devil. If they would only expend the same amount of energy loving their fellow men, the devil would die in his own tracks of ennui.
citation: Part III, Ch. 5: Literary Style

author: Alexander Pope
text: Happy the man whose wish and care A few paternal acres bound, Content to breathe his native air In his own ground.
citation: "Ode on Solitude" (c. 1700), st. 1

author: Alexander Pope
text: Thus let me live, unseen, unknown; Thus unlamented let me die; Steal from the world, and not a stone Tell where I lie.
citation: "Ode on Solitude" (c. 1700), st. 5

author: Alexander Pope
text: A little Learning is a dang'rous Thing; Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian Spring: There shallow Draughts intoxicate the Brain, And drinking largely sobers us again.
citation: "An Essay on Criticism" (1709)

author: Alexander Pope
text: They dream in Courtship, but in Wedlock wake.
citation: "The Wife of Bath her Prologue, from Chaucer" (c. 1704, published 1713), line 103

author: Alexander Pope
text: The mouse that always trusts to one poor hole Can never be a mouse of any soul.
citation: "The Wife of Bath her Prologue, from Chaucer" (c. 1704, published 1713), lines 298-299. Compare: "I hold a mouses wit not worth a leke, That hath but on hole for to sterten to", Geoffrey Chaucer, Canterbury Tales, "The Wif of Bathes Prologu

author: Alexander Pope
text: Love seldom haunts the breast where learning lies, And Venus sets ere Mercury can rise.
citation: "The Wife of Bath her Prologue, from Chaucer" (c. 1704, published 1713), line 369

author: Alexander Pope
text: Histories are more full of Examples of the Fidelity of dogs than of Friends.
citation: Letter to Henry Cromwell (19 October 1709)

author: Alexander Pope
text: I am his Highness' Dog at Kew; Pray tell me Sir, whose Dog are you?
citation: "Epigram. Engraved on the Collar of a Dog, which I gave to His Royal Highness" (1738)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night: God said, "Let Newton be!" and all was light.
citation: Epitaph intended for Sir Isaac Newton

author: Alexander Pope
text: The stoic husband was the glorious thing. The man had courage, was a sage, 'tis true, And lov'd his country.
citation: Epilogue to Rowe's Jane Shore (1714)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Well, if our author in the wife offends He has a husband that will make amends; He draws him gentle, tender, and forgiving, And sure such kind good creatures may be living.
citation: Epilogue to Rowe's Jane Shore (1714)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Luxurious lobster-nights, farewell, For sober, studious days!
citation: "A Farewell to London" (1715), st. 1

author: Alexander Pope
text: Dear, damned, distracting town, farewell! Thy fools no more I'll tease: This year in peace, ye critics, dwell, Ye harlots, sleep at ease!
citation: "A Farewell to London" (1715), st. 12

author: Alexander Pope
text: For modes of faith let graceless zealots fight; His can't be wrong whose life is in the right.
citation: An Essay on Man (1734)

author: Alexander Pope
text: I think it was a generous thought, and one that fow'd from an exalted mind, that it was not improbable but God might be delighted with the various methods of worshipping him, which divided the whole world.
citation: Letter, February 10, 1715, 16

author: Alexander Pope
text: Each finding like a friend Something to blame, and something to commend.
citation: "Epistle to Mr. Jervas" (1717), lines 21–22

author: Alexander Pope
text: Who ne'er knew joy but friendship might divide, Or gave his father grief but when he died.
citation: "Epitaph on the Hon. S. Harcourt" (1720)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Such were the notes thy once lov'd poet sung, Till death untimely stopp'd his tuneful tongue.
citation: "Epistle to Robert, Earl of Oxford and Mortimer" preface to Thomas Parnell's Poems on Several Occasions (1721)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Absent or dead, still let a friend be dear.
citation: "Epistle to Robert, Earl of Oxford and Mortimer" (1721)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Blessed is the man who expects nothing, for he shall never be disappointed" was the ninth Beatitude which a man of wit (who, like a man of wit, was a long time in gaol) added to the eighth.
citation: Letter, written in collaboration with John Gay, to William Fortescue (23 September 1725). A similar remark was made in a letter to John Gay (16 October 1727): "I have many years magnify'd in my own mind, and repeated to you a ninth Beatitud

author: Alexander Pope
text: Let me tell you I am better acquainted with you for a long Absence, as men are with themselves for a long affliction: Absence does but hold off a friend, to make one see him the truer.
citation: Letter, written in collaboration with Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, to Jonathan Swift (14 December 1725)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Know, sense, like charity, begins at home.
citation: "Umbra", first published in Miscellanies (1727)

author: Alexander Pope
text: So unaffected, so compos'd a mind; So firm, yet soft; so strong, yet so refin'd; Heav'n, as its purest gold, by tortures try'd; The saint sustain'd it, but the woman died.
citation: "Epitaph on Mrs. Corbet" (1730)

author: Alexander Pope
text: Good God! how often are we to die before we go quite off this stage? in every friend we lose a part of ourselves, and the best part.
citation: Letter, written in collaboration with Dr John Arbuthnot, to Jonathan Swift (December 5, 1732) upon the death of John Gay.

author: Alexander Pope
text: Of Manners gentle, of Affections mild; In Wit, a Man; Simplicity, a Child.
citation: "Epitaph on Gay" (1733), lines 1-2. Reported in The Poems of Alexander Pope, ed. John Butt, sixth edition (Yale University Press, 1970), p. 818. Compare: "Her wit was more than man, her innocence a child", John Dryden, Elegy on Mrs. Killegr

author: Alexander Pope
text: For he lives twice who can at once employ The present well, and e'en the past enjoy.
citation: Imitation of Martial, reported in Mr. Pope's Literary Correspondence (1737), Vol. V, p. 232; The Poems of Alexander Pope, ed. John Butt, sixth edition (Yale University Press, 1970), p. 117. Compare: "Ampliat ætatis spatium sibi vir bonus; h

author: Alexander Pope
text: I have nothing to say for rhyme, but that I doubt whether a poem can support itself without it, in our language; unless it be stiffened with such strange words, as are likely to destroy our language itself.
citation: Remark (1738?) quoted in Anecdotes, Observations, and Characters, of Books and Men (1820) by Joseph Spence [published from the original papers; with notes, and a life of the author, by Samuel Weller Singer]; "Spence's Anecdotes", Section IV

author: Alexander Pope
text: There, take (says Justice), take ye each a shell: We thrive at Westminster on fools like you; 'T was a fat oyster,—live in peace,—adieu.
citation: Reported in The Poems of Alexander Pope, ed. John Butt, sixth edition (Yale University Press, 1970), p. 832: "Verbatim from Boileau", written c. 1740, published 1741.. Compare: "Tenez voilà", dit-elle, "à chacun une écaille, Des sottises d'

author: Alexander Pope
text: Let such, such only tread this sacred floor, Who dare to love their country and be poor.
citation: Inscription on the entrance to his grotto in Twickenham, published in "Verses on a Grotto by the River Thames at Twickenham, composed of Marbles, Spars and Minerals", line 14, (written 1740, published 1741); also quoted as "Who dared to lov

author: Alexander Pope
text: Vain was the chief's, the sage's pride! They had no poet, and they died. In vain they schem'd, in vain they bled! They had no poet, and are dead.
citation: Odes, Book iv, Ode 9, reported in William Warburton, The Works of Alexander Pope, Esq (1751) p. 31

author: Alexander Pope
text: Ye Gods! annihilate but space and time, And make two lovers happy.
citation: Martinus Scriblerus on the Art of Sinking in Poetry, Chap. xi, reported in William Warburton, The Works of Alexander Pope, Esq (1751) p. 196

author: Alexander Pope
text: Here am I, dying of a hundred good symptoms.
citation: Pope's reply when told by his physician that he was better, on the morning of his death (30 May 1744), as quoted by Owen Ruffhead in The Life of Alexander Pope; With a Critical Essay on His Writings and Genius (1769), p. 475

author: Alexander Pope
text: Where'er you walk, cool gales shall fan the glade, Trees, where you sit, shall crowd into a shade: Where'er you tread, the blushing flow'rs shall rise, And all things flourish where you turn your eyes.
citation: Summer, line 73

author: Alexander Pope
text: Say, is not absence death to those who love?
citation: Autumn

author: Alexander Pope
text: Let opening roses knotted oaks adorn, And liquid amber drop from every thorn.
citation: Autumn, line 36

author: Alexander Pope
text: The garlands fade, the vows are worn away; So dies her love, and so my hopes decay.
citation: Autumn, line 70

author: Alexander Pope
text: The flying Rumours gather'd as they roll'd, Scarce any Tale was sooner heard than told; And all who told it, added something new, And all who heard it, made Enlargements too, In ev'ry Ear it spread, on ev'ry Tongue it grew.
citation: Lines 468-472

author: Alexander Pope
text: Nor Fame I slight, nor for her favors call; She comes unlooked for, if she comes at all.
citation: Line 513

author: Alexander Pope
text: Unblemish'd let me live, or die unknown; O grant an honest fame, or grant me none!
citation: Closing line

author: Alexander Pope
text: Vital spark of heav'nly flame! Quit, oh quit, this mortal frame: Trembling, hoping, ling'ring, flying, Oh the pain, the bliss of dying!
citation: Stanza 1

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I have at last come to the end of the Faerie Queene: and though I say "at last", I almost wish he had lived to write six books more as he had hoped to do — so much have I enjoyed it.
citation: Letter to Arthur Greeves (7 March 1916); in Walter Hooper, ed., The Collected Letters of C.S. Lewis: Family Letters, 1905–1931 (2004), p. 170

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I can't imagine a man really enjoying a book and reading it only once.
citation: Letter to Arthur Greeves (February 1932); in They Stand Together: The Letters of C. S. Lewis to Arthur Greeves, 1914–1963 (1979), p. 439

author: C. S. Lewis
text: For me, reason is the natural organ of truth; but imagination is the organ of meaning. Imagination, producing new metaphors or revivifying old, is not the cause of truth, but its condition.
citation: "Bluspels and Flalansferes: A Semantic Nightmare", in Rehabilitations and Other Essays (1939)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Only the skilled can judge the skilfulness, but that is not the same as judging the value of the result.
citation: A Preface to Paradise Lost (1942), Chapter 2: "Is Criticism Possible?"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: The heart of Christianity is a myth which is also a fact.
citation: "Myth Became Fact" (1944)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen. Not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.
citation: "Is Theology Poetry?" (1945)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I believe Buddhism to be a simplification of Hinduism and Islam to be a simplification of Xianity.
citation: Letter to Sheldon Vanauken (14 December 1950), quoted in Kathryn Ann Lindskoog, Sleuthing C. S. Lewis (2001), [http://books.google.com/books?id=8ZfLXXLZM9UC&pg=PA393&dq=%22I+believe+Buddhism+to+be+a+simplification+of+Hinduism+and+Islam+to+b

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I think that if God forgives us we must forgive ourselves. Otherwise it is almost like setting up ourselves as a higher tribunal than Him.
citation: Letter (19 April 1951); in Letters of C. S. Lewis (1966), p. 230

author: C. S. Lewis
text: It is Christ Himself, not the Bible, who is the true Word of God. The Bible, read in the right spirit and with the guidance of good teachers, will bring us to Him.
citation: Letter (8 November 1952); in Letters of C. S. Lewis (1966), p. 247

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I am almost inclined to set it up as a canon that a children's story which is enjoyed only by children is a bad children's story. The good ones last. A waltz which you can like only when you are waltzing is a bad waltz.
citation: "On Three Ways of Writing for Children" (1952); in Of Other Worlds: Essays and Stories (1967), p. 24

author: C. S. Lewis
text: He [the child] does not despise real woods because he has read of enchanted woods: the reading makes all real woods a little enchanted.
citation: [https://www.catholicculture.org/culture/library/view.cfm?recnum=9117 "On Three Ways of Writing for Children"] (1952)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I became my own only when I gave myself to Another.
citation: Letter (17 July 1953); Letters of C. S. Lewis (1966), p. 251

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Every story of conversion is the story of a blessed defeat.
citation: Foreword to Joy Davidman's Smoke on the Mountain (1954)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Where we find a difficulty we may always expect that a discovery awaits us. Where there is cover we hope for game.
citation: Reflections on the Psalms (1958), ch. III: Cursings

author: C. S. Lewis
text: The very man who has argued you down will sometimes be found, years later, to have been influenced by what you said.
citation: Reflections on the Psalms (1958), ch. VII: Connivance, p. 73

author: C. S. Lewis
text: A strict allegory is like a puzzle with a solution: a great romance is like a flower whose smell reminds you of something you can't quite place. I think the something is 'the whole quality of life as we actually experience it.'
citation: Letter to Lucy (11 September 1958); in C. S. Lewis' Letters to Children (1988)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: We are not necessarily doubting that God will do the best for us; we are wondering how painful the best will turn out to be.
citation: Letter (29 April 1959); Letters of C. S. Lewis (1966), p. 285

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Everything" is a subject on which there is not much to be said.
citation: Studies in Words (1960), ch. 2

author: C. S. Lewis
text: There are some things about your own village that you never know until you have been away from it.
citation: Studies in Words (1960), ch. 11

author: C. S. Lewis
text: A great myth is relevant as long as the predicament of humanity lasts; as long as humanity lasts. It will always work, on those who can receive it, the same catharsis.
citation: "Haggard Rides Again", in Time and Tide, Vol. XLI (3 September 1960)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Jove laughed to see The abyss empeopled, his bliss imparted, the throng that was his and no longer he.
citation: "Le Roi S'Amuse", st. 6; in Poems (1964), p. 24

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Leavis demands moral earnestness; I prefer morality. . . . I'd sooner live among people who don’t cheat at cards than among people who are earnest about not cheating at cards.
citation: "Unreal Estates", Conversation with Brian Aldiss and Kingsley Amis — in Spectrum IV (New York: Harcourt, Brace & World, 1965), p. 21

author: C. S. Lewis
text: The process of being brought up, however well it is done, cannot fail to offend.
citation: "The Funeral of a Great Myth", in Walter Hooper, ed., Christian Reflections (1967)

author: C. S. Lewis
text: He begins to think for himself and meets Nineteenth-century Rationalism Which can explain away religion by any number of methods.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 19–20

author: C. S. Lewis
text: If you make the same guess often enough it ceases to be a guess and becomes a Scientific Fact. This is the inductive method.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 22

author: C. S. Lewis
text: He came in sight of a pass guarded by armed men. ‘you cannot pass . . . Do you not know that all this country belongs to the Spirit of the Age? . . . Here Enlightenment, take this fugitive to our Master.’
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 44–45

author: C. S. Lewis
text: John – I'm trying to find the Island in the West. Sensible – You refer, no doubt to some aesthetic experience.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 77

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I am sorry that my convictions do not allow me to repeat my friend's offer, said one of the others. But I have had to abandon the humanitarian and egalitarian fancies. His name was Mr. Neo-Classical.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 89

author: C. S. Lewis
text: I hope, said the third, that your wanderings in lonely places do not mean that you have any of the romantic virus still in your blood. His name was Mr. Humanist.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 90

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Mr. Neo-Angular – I am doing my duty. My ethics are based on dogma, not on feeling. Vertue – I know that a rule is to be obeyed because it is a rule and not because it appeals to my feelings at the moment.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 90

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Savage – There is only one way fit for a man – Heroism, or Master-Morality, or Violence. All the other people in between are ploughing the sand.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 100

author: C. S. Lewis
text: But supposing one tries to live by Pantheistic philosophy? Does it lead to a complacent Hegelian optimism?
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 132–133

author: C. S. Lewis
text: The wraith of Sigmund said. “You know what this is, I suppose. Religious melancholia. Stop while there is time. If you dive, you dive into insanity.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 168

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Mr. Sensible learned only catchwords from them. He could talk like Epicurus of spare diet, but he was a glutton. He had from Montaigne the language of friendship, but no friend.
citation: Pilgrim's Regress 176

author: C. S. Lewis
text: And I say also this. I do not think the forest would be so bright, nor the water so warm, nor love so sweet, if there were no danger in the lakes.
citation: Hyoi, p. 76

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Try to exclude the possibility of suffering which the order of nature and the existence of free-wills involve, and you find that you have excluded life itself.
citation: Ch. II: "Divine Omnipotence"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Love is something more stern and splendid than mere kindness.
citation: Ch. III: "Divine Goodness"

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Love may forgive all infirmities and love still in spite of them: but Love cannot cease to will their removal.
citation: Ch. III

author: C. S. Lewis
text: If He who in Himself can lack nothing chooses to need us, it is because we need to be needed.
citation: Ch. III

author: C. S. Lewis
text: Everyone feels benevolent if nothing happens to be annoying him at the moment.
citation: Ch. IV: "Human Wickedness"

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: And how much better to die in all the happy period of undisillusioned youth, to go out in a blaze of light, than to have your body worn out and old and illusions shattered.
citation: Letter to his family (18 October 1918); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker. It was also published in The Oak Parker (Oak Park, IL) on 16 November 1918. Only 19 years old at the time, Hemi

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Switzerland is a small, steep country, much more up and down than sideways, and is all stuck over with large brown hotels built on the cuckoo clock style of architecture.
citation: In The Toronto Star Weekly (4 March 1922)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Somebody just back of you while you are fishing is as bad as someone looking over your shoulder while you write a letter to your girl.
citation: "Trout Fishing in Europe", in The Toronto Star Weekly (17 November 1923)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: A man's got to take a lot of punishment to write a really funny book.
citation: Letter (6 December 1924); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: The age demanded that we dance And jammed us into iron pants. And in the end the age was handed The sort of shit that it demanded.
citation: "The Age Demanded" in Der Querschnitt (February 1925); as quoted in Sylvia Beach and the Lost Generation (1983) by Noel Riley Fitch

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Write me at the Hotel Quintana, Pamplona, Spain. Or don't you like to write letters. I do because it's such a swell way to keep from working and yet feel you've done something
citation: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (1 July 1925); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: In the fall the war was always there but we did not go to it any more.
citation: "In Another Country" in Men Without Women (1927).

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: The good parts of a book may be only something a writer is lucky enough to overhear or it may be the wreck of his whole damn life — and one is as good as the other.
citation: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (4 September 1929); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: That terrible mood of depression of whether it's any good or not is what is known as The Artist's Reward.
citation: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (13 September 1929); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: I know monks masturbate at night That pet cats screw That some girls bite And yet What can I do To set things right?
citation: "The Earnest Liberal's Lament" (1924) in The Suppressed Poems (1929)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: I've been in love (truly) with five women, the Spanish Republic and the 4th Infantry Division.
citation: Letter to Marlene Dietrich (1 July 1930) [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/1547504/Hemingway-and-Dietrich-letters.html?service=print "Hemingway and Dietrich letters"], The Telegraph (April 3, 2007)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Eschew the monumental. Shun the Epic. All the guys who can paint great big pictures can paint great small ones.
citation: Letter (5–6 January 1932); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: When you have shot one bird flying you have shot all birds flying. They are all different and they fly in different ways but the sensation is the same and the last one is as good as the first.
citation: Nick Adams of "Fathers and Sons" in Winner Take Nothing (1932)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: That is what we are supposed to do when we are at our best — make it all up — but make it up so truly that later it will happen that way.
citation: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (28 May 1934); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Here is the piece. If you can't say fornicate can you say copulate or if not that can you say co-habit? If not that would have to say consummate I suppose. Use your own good taste and judgment.
citation: Letter to Esquire editor Arnold Gingrich (11 April 1935); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Certainly there is no hunting like the hunting of man and those who have hunted armed men long enough and liked it, never really care for anything else thereafter.
citation: Introduction to "On the Blue Water" (April 1936)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: However you make your living is where your talent lies.
citation: "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," first published in Esquire (August 1936); later published in The Fifth Column and the First Forty-Nine Stories (1938)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Ezra was right half the time, and when he was wrong, he was so wrong you were never in any doubt about it.
citation: On Ezra Pound, as quoted in The New Republic (11 November 1936)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: For our dead are a part of the earth of Spain now and the earth of Spain can never die.
citation: "On the American Dead in Spain", New Masses (February 14, 1939)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: As long as all our dead live in the Spanish earth, and they will live as long as the earth lives, no system of tyranny ever will prevail in Spain.
citation: "On the American Dead in Spain", New Masses (February 14, 1939)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: There are events which are so great that if a writer has participated in them his obligation is to write truly rather than assume the presumption of altering them with invention.
citation: Preface to The Great Crusade (1940) by Gustav Regler

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: I don't like to write like God. It is only because you never do it, though, that the critics think you can't do it.
citation: Letter (26 August 1940); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Go tell Mike Gold, Ernest Hemingway says he should go fuck himself.
citation: In response to Communist writer Mike Gold's criticism of Hemingway's depiction of the Spanish Civil War in For Whom the Bell Tolls; as quoted in Carlos Baker, Ernest Hemingway: A Life, New York, Scribners, 1969, p. 459.

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Cowardice, as distinguished from panic, is almost always simply a lack of ability to suspend the functioning of the imagination.
citation: Introduction to Men at War (1942)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Once we have a war there is only one thing to do. It must be won. For defeat brings worse things than any that can ever happen in war.
citation: Introduction to Men at War (1942)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: All my life I've looked at words as though I were seeing them for the first time.
citation: Letter (9 April 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: It wasn't by accident that the Gettysburg address was so short. The laws of prose writing are as immutable as those of flight, of mathematics, of physics.
citation: Letter (23 July 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: You see it's awfully hard to talk or write about your own stuff because if it is any good you yourself know about how good it is — but if you say so yourself you feel like a shit.
citation: Letter to Malcolm Cowley (17 October 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Scott took LITERATURE so solemnly. He never understood that it was just writing as well as you can and finishing what you start.
citation: Letter to Arthur Mizener (12 May 1950); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Wars are Spinach. Life in general is the tough part. In war all you have to do is not worry and know how to read a map and co-ordinates.
citation: Letter to Marlene Dietrich (27 June 1950) [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/1547504/Hemingway-and-Dietrich-letters.html?service=print "Hemingway and Dietrich letters"], The Telegraph (April 3, 2007)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Writing and travel broaden your ass if not your mind and I like to write standing up.
citation: Letter (9 July 1950); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: I still need more healthy rest in order to work at my best. My health is the main capital I have and I want to administer it intelligently.
citation: Letter (21 February 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Having books published is very destructive to writing. It is even worse than making love too much. Because when you make love too much at least you get a damned clarte that is like no other light. A very clear and hollow light.
citation: Letter to Bernard Berenson (2 October 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: I wish I could write well enough to write about aircraft. Faulkner did it very well in Pylon but you cannot do something someone else has done though you might have done it if they hadn't.
citation: Letter (3 July 1956); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Pound's crazy. All poets are.... They have to be. You don't put a poet like Pound in the loony bin. For history's sake we shouldn't keep him there.
citation: As quoted in The New York Post (24 January 1957)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: We are all apprentices in a craft where no one ever becomes a master.
citation: New York Journal-American (11 July 1961)

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: Forget your personal tragedy. We are all bitched from the start and you especially have to be hurt like hell before you can write seriously. But when you get the damned hurt use it — don't cheat with it.
citation: Letter to F Scott Fitzgerald, as quoted in Scott Fitzgerald (1962) by Andrew Turnbull (1962) Ch. 14

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: If you have a success, you have it for the wrong reasons. If you become popular it is always because of the worst aspects of your work.
citation: As quoted in That Summer in Paris (1963) by Morley Callaghan

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: I learned never to empty the well of my writing, but always to stop when there was still something there in the deep part of the well, and let it refill at night from the springs that fed it.
citation: As quoted in Reporting (1964) by Lillian Ross

author: Ernest Hemingway
text: When I have an idea, I turn down the flame, as if it were a little alcohol stove, as low as it will go. Then it explodes and that is my idea.
citation: As quoted in Charmed Circle: Gertrude Stein & Co. (1974) by James Mellow

author: George Orwell
text: This means no more than vae victis - woe to the creed that is not backed by machine-guns!
citation: Review of The Two Carlyles by Osbert Burdett, in The Adelphi (March 1931)

author: George Orwell
text: As to a pseudonym, a name I always use when tramping etc is P. S. Burton, but if you don't think this sounds a probable kind of name, what about Kenneth Miles, George Orwell, H. Lewis Allways. I rather favour George Orwell.
citation: Letter to Leonard Moore (19 November 1932) The Collected Essays, Journalism & Letters, George Orwell: An Age Like This, 1920–1940, Editors: Sonia Orwell, Ian Angus. p. 106.

author: George Orwell
text: Man is not a Yahoo, but he is rather like a Yahoo and needs to be reminded of it from time to time.
citation: Review of Tropic of Cancer, in New English Weekly (14 November 1935)

author: George Orwell
text: It is a mysterious thing, the loss of faith-as mysterious as faith itself. Like faith, it is ultimately not rooted in logic; it is a change in the climate of the mind.
citation: A Clergyman's Daughter, Ch. 5

author: George Orwell
text: The essential job is to get people to recognise war propaganda when they see it, especially when it is disguised as peace propaganda.
citation: Review of The Men I Killed by Brigadier-General F. P. Crozier, CB, CMG, DSO, in New Statesman and Nation (28 August 1937)

author: George Orwell
text: One is almost driven to the cynical conclusion that men are only decent when they are powerless.
citation: Review of The Freedom of the Streets by Jack Common, June 1938, pp. 335-6

author: George Orwell
text: If there are certain pages of Mr Bertrand Russell's book, Power, which seem rather empty, that is merely to say that we have now sunk to a depth at which the restatement of the obvious is the first duty of intelligent men.
citation: Review of Power: A New Social Analysis by Bertrand Russell in The Adelphi (January 1939) Paraphrased variant: Sometimes the first duty of intelligent men is the restatement of the obvious.

author: George Orwell
text: It is quite possible that we are descending into an age in which two plus two will make five when the Leader says so.
citation: Review of Power: A New Social Analysis by Bertrand Russell in The Adelphi (January 1939)

author: George Orwell
text: Has it ever struck you that there's a thin man inside every fat man, just as they say there's a statue inside every block of stone?
citation: Coming Up for Air, Part 1, Ch. 3

author: George Orwell
text: Perhaps a man really dies when his brain stops, when he loses the power to take in a new idea.
citation: Coming Up for Air, Part 3, Ch. 1

author: George Orwell
text: Adults are only less superstitious than children in proportion as they have more power over their environment. In predicaments where everyone is powerless (eg war, gambling) everyone is superstitious
citation: New Words (1940) The Collected Essays, Journalism & Letters, George Orwell: My Country Right or Left, 1940–1943, Editors: Sonia Orwell, Ian Angus. p. 9 (footnote)

author: George Orwell
text: We are in a strange period of history in which a revolutionary has to be a patriot and a patriot has to be a revolutionary.
citation: Letter to The Tribune (20 December 1940), later published in A Patriot After All, 1940-1941 (1999)

author: George Orwell
text: Society has always to demand a little more from human beings than it will get in practice.
citation: "The Art of Donald McGill" (1941)

author: George Orwell
text: Since pacifists have more freedom of action in countries where traces of democracy survive, pacifism can act more effectively against democracy than for it. Objectively the pacifist is pro-Nazi.
citation: "No, Not One," The Adelphi (October 1941) See his later thoughts on this statement below from "As I Please," Tribune (8 December 1944)

author: George Orwell
text: Everyone believes in the atrocities of the enemy and disbelieves in those of his own side, without ever bothering to examine the evidence.
citation: "Looking Back on the Spanish War" (Autumn 1942) The Collected Essays, Journalism & Letters, George Orwell: My Country Right or Left, 1940–1943, Editors: Sonia Orwell, Ian Angus. p. 252

author: George Orwell
text: Both men were the spiritual children of Voltaire, both had an ironical, sceptical view of life, and a native pessimism overlaid by gaiety; both knew that the existing social order is a swindle and its cherished beliefs mostly delusions.
citation: On Mark Twain and Anatole France, in "Mark Twain - The Licensed Jester" in Tribune (26 November 1943); reprinted in The Collected Essays, Journalism and Letters of George Orwell (1968)

author: George Orwell
text: In my small way I have been fighting for years against the systematic faking of history which now goes on.
citation: Letter to Frank Barber (15 December 1944) The Collected Essays, Journalism & Letters, George Orwell: As I Please, 1943-1945, Editors: Sonia Orwell, Ian Angus. p. 292.

author: George Orwell
text: Particularly on the Left, political thought is a sort of masturbation fantasy in which the world of facts hardly matters.
citation: "London Letter" in Partisan Review (Winter 1945)

author: George Orwell
text: Autobiography is only to be trusted when it reveals something disgraceful. A man who gives a good account of himself is probably lying, since any life when viewed from the inside is simply a series of defeats.
citation: "Benefit Of Clergy: Some Notes On Salvador Dalí," Dickens, Dali & Others: Studies in Popular Culture (1944) [http://orwell.ru/library/reviews/dali/english/e_dali]

author: George Orwell
text: Serious sport has nothing to do with fair play. It is bound up with hatred, jealousy, boastfulness, disregard of all rules and sadistic pleasure in witnessing violence: in other words it is war minus the shooting.
citation: [http://orwell.ru/library/articles/spirit/english/e_spirit "The Sporting Spirit"], Tribune (14 December 1945)

author: George Orwell
text: It is just thinkable that books may some day be written by machinery....
citation: Review of A Coat of Many Colours: Occasional Essays by Herbert Read, Poetry Quarterly (Winter 1945)

author: George Orwell
text: Totalitarianism demands, in fact, the continuous alteration of the past, and in the long run probably demands a disbelief in the very existence of objective truth.

author: George Orwell

author: George Orwell

author: George Orwell
text: If liberty means anything at all, it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear.

author: George Orwell
text: To see what is in front of one's nose needs a constant struggle.

author: George Orwell

author: Carl Jung

citation: "A Philologist on Esperanto" in The British Esperantist (May 1932). Years later, in an incomplete draft of a letter (1956; quoted more extensively below) he stated that Esperanto and other constructed languages like Volapuk, Ido and Novial

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: I have the hatred of apartheid in my bones...
citation: Valedictory address to the University of Oxford (1959)

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: I liked him better than all the other characters[…]
citation: Referring to Gollum. From J. R. R. Tolkien: An Audio Portrait, BBC Radio Collection (2001), {{ISBN|0-563-53692-6}}. CD 1, track 17. Originally from the 1964 interview with Denys Gueroult, first broadcast in 1971.

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: Every morning I wake up and think good, another 24 hours' pipe-smoking.
citation: A rare interview with Tolkien (1966) — [http://www.theguardian.com/books/1991/dec/28/jrrtolkien.classics "Tolkien's shire" by John Ezard, The Guardian (28 December 1991)]

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: If you really come down to any large story that interests people – holds the attention for a considerable time ... human stories are practically always about one thing, aren't they? Death. The inevitability of death.
citation: [http://www.bbc.co.uk/archive/writers/12237.shtml Tolkien in Oxford (1968)], a BBC 2 television documentary (at 21:49)

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: It gives me great pleasure, a good name. I always in writing start with a name. Give me a name and it produces a story, not the other way about normally.
citation: [http://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/1964_BBC_Interview 1964 BBC Interview] with Denys Gueroult, first broadcast on the BBC Radio 4 programme "Now Read On" (January 1971)

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: I do so dearly believe that no half-heartedness and no worldly fear must turn us aside from following the light unflinchingly.
citation: Letter to Edith, as quoted in J. R. R. Tolkien: a biography (1977) by Humphrey Carpenter, p. 66

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: I wish life was not so short," he thought. "Languages take such a time, and so do all the things one wants to know about.
citation: "Alboin Errol", in The Lost Road (1987). Compare this with "The lyf so short, the craft so longe to lerne" by Geoffrey Chaucer

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: A story must be told or there'll be no story, yet it is the untold stories that are most moving.
citation: No. 96: To his son Christopher (30 January 1945)

author: J. R. R. Tolkien
text: You can make the Ring an allegory of our own time, if you like: an allegory of the inevitable fate that awaits all attempts to defeat evil power by power. But that is only because all power magical or mechanical does always so work.
citation: No. 109: To his publisher (31 July 1947)

author: Virginia Woolf
text: I bought the blue paper book [Ulysses], & read it here one summer I think with spasms of wonder, of discovery, & then again with long lapses of immense boredom.
citation: Diary entry January 15, 1941.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The Reverend C. L. Dodgson had no life. He passed through the world so lightly that he left no print. He melted so passively into Oxford that he is invisible.
citation: Essay "Lewis Carroll" (1939); reprinted in The Moment, and Other Essays (1948)

author: Virginia Woolf
text: For some reason, we know not what, his childhood was sharply severed. It lodged in him whole and entire. He could not disperse it.
citation: Essay "Lewis Carroll" (1939)

author: Virginia Woolf
text: One cannot grow fine flowers in a thin soil.
citation: Women and Writing (New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1979), p. 54. Also in {{cite book |title=The Essays of Virginia Woolf: 1929-1932 |date=1986 |publisher=Hogarth Press |isbn=978-0-7012-0670-3 |page=122 |url=https://www.google.com/books

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Let us record the atoms as they fall upon the mind in the order in which they fall, let us trace the pattern, however disconnected and incoherent in appearance, which each sight or incident scores upon the consciousness.
citation: "Modern Fiction"

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Theirs, too, is the word-coining genius, as if thought plunged into a sea of words and came up dripping.
citation: "Notes on an Elizabethan Play"

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Humour is the first of the gifts to perish in a foreign tongue.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=lQLAv2zRY7MC&q="Humour+is+the+first+of+the+gifts+to+perish+in+a+foreign+tongue"&pg=PA36#v=onepage On Not Knowing Greek]

author: Virginia Woolf
text: For our penitence deserves a glimpse only; our toil respite only.
citation: Part II, Ch. 3

author: Virginia Woolf
text: She alone spoke the truth; to her alone could he speak it. That was the source of her everlasting attraction for him, perhaps; she was a person to whom one could say what came into one's head.
citation: Part III, Ch. 9

author: Virginia Woolf
text: A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: No need to hurry. No need to sparkle. No need to be anybody but oneself.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The beauty of the world which is so soon to perish, has two edges, one of laughter, one of anguish, cutting the heart asunder.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: If truth is not to be found on the shelves of the British Museum, where, I asked myself, picking up a notebook and a pencil, is truth?

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Have you any notion how many books are written about women in the course of one year? Have you any notion how many are written by men? Are you aware that you are, perhaps, the most discussed animal in the universe?

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Women have served all these centuries as looking-glasses possessing the magic and delicious power of reflecting the figure of man at twice its natural size.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman.
citation: Ch. 3, p. 51 Very often misquoted as "For most of history, Anonymous was a woman."

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Literature is strewn with the wreckage of men who have minded beyond reason the opinions of others.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The history of men's opposition to women's emancipation is more interesting perhaps than the story of that emancipation itself.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=CoP1GxjoNnsC&q="The+history+of+men's+opposition+to+women's+emancipation+is+more+interesting+perhaps+than+the+story+of+that+emancipation+itself"&pg=PA72#v=onepage Ch. 3, p. 72)]

author: Virginia Woolf
text: It is the nature of the artist to mind excessively what is said about him. Literature is strewn with the wreckage of men who have minded beyond reason the opinions of others.
citation: [http://books.google.com/books?id=HSRFAAAAYAAJ&q=%22It+is+the+nature+of+the+artist+to+mind+excessively+what+is+said+about+him+Literature+is+strewn+with+the+wreckage+of+men+who+have+minded+beyond+reason+the+opinions+of+others%22&pg=PA98#v=on

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Lock up your libraries if you like; but there is no gate, no lock, no bolt that you can set upon the freedom of my mind.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: He — for there could be no doubt of his sex, though the fashion of the time did something to disguise it — was in the act of slicing at the head of a Moor which swung from the rafters.
citation: Ch. 1, first lines

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Better was it to go unknown and leave behind you an arch, a potting shed, a wall where peaches ripen, than to burn like meteor and leave no dust.
citation: Ch. 2

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The sound of the trumpets died away and Orlando stood stark naked. No human being, since the world began, has ever looked more ravishing. His form combined in one the strength of a man and a woman's grace.
citation: Ch. 3

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The chief charges against her were (1) that she was dead, and therefore could not hold any property; (2) that she was a woman which amounts to much the same thing ...
citation: Ch. 4

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Only those who have little need of the truth, and no respect for it — the poets and novelists — can be trusted to do it, for this is one of the cases where the truth does no exist. Nothing exists. The whole thing is a miasma — a mirage.
citation: Ch. 4

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Society is the most powerful conception in the world and society has no existence whatsoever.
citation: Ch. 4

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Old Madame du Deffand and her friends talked for fifty years without stopping. And of it all, what remains? Perhaps three witty sayings.
citation: Ch. 4

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Thus, there is much to support the view that it is clothes that wear us and not we them; we may make them take the mould of arm or breast, but they mould our hearts, our brains, our tongues to their liking.
citation: Chapter 4

author: Virginia Woolf
text: As long as she thinks of a man, nobody objects to a woman thinking.
citation: Ch. 6

author: Virginia Woolf
text: But look — he flicks his hand to the back of his neck. For such gesture one falls hopelessly in love for a lifetime.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: For I am more selves than Neville thinks. We are not simple as our friends would have us to meet their needs. Yet love is simple.
citation: Bernard, section III

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Among the tortures and devastations of life is this then — our friends are not able to finish their stories.
citation: Ch. II

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Things have dropped from me. I have outlived certain desires; I have lost friends, some by death... others through sheer inability to cross the street.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Though we see the same world, we see it through different eyes. Any help we can give you must be different from that you can give yourselves, and perhaps the value of that help may lie in the fact of that difference.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Directly the mulberry tree begins to make you circle, break off. Pelt the tree with laughter.

author: Virginia Woolf
text: The artist after all is a solitary being.
citation: "The Historian and 'The Gibbon'"

author: Virginia Woolf
text: Lines slip easily down the accustomed grooves. The old designs are copied so glibly that we are half inclined to think them original, save for that very glibness.
citation: "A Letter to a Young Poet"

author: Virginia Woolf
text: I mean, what is a woman? I assure you, I do not know. I do not believe that you know. I do not believe that anybody can know until she has expressed herself in all the arts and professions open to human skill.
citation: "Professions for Women"

author: Virginia Woolf
text: If you do not tell the truth about yourself you cannot tell it about other people.
citation: "The Leaning Tower", lecture delivered to the Workers' Educational Association, Brighton (May 1940)

author: Virginia Woolf
text: If, then, one should try to sum up the character of women's fiction at the present moment, one would say that it is courageous; it is sincere; it keeps closely to what women feel. It is not bitter. It does not insist upon its femininity.
citation: "Women and Fiction"

author: Leonardo da Vinci
text: It is the infinite alone that cannot be attained, for if it could it would become finite.
citation: [http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/29904 Thoughts on Art and Life, by Leonardo da Vinci], (1906)

author: Leonardo da Vinci
text: Subito salse in me due cose: paura e desiderio: paura per la minacciante e scura spelonca, desiderio per vedere se là entro fusse alcuna miracolosa cosa. (Ancient Italian)
citation: At once two things came to mind: fear and desire: fear of the threatening dark cave, desire to see if there was anything miraculous within it.(referring to the "Cave of Acquabianca" or "La Ferrera" on Lake Comuntain).

author: Leonardo da Vinci
text: Tristo è quel discepolo che non avanza il suo maestro. (Modern Italian)
citation: Poor is the pupil that does not surpass his master.

author: Leonardo da Vinci
text: Whoever in discussion adduces authority uses not intellect but rather memory.
citation: Variant translations: Anyone who conducts an argument by appealing to authority is not using his intelligence; he is just using his memory. As quoted in The Book of Unusual Quotations (1957) by Rudolf Flesch, p. 12 Any one who in discussion

text: Human subtlety...will never devise an invention more beautiful, more simple or more direct than does nature, because in her inventions nothing is lacking, and nothing is superfluous.
citation: Richter II [http://books.google.de/books?id=A7dUhbBfmzMC&pg=PA126 p. 126 no. 837 books.google]

author: Leonardo da Vinci

citation: "Of servants"

author: Aldous Huxley
text: I can sympathize with people's pains, but not with their pleasures. There is something curiously boring about somebody else's happiness.
citation: Limbo (1920), "Cynthia"

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Stupidity or reason? Oh, there was no choice now. It was imbecility every time.
citation: Mortal Coils (1921), "The Gioconda Smile"

author: Aldous Huxley
text: I'm afraid of losing my obscurity. Genuineness only thrives in the dark. Like celery.

author: Aldous Huxley
text: What the cinema can do better than literature or the spoken drama is to be fantastic.

author: Aldous Huxley
text: To his dog, every man is Napoleon; hence the constant popularity of dogs.
citation: In Reader's Digest (1934){{fix cite}}

text: My sympathies are, of course, with the Government side, especially the Anarchists; for Anarchism seems to me more likely to lead to desirable social change than highly centralized, dictatorial Communism.

author: Aldous Huxley

author: Aldous Huxley
text: At least two thirds of our miseries spring from human stupidity, human malice, and those great motivators and justifiers of malice and stupidity, idealism, dogmatism and proselytizing zeal on behalf of religious or political idols.

author: Aldous Huxley
text: The trouble with fiction... is that it makes too much sense. Reality never makes sense.

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Of course I base my characters partly on the people I know—one can't escape it—but fictional characters are oversimplified; they're much less complex than the people one knows.

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Brutes are merely brutal; men and women are capable of being devils and lunatics. They are no less capable of being fully human-even, occasionally, of being a bit more than fully human, of being saints, heroes and geniuses.
citation: Introduction to You Are Not The Target by Laura Archera Huxley (1963)

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Words are good servants but bad masters.
citation: As quoted by Laura Huxley, in conversation with Alan Watts about her memoir This Timeless Moment (1968), in Pacifica Archives #BB2037 [sometime between 1968-1973])

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Music is an ocean, but the repertory is hardly even a lake; it is a pond.
citation: Interview in Time magazine (December 1957)

author: Aldous Huxley
text: It's with bad sentiments that one makes good novels.
citation: Letter (10 July 1962), quoted in Donald Watt (ed.) Aldous Huxley: The Citical Heritage (1975)

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Be gentle with them, Timothy. They want to be free, but they don't know how. Teach them. Reassure them.

citation: "Fifth Philosopher's Song", st. 1

text: Shame to have ousted your betters thus, Taking ark while the others remained outside! Better for all of us, froward Homunculus, If you’d quietly died!
citation: "Fifth Philosopher's Song", st. 3

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Beauty for some provides escape, Who gain a happiness in eyeing The gorgeous buttocks of the ape Or Autumn sunsets exquisitely dying.
citation: "Ninth Philosopher's Song"

citation: "Ninth Philosopher's Song"

citation: "Frascati's"

text: All that happens means something; nothing you do is ever insignificant.

citation: Ch. 10

text: After all, what is reading but a vice, like drink or venery or any other form of excessive self-indulgence? One reads to tickle and amuse one's mind; one reads, above all, to prevent oneself thinking.

text: Amour is the one human activity of any importance in which laughter and pleasure preponderate, if ever so slightly, over misery and pain.

text: Words — I wonder if you can realize how much I love them. You are too much preoccupied with mere things and ideas and people to understand the full beauty of words. Your mind is not a literary mind.
citation: Ch. 20 (Denis)

author: Aldous Huxley
text: The creation by word-power of something out of nothing--what is that but magic? And, may I add, what is that but literature?

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Everything that ever gets done in this world is done by madmen.

text: If you want to get men to act reasonably, you must set about persuading them in a maniacal manner.
citation: Ch. 22 (Mr. Scogan)

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Nature, or anything that reminds me of nature, disturbs me; it is too large, too complicated, above all too utterly pointless and incomprehensible.
citation: Ch. 23 (Mr. Scogan)

text: He liked to think of himself as a merciless vivisector probing into the palpitating entrails of his own soul.

author: Aldous Huxley
text: When one individual comes into intimate contact with another, she — or he, of course, as the case may be — must almost inevitably receive or inflict suffering.
citation: Ch. 24 (Mary)

author: Aldous Huxley
text: Beetles, black beetles” — his father had a really passionate feeling about the clergy. Mumbojumbery was another of his favourite words. An atheist and an anti-clerical of the strict old school he was.
citation: Ch. 1

author: Warren Buffett
text: You're dealing with a lot of silly people in the marketplace; it's like a great big casino and everyone else is boozing. If you can stick with Pepsi, you should be O.K.
citation: On being dispassionate and patient in investments, in an interview in Forbes magazine (1 November 1974); he is contrasting soft-drinks to intoxicating beverages in this example; Buffett eventually became a major investor in Coca-Cola.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Love is the greatest advantage a parent can give.
citation: As quoted in [http://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/1986/09/29/68098/index.htm "Should You Leave It All to the Children?" by Richard I. Kirkland Jr, in Fortune (29 September 1986)]

author: Warren Buffett
text: I'll tell you why I like the cigarette business. ... It costs a penny to make. Sell it for a dollar. It's addictive. And there's fantastic brand loyalty.
citation: As quoted in Barbarians at the Gate : The Fall of RJR Nabisco (1989), by Bryan Burrough and John Helyar

author: Warren Buffett
text: Someone's sitting in the shade today because someone planted a tree a long time ago.
citation: Statement of January 1991, as quoted in Of Permanent Value: The Story of Warren Buffett (2007) by Andrew Kilpatrick

author: Warren Buffett
text: Never count on making a good sale. Have the purchase price be so attractive that even a mediocre sale gives good results.
citation: As quoted in Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist (1995), by Roger Lowenstein, p. 77

author: Warren Buffett
text: I like thinking big. I always have. To me it's very simple: if you're going to be thinking anyway, you might as well think big.
citation: As quoted in Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist (1995), by Roger Lowenstein, p. 77

author: Warren Buffett
text: Wall Street is the only place that people ride to work in a Rolls Royce to get advice from those who take the subway.
citation: As quoted in The Money Adventure (1998) by Egbert Sukop, p. 128

author: Warren Buffett
text: Investors making purchases in an overheated market need to recognize that it may often take an extended period for the value of even an outstanding company to catch up with the price they paid.
citation: 1998 Berkshire Hathaway Annual Meeting, as quoted in The Essays of Warren Buffett : Lessons for Corporate America (1998), p. 92

author: Warren Buffett
text: We don't get paid for activity, just for being right. As to how long we'll wait, we'll wait indefinitely.
citation: 1998 Berkshire Hathaway Annual Meeting, quoted in Wait: The Art and Science of Delay (2012) by Frank Partnoy, p. 177

author: Warren Buffett
text: Success in investing doesn't correlate with I.Q. once you're above the level of 125. Once you have ordinary intelligence, what you need is the temperament to control the urges that get other people into trouble in investing.
citation: As quoted in [http://www.businessweek.com/1999/99_27/b3636006.htm Homespun Wisdom from the "Oracle of Omaha" by Amy Stone in BusinessWeek (5 June 1999)]

author: Warren Buffett
text: The best thing that happens to us is when a great company gets into temporary trouble... We want to buy them when they're on the operating table.
citation: BusinessWeek,[https://books.google.com/books?id=q_PPI4icLLsC&pg=PA33 5 July 1999)]

author: Warren Buffett
text: It's class warfare. My class is winning, but they shouldn't be.
citation: [http://www.cnn.com/2005/US/05/10/buffett/index.html Interview with Lou Dobbs] on CNN (25 May 2005) Buffett has made similar statements in other interviews:

author: Warren Buffett
text: It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it. If you think about that, you'll do things differently.
citation: As quoted in Corporate Survival: The Critical Importance of Sustainability Risk Management (2005) by Dan Robert Anderson, p. 138

author: Warren Buffett
text: You couldn't advance in a finance department in this country unless you taught that the world was flat.
citation: As quoted in [http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B00E1D71E3FF93AA15753C1A9639C8B63 "The Heresy That Made Them Rich" by Joseph Nocera, in The New York Times (29 October 2005)]

author: Warren Buffett
text: People will always try to stop you doing the right thing if it is unconventional.

text: I could end the deficit in five minutes. You just pass a law that says that any time there's a deficit of more than 3% of GDP, all sitting members of Congress are ineligible for re-election.
citation: [http://www.cnbc.com/id/43670783 Interview on CNBC] (1 July 2011)

author: Warren Buffett
text: Anyone who has become rich twice is dumb. Why would you risk what you need and have for what you don’t need? If you are already rich, there is no upside to taking on a lot more risk, but there is disgrace on the downside.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Can you really explain to a fish what it's like to walk on land? One day on land is worth a thousand years of talking about it, and one day running a business has exactly the same kind of value.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Our performance, relatively, is likely to be better in a bear market than in a bull market ... in a year when the general market had a substantial advance, I would be well satisfied to match the advance of the averages.

text: Management's objective is to achieve a return on capital over the long term which averages somewhat higher than that of American industry generally — while utilizing sound accounting and debt policies.
citation: 29 March 1974

text: We will reject interesting opportunities rather than over-leverage our balance sheet.

text: After all, you only find out who is swimming naked when the tide goes out.
citation: [http://www.berkshirehathaway.com/2001ar/2001letter.html 2001 Chairman's Letter]

author: Warren Buffett
text: Investors should remember that excitement and expenses are their enemies. And if they insist on trying to time their participation in equities, they should try to be fearful when others are greedy and greedy only when others are fearful.
citation: [http://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2004.html 2004 Chairman's Letter]

author: Warren Buffett
text: Size seems to make many organizations slow-thinking, resistant to change and smug.
citation: [http://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2006ltr.pdf 2006 Chairman's Letter]

author: Warren Buffett
text: I've reluctantly discarded the notion of my continuing to manage the portfolio after my death — abandoning my hope to give new meaning to the term "thinking outside the box.
citation: 2007 Chairman's Letter

author: Warren Buffett
text: Long ago, Ben Graham taught me that “Price is what you pay; value is what you get.” Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down.
citation: [http://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2008ltr.pdf 2008 Chairman's Letter]

author: Warren Buffett
text: Putting people into homes, though a desirable goal, shouldn't be our country's primary objective. Keeping them in their homes should be the ambition.
citation: 2008 Chairman's Letter

author: Warren Buffett
text: We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow's obligations. When forced to choose, I will not trade even a night's sleep for the chance of extra profits.
citation: 2008 Chairman's Letter

author: Warren Buffett
text: Upon leaving [the derivatives business], our feelings about the business mirrored a line in a country song: "I liked you better before I got to know you so well.
citation: 2008 Chairman's Letter

author: Warren Buffett
text: I eat like a normal 6-year-old, but if you look at the mortality statistics, I mean, 6-year-olds don't die very often.
citation: [http://www.pbs.org/newshour/bb/part-2-billionaire-warren-buffett-says-gop-health-reform-bills-relief-rich/ "Part 2 — Billionaire Warren Buffett says GOP health reform bills are relief for the rich"] PBS Newshour (27 June 2017)

author: Warren Buffett
text: In terms of cryptocurrencies, generally, I can say with almost certainty that they will come to a bad ending.
citation: Quoted in [https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/warren-buffett-predicts-bad-ending-bitcoin-it-doomed-investment Warren Buffett Predicts ‘Bad Ending’ for Bitcoin — Is It a Doomed Investment?] (2018)

author: Walt Disney
text: That's a 30-year-old woman you're bringing me.
citation: 1936 during the casting for 1937's Snow White and the Seven Dwarves, referring to eleven-year-old actress Deanna Durbin, according to Adriana Caselotti (the 19-year-old actress who got the role of Snow White) in a [https://web.archive.org/w

author: Walt Disney
text: All the adversity I've had in my life, all my troubles and obstacles, have strengthened me... You may not realize it when it happens, but a kick in the teeth may be the best thing in the world for you.
citation: As quoted in The Story of Walt Disney (1957)

author: Walt Disney
text: I suppose my formula might be: dream, diversify and never miss an angle.
citation: "Walt's Profit Formula: Dream, Diversity, and Never Miss an Angle" in Wall Street Journal (4 February 1958)

author: Walt Disney
text: We are not influenced by the techniques or fashions of any other company.
citation: Interview with David Griffiths (1959); as quoted in Walt Disney : Conversations (2006) edited by Kathy Merlock Jackson Paraphrased variant: I am not influenced by the techniques or fashions of any other motion picture company.

author: Walt Disney
text: That’s a pretty sexy little girl, Ollie.
citation: November 1966 statement to Ollie Johnston, regarding Mowgli's love interest Shanti) during work on The Jungle Book prior to its 1967 theatre debut; as quoted in a 2003 interview that Michael Mallory had with Ollie prior to Ollie's death in

author: Walt Disney
text: Girls bored me — they still do. I love Mickey Mouse more than any woman I've ever known.
citation: As quoted in You Must Remember This (1975) by Walter Wagner

author: Walt Disney
text: There is more treasure in books than in all the pirates' loot on Treasure Island and at the bottom of the Spanish Main... and best of all, you can enjoy these riches every day of your life.
citation: As quoted in Peter's Quotations : Ideas for Our Time (1977) by Laurence J. Peter

author: Walt Disney
text: We allow no geniuses around our Studio. .. It's kind of fun to do the impossible.
citation: As quoted in Animated Architecture (1982) by Derek Walker, p. 10

author: Walt Disney
text: We're not trying to entertain the critics … I'll take my chances with the public.
citation: As quoted in "Disneyland, 1955: Just Take the Santa Ana Freeway to the American Dream" by Karal Ann Marling, in American Art (Winter-Spring 1991) Variant: We are not trying to entertain the critics. I'll take my chances with the public.

author: Walt Disney
text: I could never convince the financiers that Disneyland was feasible, because dreams offer too little collateral.
citation: As quoted in The Stuff Americans Are Made Of : The Seven Cultural Forces that Define Americans — A New Framework for Quality, Productivity, and Profitability (1996) by Joshua Hammond and James Morrison

author: Walt Disney
text: All right. I'm corny. But I think there's just about a-hundred-and-forty-million people in this country that are just as corny as I am.
citation: As quoted in The Magic Kingdom : Walt Disney and the American Way of Life (2001) by Steven Watts, p. 401

author: Walt Disney
text: What are you doing with a car here in 1860?
citation: To a company publicist at Frontierland in Disneyland, As quoted in Be Our Guest: Perfecting the Art of Customer Service (Disney Editions, 2001) p. 62

author: Walt Disney
text: When we do fantasy, we must not lose sight of reality.
citation: As quoted in Be Our Guest: Perfecting the Art of Customer Service (Disney Editions, 2001) p. 102

author: Walt Disney
text: For every laugh, there should be a tear.
citation: As quoted in The New York Times (2 November 2001); also in The Victory Letters : Inspiration for the Human Race (2003) by Cheri Ruskus, p. 79

author: Walt Disney
text: I do not like to repeat successes, I like to go on to other things.
citation: As quoted in Success (2003) by Ariel Books

author: Walt Disney
text: All you've got to do is own up to your ignorance honestly, and you'll find people who are eager to fill your head with information.
citation: As quoted by Mike Strickland, Director of Photographers at Walt Disney, Co. in Power Marketing for Wedding and Portrait Photographers (2004) by Mitche Graf, p. 19

author: Walt Disney
text: We like to have a point of view in our stories, not an obvious moral, but a worthwhile theme. … All we are trying to do is give the public good entertainment. That is all they want.
citation: As quoted in The Gospel According to Disney : Faith, Trust, and Pixie Dust (2004) by Mark I. Pinsky, p. 2

author: Walt Disney
text: I am interested in entertaining people, in bringing pleasure, particularly laughter, to others, rather than being concerned with "expressing" myself with obscure creative impressions.
citation: Quoted in [http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4191/is_20050507/ai_n14625292/print "The man behind 'The Magic Kingdom'" in The Gazette [Colorado Springs] (7 May 2005)]

author: Walt Disney
text: When I started on Disneyland, my wife used to say, "But why do you want to build an amusement park? They're so dirty." I told her that was just the point — mine wouldn't be.
citation: As quoted in [http://www.viamagazine.com/top_stories/articles/ride_yourlife05.asp "The Rides of Passage" in Via magazine (July 2005)]

author: Walt Disney
text: Animation can explain whatever the mind of man can conceive. This facility makes it the most versatile and explicit means of communication yet devised for quick mass appreciation.
citation: As quoted in OpenGL Shading Language (2006) by Randi J. Rost, p. 411

author: Walt Disney
text: Around here, however, we don't look backwards for very long. We keep moving forward, opening up new doors and doing new things, because we're curious… and curiosity keeps leading us down new paths.
citation: As quoted in the ending credits of the movie Meet the Robinsons (2007)

author: Walt Disney
text: Animation offers a medium of story telling and visual entertainment which can bring pleasure and information to people of all ages everywhere in the world.
citation: As quoted in [http://www.the-review.com/news/article/2344671 "COSI exhibit explores world of cartoons" by Jeffrey Zupanic in The Review (2 August 2007)]

author: Walt Disney
text: Disneyland will never be completed. It will continue to grow as long as there is imagination left in the world.
citation: A similar quotes about EPCOT and other similar statements about Disneyland also exist.

author: Walt Disney
text: All our dreams can come true — if we have the courage to pursue them.
citation: Ch. 3 : Imagination Unlimited, p. 63; Unsourced variant: All your dreams can come true if you have the courage to pursue them.

author: Walt Disney
text: Leadership means that a group, large or small, is willing to entrust authority to a person who has shown judgement, wisdom, personal appeal, and proven competence.
citation: Ch. 4 : Animated Leadership, p. 102 Unsourced variant: Leadership implies a strong faith or belief in something. It may be a cause, an institution, a political or business operation in which a man takes active direction by virtue of his fai

author: Walt Disney
text: Do a good job. You don't have to worry about the money; it will take care of itself. Just do your best work — then try to trump it.
citation: Ch. 6 : Triumph to Tragedy

author: Walt Disney
text: A man should never neglect his family for business.
citation: Ch. 14 : The Real Walt Disney, p. 361

author: Rumi
text: He whose intellect overcomes his desire is higher than the angels; he whose desire overcomes his intellect is less than an animal.
citation: Kabir Helminski (ed.) The Rumi Collection: An Anthology of Translations (2000)

author: Rumi
text: The fault is in the one who blames. Spirit sees nothing to criticize.
citation: Timothy Freke, Rumi Wisdom: Daily Teachings from the Great Sufi Master (2000)

author: Rumi
text: This discipline and rough treatment are a furnace to extract the silver from the dross. This testing purifies the gold by boiling the scum away.
citation: I, 232-3 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: Fortunate is he who does not carry envy as a companion.
citation: I, 431 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: The idol of your self is the mother of all idols. To regard the self as easy to subdue is a mistake.
citation: I, 760-2 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: If you wish mercy, show mercy to the weak.
citation: I, 822 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: If you dig a pit for others to fall into, you will fall into it yourself.
citation: I, 1311 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: Many of the faults you see in others, dear reader, are your own nature reflected in them.
citation: I, 1319 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: The lion who breaks the enemy's ranks is a minor hero compared to the lion who overcomes himself.

author: Rumi
text: Whoever gives reverence receives reverence.
citation: I, 1494 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: Were there no men of vision, all who are blind would be dead.
citation: I, 2133 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: If you are wholly perplexed and in straits, have patience, for patience is the key to joy.
citation: I, 2908 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: If you are irritated by every rub, how will your mirror be polished?
citation: I, 2980 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: Anyone in whom the troublemaking self has died, sun and cloud obey. As his heart is afire with knowledge and love, the sun cannot burn him.
citation: I, 3004-5 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: If you wish to shine like day, burn up the night of self-existence. Dissolve in the Being who is everything.
citation: I, 3009-12 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: There is no worse sickness for the soul, O you who are proud, than this pretense of perfection. The heart and eyes must bleed a lot before self-complacency falls away.
citation: I, 3213-5 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: God turns you from one feeling to another and teaches by means of opposites, so that you will have two wings to fly, not one.
citation: II, 1552; 1554 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: When the remedy you have offered only increases the disease, then leave him who will not be cured, and tell your story to someone who seeks the truth.
citation: II, 2067 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

author: Rumi
text: Whoever enters the Way without a guide will take a hundred years to travel a two-day journey.
citation: III, 588 (tr. W. C. Chittick, 1983)

author: Rumi
text: Whoever undertakes a profession without a master becomes the laughingstock of city and town.
citation: III, 590 (tr. Chittick)

author: Rumi
text: Even though you're not equipped, keep searching: equipment isn't necessary on the way to the Lord.
citation: III, 1445-49 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

author: Rumi
text: If an ant seeks the rank of Solomon, don't smile contemptuously upon its quest. Everything you possess of skill, and wealth and handicraft, wasn't it first merely a thought and a quest?
citation: III, 1445-49 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

author: Rumi
text: Come, seek, for search is the foundation of fortune: Every success depends upon focusing the heart.
citation: III, 2302-5 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

author: Rumi
text: Many have been led astray by the Qur'an: by clinging to that rope many have fallen into the well. There is no fault in the rope, O perverse man, for it was you who had no desire to reach the top.
citation: III, 4210-11 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

author: Rumi
text: The eye of outward sense is as the palm of a hand, The whole of the object is not grasped in the palm. The sea itself is one thing, the foam another; Neglect the foam, and regard the sea with your eyes.
